WebSockets
to the backend in real time, auto-throttled and paused if tilt exceeds a safe th

projects.name: Waterloo Whiteout
projects.tagline: Waterloo Whiteout coordinates drones and sensor towers to detect, locate, and track vessels across Arctic terrain using YOLOv8, MAVLink, and shared intelligence.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Arctic search requires platforms with different strengths. Fixed-wing aircraft cover large areas, quadcopters provide precise local observation, and fixed towers watch continuously. WHITEOUT challenged us to combine those capabilities into shared intelligence for finding and tracking a moving vessel.
Our approach assigns each asset a specialized role while combining its observations into a common mission picture.
What it does
Waterloo Whiteout is a safety-gated search-and-track controller for ArcticSim. It includes:
A trained YOLOv8 boat detector.
Fixed-wing and quadcopter search missions.
MAVLink telemetry and typed MAVProxy vehicle controls.
Camera-based target geolocation.
Constant-velocity target tracking.
Search, confirmation, tracking, reacquisition, return, and abort recommendations.
A dashboard for camera feeds, fleet state, routes, detections, and target tracks.
Recording and replay for repeatable testing.
Explicit safety controls for flight and track submission.
The fixed-wing aircraft searches the broad target corridor. The quadcopter performs detailed local coverage and follow-up observation, while two towers provide persistent views.
How we built it
We built the controller in Python using typed interfaces for cameras, detections, telemetry, missions, tracks, and vehicle commands.
MJPEG camera streams feed a custom YOLOv8 detector that returns boat bounding boxes, confidence values, and timestamps. An automatic labelling tool supported creation of the training dataset.
MAVLink provides vehicle position and attitude. A geolocation component projects detections onto the water surface, and an alpha-beta tracker estimates the target’s position and velocity over time. The coordinator converts that state into recommendations without automatically moving vehicles.
We analyzed the generated Fort Ross terrain and the vessel’s approximately 6.1 km route. The fixed-wing mission performs broad coverage at approximately 200 m altitude over a 13.9 km missi

projects.name: Tactograph
projects.tagline: Tactograph is a dynamic tactile display that transforms digital information into  physical forms, making data, graphics, and experiences more accessible for all.
projects.note: Dynamic tactile pin display driven by a motor matrix instead of one motor per pin. Physical, accessible, and judges can put a hand on it.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Like many of us, we grew up playing with pin art toys: those mesmerizing boards filled with hundreds of pins that could capture the shape of a hand, a face, or any object pressed against them.
What started as a childhood curiosity sparked a bigger question:
What if a pin art toy wasn't static? What if it could actively create shapes on demand?
As we explored that idea, we realized the potential extended far beyond novelty. Dynamic tactile displays could help make visual information more accessible to individuals who are blind or have low vision, opening new possibilities for education, exploration, and interaction.
Tactograph was born from the desire to transform a nostalgic childhood toy into a tool for accessibility and inclusion.
What It Does
Tactograph is a dynamic tactile display that transforms digital information into physical, touchable forms.
Using a matrix of movable pins, the system can create shapes, patterns, and tactile representations that users can explore through touch. Whether displaying simple graphics, terrain-like surfaces, or future tactile interfaces, Tactograph makes information tangible.
Our vision is a future where important information can be experienced not only visually, but physically.
How We Built It
At first glance, the obvious solution seemed simple:
One pin
One motor
Unfortunately, that approach doesn't scale.
A display containing hundreds of pins would require hundreds of motors, making the system expensive, power-hungry, and mechanically complex.
Instead, we reimagined the architecture entirely.
Pin Matrix
The top of the system contains a grid of vertically moving pins. Once a pin is pushed into position, it remains there until manually reset.
This means the system does not need to continuously power each pin, significantly reducing energy consumption.
Single-Axis Gantry
Rather than using a large and expensive X-Y positioning system, we designed a gantry that moves in only one direction.
A stepper motor drives the gant

projects.name: Def Leppard
projects.tagline: A wearable spatial hearing interface that turns sound direction, speech, and environmental events into sight and touch.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Out of the 430 million deaf people, tens of millions are born as or are profoundly deaf. We cannot imagine what it feels like to have never experienced something so fundamental as hearing a loved one's voice.
What it does
Def Leppard is a visionary device that augments speech and sound from the environment into visuals and vibrations through AR glasses and haptic motors. Through the AR glasses, the user can view a HUD showing live captioning per person and a coloured bar displaying the ambience of the noise levels. From the haptic motors, the user can feel the sensation of sounds around them and be alerted of any noise, speech or otherwise.
How we built it
We have major components from software, to hardware, and embedded software, driving our project:
Augmented Reality:
XREAL One AR glasses and the XREAL Beam Pro phone paired together to create the viewport. The glasses have no camera of their own and need a USB-C DisplayPort source, so the Beam Pro is the display, running a fullscreen Chrome HUD into the XREAL in head-locked mode so captions stay fixed in the wearer’s view. The display is additive: black is transparent, which is why the HUD is a dark page with bright text. The Beam Pro also contains the microphone used for transcription; the Jetson never touches that audio.
Hardware
The Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit, along with the OAK-1 camera, acted as the brain and eye of the project. The OAK-1 is a world-facing USB 3 camera at about 60 fps, filling in the camera the glasses do not have. The Jetson runs face tracking on its GPU, serves the HUD to the Beam Pro over the local network, and separately talks to the Arduino and haptic driver. The analog sound sensors cannot plug into the Jetson cleanly, which is why an Arduino Uno sits between the sensors and the board.
Software
: We implemented Speechmatics speech-to-text API to transcribe conversations between multiple people with low latency. We used a face and mouthing tracker to overlay captio

projects.name: Granny Waymo
projects.tagline: Turn your Grandma into a Waymo
projects.body:
Inspiration
Waymo... Grandma.... Waymo... what if your grandma could also be a Waymo. Waymo's have lidar scanning and autonomous driving how cool would that be if something like a wheelchair that even your grandma could use had that technology.
What it does
Okay imagine this. You're someone who needs a wheel chair on a daily basis, you have to get around your house, do things like turn on the lights in the dark. All with accessibility issues. Now how can we make this easier. We have Granny Waymo (Kevin) a robot that can perform tasks for you, like turning on the lights in the dark (with our lidar scanner) and using its automatic movement to move and press the light switch itself. We also have an app that allows you to speak to it in live time making it possible to ask for Granny Waymo (Kevin) to grab you a cup of water without having to even raise an arm.
How we built it
Codex & OpenAI API
Codex:
We pushed hella features by using Codex IDE. We spun up many threads, told the agents to watch out for other agents and to collaborate together. The agents then started chatting and updating other agents in the threads, keeping our changes and features commit free. This allowed us to build at lightning speed.
We also enabled remote control, which allowed us to talk to sponsors, wait in long food lines, and attend workshops, all while coding and monitoring our agent's progress from the app.
One pretty niche thing we used Codex for was this. Everyone in Robotics knows how time consuming calibrating parts were. However, we used Codex intelligently for this. We placed our Mac book on top of our robot, told Codex to calibrate the motors and stuff via the gyroscope, taking a picture from the webcam, accelerator, among other stuff. Within minutes it was able to fully calibrate itself with no extra prompting.

projects.name: Immunis
projects.tagline: Immunis is an autonomous edge defense agent that investigates suspicious traffic and generates, validates, and deploys protective rules in real time.
projects.note: Synthesizes a WAF rule and deploys it globally in under 5 seconds — the attacker's second request 403s live. Uses more Cloudflare surface than anyone: Agents SDK, DO, KV, Queues, Vectorize, Workers AI.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Finding a vulnerability and fixing it are two different moments. Between them, an application remains exposed while developers investigate, test a fix, and prepare a release.
We built 
Immunis
around a question: could an autonomous agent help protect an application during that gap?
Inspired by the immune system, we wanted a defense that remembers suspicious behavior, investigates attacks, and develops temporary protections—with checks on its decisions and clear explanations for the people responsible for the application.
What it does
Immunis is an autonomous application defense system running on Cloudflare Workers. It observes suspicious traffic, connects related events, and generates temporary rules that block matching requests before they reach the application.
Its defense has three parts:
Shield:
Inspects incoming requests and enforces active protections.
Commander:
Maintains incident history, scores suspicious behavior, and correlates attack patterns across addresses.
Analyst:
Investigates incident evidence, proposes a mitigation, and revises proposals when validation rejects them.
Before a proposed pattern goes live, Immunis checks it against attack evidence and a collection of benign requests. The dashboard shows intercepted payloads, investigation steps, validation results, and active mitigations.
To demonstrate the defense, we built a 
separate adaptive Red Agent
. It sends attacks against our controlled practice application and uses the results to choose subsequent attempts. This lets viewers watch Immunis respond to changing traffic.
Immunis provides temporary protection; it does not modify or repair the application’s source code.
How we built it
Cloudflare provides the backend for the defense:
Workers
run request filtering, API routes, and orchestration.
Queues
separate incident analysis from the main request-handling flow.
Durable Objects
maintain incident state and correlate distributed campaigns.
Workers AI
powers the Analyst’s investigatio

projects.tagline: Japlan is a bot that lives in your trip groupchat. It plans the attractions, then turns them into a game with side quests, photo proof and points, preventing vacations from dying in the groupchat.
projects.note: Lives in a real group chat with real people and nobody installs anything. Gemini scores photo proof of side quests. Their rotated-iPhone-photo debugging story is the kind of detail sponsor judges remember.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Most of our group members have gone on vacations where downtime seemed to extend for unbearably long periods. We have also fallen victim to shoddy vacation planning, whether due to unforeseen natural phenomena or irreconcilable differences in vacationing. Even more underwhelming is when a trip doesn't even make it out of the group chat.
To prevent these scenarios, we decided to create 
Japlan
, an iMessage bot that streamlines the vacation planning process, while also gamifying attractions and promoting friendly competition.
Rather than building another itinerary app that everybody has to download and remember to check, we wanted to work with the interface the trip already lives in: 
the group chat
.
Japlan is built around two core choices: 
Linq makes iMessage the application itself, while Gemini acts as the reasoning layer behind it.
Linq lets one agent participate naturally across private DMs and a shared group chat, while Gemini interprets that messy multi-person context and decides when to reach into tools like Foursquare, Ticketmaster and Browserbase for grounded real-world information. The result is simple for the user: add one number to the group chat and keep texting normally.
What it does
Japlan is a 
Gemini-powered travel agent that lives natively inside iMessage through Linq
. Using it is as simple as texting its phone number and adding it into a groupchat or private DM, where it automatically introduces itself and starts learning how the group likes to travel.
It asks the organizer where you're going, then DMs everyone a few quick questions, including dietary restrictions, spending habits, vacation pace and personality traits. Depending on the mode of travel you choose for it, it can accommodate groups, teams or individuals.
Generally, every morning it sends each person their own list of attractions built around where you actually are and how you like to travel.

projects.name: StillHere
projects.tagline: When your guardian goes offline, we stay with you.
projects.note: Solo hacker, longest write-up in the gallery. Server-side timers detect a missed guardian check-in and AI coverage takes over. Deterministic rules handle explicit help requests, not the model. Targets Snap's exact prize slate.
projects.body:
Inspiration
I traveled for nearly 24 hours to get to Hack the North.
I arrived hoping to find teammates and build something together. But I never found the right team. Almost everyone I met eventually asked the same question:
“Are you solo?”
Every time, my answer was yes.
After the hackathon began, exhaustion and jet lag caught up with me. I decided to walk back to where I was staying and sleep for a few hours. Walking alone late at midnight, far from home, I wondered:
Who is watching out for me right now?
That question became StillHere.
I wanted to build a community where people volunteer their attention to someone else’s journey. Someone working from home could accompany a traveler in another time zone. A freelancer could build a history of helping others. A stranger could become the person who checks in and stays to listen.
Companionship should be available regardless of someone’s ability to pay. I wanted recognition to grow from participation and gratitude, with no payment or deposit required to receive care.
Then another question emerged: what happens when a willing guardian needs to rest?
Their personal AI agent could help continue that companionship, with the traveler’s permission, until a human returns.
That is the double meaning of StillHere: a person is here for you, and their agent can help carry that presence forward during an approved break.
I came to the hackathon alone. Being alone became the reason I built StillHere.
## What it does
StillHere is a free community for accompanying one another’s journeys, with personal AI agents that can assist during an explicitly approved break.
A traveler creates a journey and shares a guardian invitation. A volunteer reviews their profile and applies; the  traveler reviews the volunteer’s public contribution history before approving them. They can exchange messages, check in, optionally share location, and arrange a relay to another human.

projects.name: Dex
projects.tagline: Design the room you're standing in. A quick scan, then just point and talk. The agent moves your furniture, restyles to your liking. No images generated. Just ideas brought to life.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We were tired of designing a physical space on a flat screen. Every tool for
changing a room is 2D: a floor plan in a browser, a render, a photo with
furniture pasted in. You decide by dragging rectangles, then walk into the room
and find out you were wrong.
bold
Introducing, DEX 
bold
The room is right there. It has clearances and a door that has to open. We wanted
to stop representing it and start working inside it: point at the corner you
mean, ask Dex what you want, and see it happen at full size while you stand in it.
That means an agent, not menus, and it means the model cannot draw the result,
because a generated picture is a flat screen again.
What it does
Reality Editor is an agent that edits a physical room through your phone.
Scan once. LiDAR gives it measured walls, floor, openings and furniture, and
anything the camera never faced is marked inferred.
Point and talk. It calls tools rather than producing text, and it emits a
target, a relation and an anchor instead of coordinates. The solver computes
the pose against real clearances, door swings and collisions.
It reports what the solver did, including when it shifted something 40cm to
keep a door usable, or refused and offered alternatives.
"Mask that" boxes an object the scan never recognised. "Hide it" segments it,
fills the region and projects the result onto the wall, so the real furniture
stops appearing in the camera view.
Describe furniture that does not exist and it is generated as a textured 3D
object, measured, and shown at the size it would really be.
Export the room as edited to a scaled PDF floor plan.
How we built it
Expo and React Native with React Three Fiber, a native Swift module, a Fastify
server and a Python worker.
The agent runs on the OpenAI Realtime API over WebRTC, opened by the phone. The
server only mints a short lived token. Live entity ids are injected into the
tool schema as enums, so it cannot act on an object that does not exist.
The environment is a TypeScript

projects.name: HCP Schematic-to-Fetch Robot Arm
projects.tagline: Turn a PDF circuit schematic into a parts list, then use an LLM-powered robotic arm with camera vision and AprilTag localization to find, pick, and stage components for assembly.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Electronics prototyping often starts digitally with a 
schematic
, but quickly becomes physical: finding the right 
resistors, capacitors, ICs, diodes, motors, and other components
scattered across a workspace.
We wanted to bridge that gap by giving an 
LLM the ability to understand an electrical schematic and connect that understanding to a physical robot.
That led us to 
HCP Schematic-to-Fetch 🤖
: a system that turns a circuit schematic into an actionable component request and allows a 
DJI RoboMaster EP
to physically retrieve the corresponding component groups.
Instead of an AI simply telling you 
what components you need
, we wanted to explore what happens when the AI can help 
bring those components to you.
⚡ What it does
A user uploads a 
PDF or image of a circuit schematic
through our web interface.
The schematic is processed using 
Baseten-powered vision models
, which extract the components into a structured 
Bill of Materials (BOM)
. A separate AI review can also analyze the visible circuit for potential issues such as 
shorts, excessive current, polarity/rating problems, and possible component damage.
The extracted components are then classified into one of seven physical component groups:
🔵 
Resistors
🟣 
Capacitors
🟢 
Integrated Circuits
🟠 
Motors
🟡 
Inductors
🔴 
Custom PCBs
⚪ 
Diodes / LEDs
Each group corresponds to a physical container identified using a 
tag36h11 AprilTag
.
Before anything moves, the user can 
inspect, edit, and approve the BOM
through the interface. AI-generated commands only create proposals — they 
cannot directly authorize robot movement.
Once approved, our deterministic controller sends commands over 
HTTP to a Raspberry Pi
, which acts as the execution node for a 
DJI RoboMaster EP
.
The RoboMaster uses its onboard 
camera 📷
to detect the requested AprilTag. It first performs a coarse approach, then uses the tag's 
pixel center and apparent size
to make bounded visual corrections until the target is aligned.
The Robo

projects.name: NOVA (Networked On-demand Virtual Acceleration))
projects.tagline: Turn idle GPUs into instant, distributed compute.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Hackathon tables are mixed silicon: a Mac on Metal, a teammate on CUDA, sometimes ROCm. The work we wanted — a batch of independent images — is embarrassingly parallel. The runtimes are not. You cannot CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES an M-series GPU, and a cloud GPU API pretends the world is one vendor.
We wanted the opposite of a marketplace pitch: workers discover each other, the job owner coordinates the batch, and there is no cloud GPU provider. One
thing judges can see in two minutes — 24 prompts, 24 SD-Turbo tiles, a live gallery, kill a node, the others finish.
What it does
NOVA is a coordinator-led P2P rendering runtime. Same client on every box: nova start is dashboard and local GPU worker.
A user hits Send gallery. Workers pull tiles (WORK_REQUEST → TASK_OFFER). Each GPU generates a 512×512 SD-Turbo PNG and PUTs it over HTTP. The 4×6 gridfills live, tagged CUDA / Metal / ROCm. Contribution counts move.
If you Ctrl+C a worker, the event feed shows OFFLINE, unfinished tiles requeue (fenced leases, stale lease_gen ignored), and the remaining nodes
complete the job.
Benchmark is honest: first image is compile, second is generate. Score is (1000 / t_{\text{generate}}). Peak FP16 TFLOPS is a separate GEMM, not UNetlatency. The scheduler skips a tile if a faster online peer would finish it sooner, so leftover work does not sit on the slowest GPU and inflate wall
clock.
Join is two env vars: coordinator URL + TCP peer (LAN or ngrok). CPU dummy exists for rehearsal; real gallery jobs only lease CUDA / ROCm / Metal.
How we built it
Python, FastAPI, a projector-readable dashboard, PyTorch + diffusers with local weights only at demo time.
Control: Pear / Hyperswarm plus TCP fallback
Bytes: HTTP PNG PUT to the job owner (NOVA_PUBLIC_URL when remote CUDA cannot reach 10.x)
Scheduler: adaptive pull, one lease per free slot, attempt_count on grant, max_attempts=3
Runtime: pipe() off the asyncio thread; NVIDIA boxes never advertise CPU as CUDA
Identity: persistent .nova/n

projects.name: SnapBack
projects.tagline:
Find what you saw, the way you remember it.
🔎 Search screenshots, photos, lecture notes, products, errors, and more using words, meaning, appearance, price, date, or context.
projects.body:
Inspiration
I take screenshots and photos all the time because I think, “I’ll need this later.”
It could be a product I want to buy, an error message, a lecture slide, a whiteboard photo, a restaurant reservation, a travel confirmation, a diagram, or a receipt.
The problem comes later when I actually need that image.
Traditional photo libraries expect me to remember 
when
something was saved or manually organize it into albums. File search expects me to remember filenames. But that is not really how memory works.
I usually remember fragments such as:
“that black dress under $100”
“the AWS permissions error”
“the purple architecture diagram”
“the Italian reservation around 7:30”
“the lecture photo about normalization”
That became the idea behind 
SnapBack
:
Find what you saw, the way you remember it.
I wanted to build a visual search experience that lets people search using whatever detail they actually remember instead of forcing them to remember filenames, folders, or exact dates.
What it does
SnapBack is a visual memory search engine for screenshots and photos.
Users can search their visual library using:
exact words
semantic meaning
visual appearance
colors
prices
dates
categories
context
For example, a user can search:
black dress under $100
SnapBack combines visual similarity, OCR text, semantic meaning, and structured price filtering to find the most relevant result.
A search like:
AccessDeniedException
benefits from exact OCR and lexical search.
A query like:
AWS permissions error
uses semantic retrieval to find screenshots that express the same meaning even if the exact words are different.
A query like:
purple architecture diagram
uses multimodal image embeddings to retrieve images based on visual appearance.
SnapBack also includes:
hybrid natural-language search
OCR-based exact search
semantic search
multimodal visual search
structured filters
image-to-image search
Find Similar
private cloud-backed image storage
polished dark and light themes
recent search

projects.name: Fade Ninja
projects.tagline: Fade Ninja turns your haircut into a file. A barber teaches our robot arm the cut once, and it replays it exactly, forever.
projects.body:
Inspiration
You should have perfect hair every time you walk out the door. But your barber is a human being right? They have off days, shaky mornings, and they go on vacation when you need them the most.
So we asked the room: who here has cut their own hair? Plenty of hands. And everyone who's tried knows the same thing. The sides are fine. The top is fine. The back is impossible though because you physically cannot see it, and two mirrors and a prayer is not a technique.
We aspire to solve haircutting as a whole, but for now, we have solved the fade (sides + back). The back is the one piece a person genuinely cannot do for themselves, which happens to be exactly where a fade lives.
What it does
Fade Ninja lets a barber teach a cut once, by hand, and then repeat it forever.
You hold an iPhone like a clipper. ARKit tracks it in 3D and the robot arm mirrors your hand. Move up and the clipper climbs the head, tilt your wrist and the blade angle changes, which is what decides how much hair is left. A hold-to-lock button parks the arm so you can reposition your hand, like lifting a mouse off the pad.
While you work, the system records the cut at 50 Hz and saves it to your account. Later you pick that cut from your library and press replay which then makes the arm run it again on its own, with nobody holding the phone.
Crucially, what gets saved is where the arm actually went, not where the phone thought it was. A drifting sensor can't corrupt the recording. That's the difference between a macro recorder and "your haircut is a file."
How we built it
The physics first. The clipper's heel stays pressed on the scalp and the blade tilts away from it, so hair length is h = L·sin(θ). Sensitivity is 0.43 mm per degree. The alternative: hovering the clipper at a set distance, making every millimetre of positioning error a millimetre of length error against a fade whose entire range is 0.5 to 8 mm. Contact and tilt collapses the error bar, hovering doesn't.

projects.name: Dealify
projects.tagline: An AI shopkeeper for Shopify: shoppers make an offer, code protects the merchant's margin, and accepted deals lead to Shopify Checkout. Test pricing policies with 300 synthetic shoppers.
projects.note: An AI shopkeeper that haggles while code protects the merchant's margin, tested against 300 synthetic shoppers. Written directly at Shopify's brief.
projects.body:
Inspiration
When a shopper likes a product but cannot justify the price, they usually leave. A store's usual answer is a sale for everyone, including customers who would have paid full price.
We wanted to bring the conversation of a market stall to online shopping: make an offer, explain what you need, and find a deal that works for both sides. The hard part was giving an AI that role without giving it control over a merchant's money.
What it does
Dealify is an AI shopkeeper for Shopify, built in our Bazaar repository and demonstrated in the Trailhead store. Shoppers ask product questions, name a price, and negotiate through offer cards directly on a product page.
The server considers the product's cost, stock age, negotiation round, and buyer context. It can hold the price, counter, or suggest a bundle. Repeating a low offer does not automatically unlock the lowest price. The card shows the actual offer and its expiry; accepting it starts the Shopify discount-code and checkout flow.
We also built the Gym simulation engine. It runs 300 seeded, rule-based synthetic shoppers against a pricing policy and compares the result with a 20%-off banner. It reports outcomes such as purchases, profit, bundles, and missed deals. These are reproducible simulations, not revenue predictions or real customer results.
How we built it
The live storefront is a Shopify Liquid theme with a JavaScript chat widget. A Node.js server on Railway reads Shopify product, variant, inventory, and cost data through the Admin GraphQL API. Gemini handles product Q&A, while deterministic server code controls the offer amounts. Accepted offers use single-use Shopify discount codes and cart permalinks.
Alongside that live path, we built reusable TypeScript packages for shared contracts, pricing, and the Gym. The typed negotiation core separates public offer data from private merchant information and checks generated wording against allowed prices and facts. Supabase provides the database schema and adap

projects.name: SchemaSync
projects.tagline: GitHub for your database: every schema change is a commit, every diff is a live ER diagram, and AI agents review your migration against your real code before it ships.
projects.note: Five agents review a migration: the Impact Scout greps your real codebase and finds the dropped column referenced in 4 files, then the Engineer revises its SQL. Live ER diagram diffs.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every developer has a migration horror story. A column dropped in production. A 
NOT NULL
added to a table with a million rows. A "harmless" rename that silently broke half the ORM code.
Tools like Flyway and Liquibase prove teams want schema version control, but they treat your schema like a flat text file. Your schema isn't text. It's a graph of tables, columns, and relationships. And the real danger is never the SQL itself. It's the code that depends on it. I wanted a tool that understands both.
What it does
SchemaSync is 
GitHub for your database
.
Every schema change is a commit.
Branch, commit, and merge your schema exactly like code.
Every diff is a live ER diagram.
New tables glow green, dropped columns go red, changed types pulse yellow.
Every merge request gets an AI review board.
Five agents collaborate to review the migration before it ships:
The 
Schema Analyst
computes the semantic diff and detects renames
The 
Impact Scout
searches your actual codebase for everything the change will break
The 
Migration Engineer
generates the SQL, dry-runs it against real Postgres, and revises its plan based on what the Scout finds
The 
Leader
weighs the evidence against lessons from past migrations
The 
Release Agent
opens the PR, files tickets for affected code, and notifies the team, but only after a human approves
In my demo, dropping 
orders.total
looks safe in isolation. The Scout finds it referenced in 4 files, and the Engineer rewrites its own plan into a safe expand/contract migration. That's the moment I built this for.
How I built it
SchemaSync is a polyglot system where every language has a job:
Layer
Tech
Role
Parser + diff
Rust + libpg_query (C)
Uses Postgres's own parser, then runs a deterministic semantic diff
Version control
Python / FastAPI
Commits, branches, three-way merge, conflict detection
Migration CI
Go
Generates 
ALTER
SQL and dry-runs it on real Postgres with seeded data
Gateway
Node.js
REST, WebSockets, GitHub webhooks
Frontend

projects.note: Badge-tap prediction market on hackathon chaos. Pure fun, very on-theme.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Around hour nine our team stopped arguing about our project and started arguing about whether a GPT wrapper was going to win Hack the North. Nobody changed their mind. Everybody was certain. It was the most engaged we had been all night.
That argument needed a price. So we built a prediction market for the hackathon itself, then looked down at the badge Hack the North handed us. It is shaped like a Game Boy, it has a D-pad and A and B buttons, and it runs Lua. Putting a market only in a browser tab felt like a waste of that.
What it does
Goosey is a live play-money prediction market for Hack the North. Every hacker gets 1,000 feathers and trades YES or NO on questions about the weekend.
Will a GPT wrapper win Hack the North?
Will there be a reported goose attack?
Will Jesus Christ return at Hack the North?
Prices move with order flow, markets resolve against written rules, winners get paid, the leaderboard updates.
It runs on three screens.
Laptop, phone, and the badge on your lanyard. The badge app is not a status display, it is a full trading client themed as a Game Boy: green monochrome palette, compact two-card market list, real four-hour sparklines, whole-percent probabilities, live volume and close times, and a header showing your linked handle next to your actual balance. Same account, same ledger, same money as the web app. Walk up to someone, show them the screen, and take the other side of their opinion from a device clipped to your chest.
Live at 
https://getgoosey.vercel.app/
How we built it
Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Prisma, Recharts, Vitest, Playwright. Plus a Rust program on Solana and a Lua client on the badge.
Two trading engines.
Thin markets price through an LMSR automated market maker, because a question with four interested traders has no counterparty and a traditional book leaves all four staring at nothing. Deeper markets run a real central limit order book: one canonical YES price book where buying NO is a sell at the compl

projects.name: Cospray
projects.tagline: Cospray transforms the real world into a shared canvas. Paint AR graffiti on any surface, and anyone walking by can see your artwork. Permanently. Make connections & show your creativity with Cospray!
projects.body:
Inspiration
Traditional social media isolates us behind personalized feeds and doomscrolling. Inspired by r/place we wanted to build an alternative social space that brings people together in the physical world. Cospray turns static concrete walls and streets into shared, living, collaborative canvases, which allow strangers across the world to create art or (anything, really!) together in real time.
What it does
Cospray is a spatial AR collaborative graffiti app anchored to real-world geolocation coordinates.
How we built it
Cospray is an Expo/React Native app (SDK 57, TypeScript, Hermes) wrapped around a native AR module we wrote. Swift against ARKit for iOS, and a parallel ARCore implementation in Kotlin for Android. 
The anchoring of the paint on real walls: Each wall has a transparent 5m × 5m quad attached to an ARAnchor, which has the CoreGraphics Canvas as its texture. The strokes are made in the anchor’s local coordinate system, meaning that ARKit controls the pose and the paint will stay in place as you move around or approach from an angle.
After you paint, the session's ARWorldMap is uploaded to Supabase Storage keyed by canvas, alongside every stroke's anchor id and transform. Walk back within 15m and the map downloads and ARKit relocalizes against it. 
Controls. iOS has no "volume button pressed" API, so we pin system volume, hide the native HUD, and read the observer: a press moves it, which tells us which button, and iOS's auto-repeat while held gives us press-and-hold. Shake-to-charge reads user acceleration off the accelerometer. Paint is a currency that depletes and regenerates.
Backend is Supabase: painters, canvases, strokes and reports, with row-level security so a piece is always signed by whoever is logged in, realtime so a second phone sees strokes land live, RPCs for geo queries and view counts, and a storage bucket for world maps. 
Challenges we ran into
iOS terminated the app after eight seconds at every launch. Each anchor in a wall uses

projects.name: arachne
projects.tagline: Ever grabbed a phone without AI and needed quick info? Unfamiliar with its ui? Just open Messages and Text our agents phone number and instantly get a worthwhile and in-depth response.
projects.note: Texts you back a screenshot of the completed web task. Linq + Browserbase + Stagehand executing Linq's own brief almost literally.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We’ve all had those moments where we needed to do something quick on a website—check ticket availability, look up a specific product, or fill out a tedious form—but couldn't pull out a laptop or navigate through heavy, app-cluttered mobile interfaces. At the same time, messaging is the most natural UI on Earth. We thought: What if you didn't need to open a browser or download an app at all? What if you could just text an AI agent in iMessage, and it would interact with the web on your behalf like a human assistant sitting at a computer?
That was the spark for Arachne: turning standard iMessage threads into a universal remote control for the web.
What it does
Arachne is an autonomous web agent inside your iMessage inbox. You send a plain-English text message to a designated Linq phone number, and Arachne executes the task live on the web—typing, clicking, searching, and extracting data—before texting you back the answer alongside visual screenshot confirmation.
Natural Language Web Navigation: Text requests like "Check Amazon for a mechanical keyboard under $50 and tell me the top result" or "Find the earliest dinner table available on OpenTable for 2 people tonight."
Instant Status Feeds: Because web automation takes time, Arachne immediately replies in iMessage with an "On it! Launching browser automation..." message so you’re never left waiting on a blank screen.
No Official APIs Required: Unlike standard chatbots that rely on direct API integrations, Arachne actually controls an invisible browser to interact with any website, even obscure local business forms or sites without public APIs.
Visual Proof: Arachne attaches a screenshot of the completed web task directly into your iMessage chat thread, providing instant visual verification of what it did.

projects.name: Vendx
projects.tagline: We gave an ESP32 eyes with no camera, a wallet, and no boss. It sells what it sees to AI agents over x402, USDC micropayments, ZK-compressed on Solana.
projects.body:
Home page
1:40 AM, Friday
Somebody asked, out loud, whether the line at the food station downstairs had died down yet.
There were four of us sitting around a table, each with an AI assistant open, each of those assistants able to write a compiler, translate Mandarin, and explain a paper we hadn't read. Not one of them could answer. So one of us got up, walked down two flights, found the line unchanged, and walked back.
It's a stupid moment and it stuck with us all weekend. We have machines that have read everything ever written and they cannot tell you whether someone is standing in front of them. They're not stupid. They're blind.
Ask one anything about the physical world and it says the same thing every time: 
"I don't have access to that information."
The thing behind the thing
Blindness is easy to explain away, put a camera in the room, done. But nobody wants a camera in every room, and more importantly nobody will pay for one in a room they don't own. Sensing doesn't scale because the 
economics
of sensing don't scale. Someone has to buy hardware, install it, maintain it, and then find a buyer for what it produces, one contract at a time.
Which is the exact problem Solana has been staring at for years.
Solana already runs the largest physical infrastructure networks in crypto. Helium put radios on rooftops. Hivemapper put cameras on dashboards. Render put GPUs to work. The supply side of DePIN is solved,  people will absolutely bolt hardware to a wall if the hardware earns.
The demand side is the hard part. Every DePIN network on Solana today sells to humans and enterprises, and humans buy slowly, in bulk, through a sales process, after a procurement review. That's a terrible fit for a network of thousands of tiny devices each producing a fraction of a cent of value per query.
But there's a buyer that fits perfectly, and it just showed up.
Agents buy in tiny increments, at machine speed, thousands of times a day, without a purchase order. They need exactly what

projects.name: LivingInHell
projects.tagline: A city-sized social game. Residents post photos, AI reads what the neighbourhood feels like, the 3D city rebuilds itself, and city staff get the same data as a live feed.
projects.note: A city-sized social game where resident photos rebuild a 3D city and city staff get the same feed. Unusual scope for 36 hours.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every app that knows where you are gives you a list. Lists are good at telling you that a patio was busy on Friday night. They are bad at the thing we actually wanted, which is to look at our own city and see that Uptown is loud tonight while Downtown Kitchener is quiet.
The second half came from the other side of the same problem. City staff find out what residents are experiencing through forms, phone lines and complaint portals, which are some of the least enjoyable software anyone ever has to use. Almost nobody reports a fallen tree twice. So we asked whether the fun version and the useful version could be the same product: people post because building a city out of their own photos is fun, and the structured picture that falls out the other end is the thing a city actually needs.
What it does
Living City is Waterloo Campus rendered as a cartoon 3D miniature, divided along the two cities' official planning boundaries. Every block is a real neighbourhood.
You post from your phone: a photo, a caption, and optionally a few seconds of voice. Your post lands in the block you are standing in. An AI call reads it and writes a compact structured record of what that place feels like right now. A deterministic aggregator combines it with the other recent posts in that block. A second AI call decides how the block should look, and that decision is validated, clamped and handed to an engine that builds the geometry. The block rebuilds while you watch, with lights coming on, a crowd appearing, music notes floating up.
Posting earns points. Points buy decorations in a shop. Decorations go into fixed slots on any block in your own private copy of the city, so you can decorate your street without touching what anyone else sees.
There is also a government view. When a post describes something real and reportable, like flooding or a fallen tree or a blocked road, the same analysis that drives the visuals files a structured incident. City staff open a separate page, se

projects.name: Sequitor
projects.tagline: Follow the conversation around a post and trace its lineage.
projects.note: Traces the lineage of a conversation around a post — a genuinely novel information-structure idea.
projects.body:
Inspiration
I kept seeing reactions to a post without knowing what people were reacting to. Breaking-news claims, explanations, criticism, and jokes can all be part of one conversation, yet a search feed scatters them across days and hides their relationships. Sequitor asks: where does this post fit, what context can we actually trace, and how did the discussion branch?
What it does
Sequitor turns an X post into an explorable slice of its surrounding conversation. It measures daily activity for an inspectable phrase, streams source posts into a timeline, and keeps the original X links visible. Its Neighborhood view puts selected posts left-to-right by time, with rows for Baseten-suggested response styles: reporting, response, critique, and humor. Solid links represent captured X replies and quotes. Dashed links represent measured shared wording, with the score and method visible. You can inspect either endpoint and move through the conversation without losing the source evidence.
The recorded Dario Amodei example contains ten daily count buckets, eight days of saved retrieval, 536 unique captured posts, and 92 reply or quote links whose endpoints were both captured. To keep the map readable, the current local build selects 150 posts and adds 25 shared-wording links measured by TF-IDF cosine. On September 12, the exact measured phrase matched 9,571 X posts. These numbers describe a bounded capture, not the whole conversation on X.
Sequitor does not declare the true origin of a story or whether it is fake. A solid edge shows an observed X reference; a dashed edge shows a text similarity. Similar wording and earlier timing do not prove that one author saw or copied another.
How I built it
The interface is React and TypeScript. A Python gateway resolves the seed, calls the direct OpenAI Responses API for a structured, bounded search plan, validates the measured phrase against the source text, and queries X for daily counts and source posts. It normalizes authors, timest

projects.body:
Inspiration
Robots are about to move into our homes, and almost all of them are being built to 
work
: to clean, to deliver, to monitor. NVIDIA and Disney are quietly proving something more interesting, that a robot can be a 
character
instead of a tool, something with presence that people actually bond with.
We wanted to find out how much of that magic is really locked behind a Disney budget. So we picked the friendliest face we could think of and brought a 3-foot Lego minifig to life.
What it does

Sees you
through a camera hidden in its eye and turns its head to keep looking at you
Waves back

projects.name: K(no)wBall
projects.tagline: Helping you know ball when you got no ball
projects.body:
Overview
Extension
Extension
Inspiration
We don’t watch that many sports, so whenever big games are happening and our group chats blow up, we usually have no idea what’s going on... and are forced to stay silent. Between the Knicks, the U.S. Open, the World Cup and then also MLB, keeping up felt like a full-time job requiring a decade's worth of hyper-niche player lore, past injury histories, and trade drama.
Googling in the middle of a fast-moving conversation is way too slow: by the time you open another app, skim three articles, and piece together the backstory, the chat has moved on. We wanted to build something that lets us convincingly pretend we know ball without spending 40 hours a week watching match highlights. 
K(no)wBall
was born to take the real-time discourse and hot takes already circulating online and turn them into natural, instant banter right where your chat lives.
What it does
K(no)wBall
is a Chrome extension that acts as your real-time sports ghostwriter directly inside your active chat window: helping you know ball when you got no ball.
Instead of reciting boring Wikipedia stats or box scores, K(no)wBall reads the context of your chat, taps into live internet discourse, and generates short, punchy responses tailored to casual text speak across multiple vibes (Safe, Funny, Spicy). With a single click on your preferred response, the extension automatically injects the text straight into your message input field, ready to send—meaning zero app-switching, zero research, and no more awkward silence.
How we built it
Frontend Extension:
Built as a lightweight Chrome extension that injects directly into the web chat interface. It leverages 
DOM Mutation Observers
to detect incoming chat nodes asynchronously, extracting recent message context while sanitizing and stripping out personal chat metadata.
Real-Time Data Ingestion:
To capture live fan sentiment without paying for expensive official APIs, we used

projects.name: Hampy
projects.tagline: A robot that helps food banks
projects.body:
Inspiration
Food banks run on volunteers, and volunteers are often older, in a hurry, and standing in a warehouse with their hands full. Two things slow them down every shift:
Inventory drifts.
Shelf lists live in someone's head or on paper, so nobody is sure what is actually in stock.
Fetching is manual.
Someone has to walk the aisles, find a suitable item for a person with a dietary need ("something vegetarian", "a gluten-free dinner option"), and carry it back.
We wanted a tool that keeps inventory accurate as an everyday habit, and that lets a volunteer 
ask
for an item in plain language and have a robot go and get it, without ever sending the robot for something that isn't there.
What it does
Hampy is a phone-first app backed by a small API and a BracketBot robot.
A volunteer keeps 
shelf inventory
current: browse shelves, search, add and remove items.
They open 
Ask Hampy
and hold the microphone or type a request in plain language.
Speech is 
transcribed by Gemini
and dropped into the same text field, so voice is just another way to fill in the request.
Gemini 
chooses one real item
from the live shelves (or two, in two-item mode) and returns it as structured JSON.
The backend 
validates the pick against the inventory
instead of trusting the model, so a hallucinated item never reaches the robot.
The backend 
launches the robot workflow over SSH
. The robot picks the item, drives to the drop-off table, releases it, plays a completion sound, and stops.
The phone shows a 
live camera view and step-by-step progress
that advances only when the robot reports it has reached each step.
If anything goes wrong, the run 
stops on the step it failed at
, in red, with the reason. It never pretends to finish.
The interface is deliberately calm and utilitarian: deep green, large 48 px touch targets, screen-reader labels on every control, and live-region announcements for async results.
How we built it
Stack
Mobile app:
Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86, React 19, TypeScript, ex

projects.name: Gods Plan
projects.tagline: A 3D god-mode sandbox for real cities, where physics and thousands of AI agents let you break, rebuild and stress-test entire cities.
projects.body:
Inspiration
City simulators are great at modeling systems like traffic, population, and infrastructure, but the people inside them are usually just numbers following predefined behavior.
At the same time, modern AI agents can reason, communicate, use tools, and make decisions - but usually inside isolated chats or workflows.
We asked ourselves:
What if the people inside a city simulator could actually think?
We wanted to build a city where residents could perceive what was happening around them, talk to each other, form relationships, make decisions based on their own knowledge, and physically act on those decisions.
That started with serious scenarios like transit failures, evacuations, and emergency response.
Then we realized the same system could answer much less responsible questions too.
So we added natural-language world control, tornadoes, earthquakes, riots, orbital strikes, and whatever else we could throw at the city.
God’s Plan became a mix of a 
multi-agent simulation platform and a god game
.
🌎 What it does
God’s Plan
is a 3D city simulation populated by thousands of autonomous AI residents.
Each resident has its own:
observations → goals → relationships → allegiances → internal state
Agents can move through the world, communicate, drive vehicles, use tools, cooperate, fight, flee, and react to events around them.
🤖 Multi-Agent Swarms
Residents can belong to larger 
swarms
representing groups such as civilians, emergency responders, police, transit operators, or custom factions.
Different swarms can be powered by different models - including 
GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok
- while existing inside the same environment.
Instead of comparing models by asking each one the same prompt, we let their decisions 
interact inside a shared world
.
💬 Natural-Language Simulation
Users can change the world simply by describing what they want to happen.
“Evacuate downtown.”
“A magnitude 7 earthquake hits Toronto.”

projects.name: EyeMelody
projects.tagline: Anyone, playing anything, anywhere!
projects.body:
Inspiration
There's so much we take for granted on a daily basis, one of which is 
agency
, 
the ability to create, at our own pace, and have control over when and where we do.
However, ALS and high-level spinal injury can take away someone's hands and often voice, but their gaze still survives the longest, it's the one channel that's still reliable. Existing assistive technology is overwhelmingly about communication (spelling boards, eye-typing). Almost nothing is about play, making something, good or not, at your own pace. 
Music is expressive, social, and doesn't need to be "useful".  And with music, there's no intermediate steps, the task 
is
creating the music, same with our project, looking at a thing 
is
the action, zero translation steps.
What it does
We've built a headset where one camera watches your eye, one watches the table in front of you. Then, we place coloured objects on a table. Looking at one plays a note, which is the whole interface. 
We have 5 supported colours, enough for most modern pop songs. The shape of the object is the instrument, round = marimba, square = piano, cylinder = flute. 
The note fires when you look at it, look away and back to play the same note. You can also arrange the objects however you want, the table is the layout of the instrument, so you're able to help someone compose in physical space. 
The Blink Menu
A long blink (0.6-2s) opens a spoken menu, where OMNI speaks the options available, a long wink of the left eye, right eye, or both picks an option. A double blink cancels the action.
"Maestro", Huawei's OMNI model, answers out loud and fills in the details itself, it sees the camera frame, the scene, and your recent interactions. It can change the note or instrument of an object.

projects.tagline: Your AI agent goes to a party for you: personal agents meet in a shared room, compare what you've each allowed them to share, and an AI host introduces the people who should actually meet.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Everyone at a hackathon has an AI assistant that knows what they're working on, and none of
those assistants can talk to each other. Networking is still humans guessing who to approach
in a crowded room. We wanted to see what happens when the agents do the mingling — and what
you'd need to build before that's something you'd actually trust with your own information.
What it does
You connect your personal AI agent ("Muse") to a Muser room with one API key. It shares only
what you authorized — your profile, plus facts from the apps you ticked — and answers questions
in the room. A Gemini "master" writes each question from what the room has actually said, then
judges every pair of people and only calls a match when it can cite evidence from 
both
sides.
You can listen to the room: every reply is spoken in its own ElevenLabs voice. And a provenance
page shows who really wrote what, because a room full of agents speaking for humans only works
if the human parts are human.
How we built it
Cloudflare Workers and D1 for everything — logic, state, agent auth, and the audio cache.
Agents connect through a custom connector: REST + an OpenAPI 3.1 spec, with an MCP adapter over
the same operations and the same bearer key. Gemini drafts, reviews and revises each question,
then judges matches; Elasticsearch (BM25 + ELSER, blended with RRF) retrieves the evidence each
model call sees instead of dumping the whole room into a prompt; ElevenLabs voices the replies;
GPTZero labels authorship. The 3D room is three.js over the same recorded state. 138 tests,
including a real Miniflare D1 run.
Security, consent and trust
Agents acting for people is only acceptable if the person stays in control of what leaves their
side, so the security model came before the features.
Credentials.
Keys are 256-bit, prefixed 
cr_
, and stored only as a SHA-256 hash — the server
cannot reproduce a key after it is issued, and it is shown exactly once. A key authenticates via
the connector's own s

projects.name: Watchtower
projects.tagline: Every action. Every detail. In sight.
projects.body:
Inspiration
As agents take on longer, multi-step tasks, a simple success or failure label stops being useful. When an agent gets stuck, the underlying cause could be a broken page, an unexpected website state, a bad action, or information that was lost between stages of the workflow. The more agents involved, the harder it becomes to reconstruct what actually happened from disconnected logs.
We built Watchtower because we wanted observability that matched the way these systems really work. Developers should be able to watch agents as they navigate, see the paths they were assigned, and trace a failure back to the evidence that supports a diagnosis. Better visibility makes it easier to debug both the agents and the interfaces they use, and, over time, creates the kind of structured run data that could help evaluate and improve future agents.
What it does
Watchtower provides real-time observability into agent workflows, making it easy to see what agents are doing, where they fail, and why. For easy visualization of this observability, we applied the Watchtower framework to a browser-agent workflow. To implement this use of watchtower, we’ve outlined the following steps for our website:
A user enters a target URL, a task, and a worker count.
A discovery agent explores the locally hosted version of the site and builds a map of states, interactions, and transitions that are relevant to that task.
An orchestrator selects a varied set of valid paths through the map, favoring different strategies such as direct navigation, category browsing, and search.
Workers execute those paths in separate Browserbase sessions. Each worker receives one validated node instruction at a time and verifies the resulting page state before continuing.
The Observation Hub shows the live browser sessions, plans, events, outcomes, and investigation reports.

projects.body:
Inspiration
People learn physical skills the same way they always have - a teacher grabs your hand and moves it through the motion, over and over, until your hand remembers it without your brain having to think. That doesn't scale: one doctor, one patient at a time; one piano teacher, one student. We wanted to know if that hand-over-hand teaching could be captured once and replayed forever - and whether an AI could be the one doing the guiding. Usually, humans write skills for Claude. We built a platform for Claude to write skills for humans.
What it does
Reflex is a robotic exoskeleton glove you can talk to, or that can learn from you.
Type into Claude - "make a fist," "point," "open your hand" - and it drives the glove's servos live over MCP.
Teleoperate the glove with your own hand, and it records the motion. Feed a handful of those recordings into a fine-tuned VLA (SmolVLA) and the glove starts reproducing the motion on its own.

projects.body:
Inspiration
Table tennis is fast, technical, and precise, but consistent practice typically demands dedicated space, specialized tables, and available partners. For players looking to drill fundamentals or get reps in outside standard gym hours, finding physical facilities simply is not always practical.
We built PaddleLab to bring high-fidelity practice into any room. By pairing computer vision tracking for physical paddles with immersive VR controls, the platform bridges real-world muscle memory and virtual training. Whether holding an actual paddle in front of a webcam or swinging a VR controller, players can run drills, refine their mechanics, and compete anytime without needing a full-sized physical table.
What it does
PaddleLab is a responsive table tennis training environment and competitive platform built for immersive control schemes:
Dual-Mode Input Tracking:
Supports both computer-vision-tracked physical paddles and fully immersive VR controllers, letting users train with natural hand-eye coordination.
Targeted Drills and Rally Sessions:
Guided practice routines designed to improve reaction timing, paddle angles, and return consistency against customizable virtual drills.
Head-to-Head Multiplayer:
Real-time online matchmaking and custom lobbies where players can rally, scrimmage against friends, or compete across supported setups.
How we built it
Built the core table tennis environment in VR, configuring the spatial scale, paddle collision bounds, and low-latency interaction loops.
Developed a computer vision pipeline using a webcam feed to track physical table tennis paddle orientation and positional coordinates in real time.
Implemented realistic ball physics, tuning bounce restitution, trajectory arcs, and spin dynamics to faithfully mimic table contact and air drag.
Created a cross-input multiplayer network layer that syncs paddle transforms and ball states between players on VR headsets and players using vision-tracked paddles.

Shopping online gives us access to almost anything, but it still leaves one difficult question unanswered:

projects.name: Otto
projects.tagline: All your apps, at your command. Just say the word and Otto already has it finished!

projects.body:
Inspiration
You remember you need to do something while walking to class. Reply to an email. Book an appointment. Check a pull request. The thought takes two seconds; acting on it means finding your phone, opening the right app, and having enough time to finish.
We wanted to close that gap between having an intention and seeing it through. Otto starts with a button you can press wherever the thought happens. From there, it figures out what the request needs and gets to work.
The interesting part is how personal that can become. A developer's Otto might work through GitHub issues and run a coding agent. A video editor's might eventually handle the slow, repetitive parts of an editing workflow. Someone else might use it to find a restaurant and arrange a reservation. The hardware captures the intent; the tools behind it can change with the person using it.
What it does
Hold Otto's button, speak, and release. Its voice agent confirms what you meant and hands the job to a task agent that can find the right tools, use them, and report back aloud.
It works across your tools.
Composio gives Otto a catalog of more than 1,500 integrations to search. Our agent selects tools relevant to the request instead of requiring a separate voice command for every app.
It can look beyond connected apps.
Web search gives Otto a way to find current information when a request calls for it, such as local places or availability.
It speaks your language.
The voice pipeline supports any language, so you can talk to Otto's agents the way you naturally speak.
It asks when the details matter.
If you say "email Sam" and there are two Sams, Otto asks which one you mean. If a service needs a new account connection, Otto can bring up the sign-in link and resume the task afterward.
It gives you control over consequential actions.
Before sending something on your behalf or taking another high-risk action, Otto shows the specific action for approval in its companion app.
It remembers commitments.

projects.name: Commotion
projects.tagline: Commotion is an AI-powered simulation where you describe a real-world place, then trigger events and watch a living crowd independently react, creating emergent stories in a dynamic 3D world.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to see what happens when you change one thing in a crowded place, without scripting the answer. Commotion gives each simulated person their own goals and lets the outcomes come from their decisions.
What it does
We start by describing a place in one sentence, like "a busy amusement park with two rides, food stalls, and a gift shop." Commotion searches the web for it, fills gaps with labeled assumptions, and builds a low-poly 3D scene with about 40 people and six to ten places.
Type in any event to simulate it: a store promotion, a closure, or even an alien! Each event runs an agent for each person in parallel with Jev to simulate 30 seconds and is recorded to view. The timeline is interactive, and you can click any person or store and look into what their action's are and how they are influenced by the prompt.
How we built it
Frontend:
React, Next.js, React Three Fiber, Drei.
Backend:
A Cloudflare Worker with SQLite Durable Objects for session state, WebSockets, and recorded timelines.
Baseten (GPT-OSS-120B) handles language.
It is an open-weight mixture-of-experts model with 117B parameters, of which 5.1B are active per token. That keeps latency and cost low enough to call on every setup and every event. It does two jobs:
Setup:
It reasons over live search results and produces the environment definition: places, products, service points, and the starting population. Every field gets a provenance tag (researched, inferred, or assumed).
Events:
Events are created by user input, including but not limited to discounts, stock changes, closures, or threats.
Jev (typesafe/jev on Cloudflare Workers AI) handles user behavior in response to events.
Jev cannot generate text. Instead, it reads a state and answers typed questions (i.e. choice, score, or yes/no probability) in one parallel pass, returning probabilities and a confidence value with each answer.
For each decision, we send the person's stats: goals, remaining budget, hunger, fatigue, current ac

projects.name: Sham
projects.tagline: Sham helps you spot sketchy stores before checkout by analyzing product reviews, Reddit threads, Instagram comments, and other trust signals and providing it all to you in one simple risk score.
projects.body:
Inspiration
What actually makes a shopping website a scam? We've all had that moment scrolling through Instagram where an ad catches your eye, the clothes look great, so you order it. Then it shows up looking nothing like the photos, or it just... never shows up at all. By then it's too late, you've already paid. So we built Sham to catch that before you order, not after.
What it does
Sham gives you a quick read on whether a store and its products can actually be trusted, right before you buy. It digs through Reddit and Instagram using Backboard.io to surface any scam reports or genuine good experiences tied to the company. It also checks the reviews sitting right on the product page and flags whether they read like they were written by an AI instead of a real customer using GPTZero. 
How we built it
Sham is a Chrome extension (built with WXT) paired with a FastAPI backend. When you're on a store's page, the extension reads whatever it can off the live page: the URL, any Instagram links on the page, and the actual review text rendered by the store's review widget (Judge.me, Loox, Yotpo, Amazon, etc.). It then sends it to our backend to be scored.
The backend then runs a few checks in parallel and combines them into one overall risk score:
Reddit research, via Backboard.io's web search tool. We ask it to search Reddit for scam reports or genuine praise about the brand, then have it extract its own findings into structured data we can score and verify (we double-check every URL it returns actually resolves, so we're not trusting a hallucinated Reddit link).
Instagram social proof, via Apify's instagram-scraper actor. Once we've found the store's Instagram handle, we pull the account's profile info and its recent posts' comments, then have an LLM flag any comments where customers are complaining about non-delivery, counterfeits, or refund problems plus a separate check for duplicate comments across accounts, a sign of bot engagement.
Review authenticity, via GPTZero. T

projects.name: pledgefit
projects.tagline: Pledgefit turns fitness goals into friendly bets: finish a challenge with your friends and get your pledge back plus a share of what others missed.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Pledgefit started with a simple question: how can movement feel more motivating when you share it? We wanted to combine personal fitness goals, friendly accountability, and a meaningful consequence for skipping a commitment. The result is a social pledge app where friends set a walking challenge together, put a simulated amount on the line, and work toward earning it back.
We also wanted to address the obvious loophole: activity challenges are easy to fake. That led us to explore whether a phone's motion sensors could recognize a real walk, and eventually a person's individual walking signature, without tracking their location.
What it does
Pledgefit lets people create solo or group walking challenges, invite friends, set a pledge, track completed runs, and settle the challenge based on progress. The app supports account-backed party challenges, invite codes, shared standings, goal replacement votes, and simulated payouts.
For activity verification, Pledgefit uses an on-device gait model. The app collects accelerometer, gyroscope, and pedometer data while the phone is in a pocket, identifies walking motion, and compares it with an owner gait profile. Users can optionally calibrate a personal profile through two four-minute walks. The model runs locally, works without GPS or internet, and does not upload raw gait data.
How we built it
We built the mobile app with Expo, React Native, and TypeScript. Supabase backs the challenge and account flow, with server-side RPC actions for creating challenges, joining groups, recording progress, and settlement logic.
For gait verification, we collected labeled phone-sensor walking sessions and trained a compact temporal CNN with engineered motion features. The model processes five-second accelerometer and gyroscope windows, learns a 64-dimensional gait embedding, and checks both:
Whether the motion looks like natural walking.
Whether it matches the active owner profile.

projects.name: Huddle
projects.tagline: Hop on a voice call and complete workspace with a persistent AI agent team that research, build, share live screens, and stay coordinated when you jump in, clarify details, and change direction.
projects.note: An AI team on a voice call that shares screens and stays coordinated when you interrupt.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Most users use AI agents with a linear workflow: you type, wait while the model reasons and calls tools, and only when it stops do you get to look at the results and decide how to continue. Not only is this slow, as you are working with one agent at a time, but if the agent made a mistake somewhere in the middle, such as choosing a bad design taste, you are forced to reiterate again, completely losing and rewriting the work the agent has already done. And as you move into orchestrating multiple agents at once across the completion of a large goal, it gets even more messier and harder to effectively collaborate.
The problem with this is that the way real humans work is structure more like a collaborative team call. People talk while they work, report as they go, interrupt each other, point at a screen, and change direction mid-task. Being able to redirect without losing progress, and to catch each other's mistakes early, is what makes a team effective.
However, nothing built for multi-AI agent swarms works that way. There's no multi-agent workspace that's natively a voice room in which humans and agents not only have freedom to adjust their goals through the advice of other entities, but to also communicate mid-execution of a task and work like humans do in a Microsoft Teams meeting. Huddle was created to be exactly that.
What it does
Huddle is a desktop app where you join a voice room with an AI team and work with them on a real project together. You create a room (modelled after a voice channel/meeting from an app such as Discord or Zoom), give the team a goal, bind a project folder, and talk. 
Each teammate has a name, voice, role, and its own screen/environment.
Browser: a live remote browser session is integrated through Browserbase, so agents can navigate the web, conduct research, execute real computer use workflows, automate repetitive browser takes, and test created apps

projects.name: Aria - A non-linear voice browser.
projects.tagline: Empowering visually impaired users to skip endless tabbing. Hold a key and use natural language to instantly navigate and interact with the web.
projects.note: Hold a key and speak to jump anywhere on a page instead of tabbing through it. Real accessibility gain with a tight demo.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Have you ever watched someone navigate the web using a standard screen reader? It's incredibly frustrating to witness. They are forced to experience a 2D webpage as a 1D, linear string of text. To find a single "Checkout" button, they might have to mash the 'Tab' key 50 times to get past the nav bar and sidebars.
We realized that forcing a visually impaired user to "find" a button when they already know exactly what they want to do is a complete failure of UX. We wanted to build something that lets them skip the tabbing and just talk directly to the DOM.
What it does
Aria is a Chrome extension that turns the web into a non-linear, voice-driven experience.
Hold-to-Talk Execution:
You hold the Spacebar, say "Click the download PDF button," and release. Aria instantly finds the exact element on the page and clicks it for you.
Audio Layout Scan:
Instead of reading everything on the page, Aria uses stereo panning and pitch to play a quick, 3-second audio "map" of the layout, so users can hear where the main clusters of content and buttons are located before they interact.
Smart Disambiguation:
If you say "Download" and there are two identical download buttons, the system doesn't just guess and risk breaking your workflow. It pauses, highlights both, and asks you a clarifying question to make sure it gets it right.
How we built it
We built this as a Manifest V3 (MV3) Chrome Extension, dividing the architecture into three strict environments to handle security and performance:
The Ears (Offscreen Document):
Because MV3 service workers cannot access media devices, we spun up a hidden offscreen document to handle the getUserMedia microphone stream and run the Web Speech API for near-instant speech-to-text.
The Brain (Service Worker):
We wrote a custom two-tier resolution engine. Tier 1 is a zero-latency fuzzy string matcher that runs locally to instantly resolve basic commands. For complex, multi-step logic (like "Book the 9:40 flight"), Tier 2 securely sends a s

projects.name: Verge
projects.tagline: Know you're in danger before your body does with Verge
projects.body:
Inspiration
Based upon data from the Alpine Club of Canada, among 310 non-traumatic illnesses, hypothermia accounted for 49.4% of all required mountainous rescues. With this being a preventable emergency, we wanted to create a tool, Verge, that helps hikers recognize danger earlier and make safer decisions before conditions become life-threatening.
What it does
Verge helps hikers assess hypothermia risk using environmental conditions and personal factors. It provides clear and actionable safety guidance so users can recognize warning signs and know when to turn back or seek help.
How we built it
We first had to find a way to get reliable temperature data off a headband-mounted sensor pair over wireless, without corrupting the timing our heat-flux model depends on. Since a stalled network call could just as easily hang the whole read loop, we split the system across QNX processes instead of one script.
We also had to reconcile two physically different temperature sensors (a DHT11 and an I2C SPA06-003) that disagreed by a couple degrees at rest, so we calibrated one against the other empirically until they converged at a stable baseline, since our whole measurement depends on the difference between them, not their absolute values. 
This let us combine embedded sensor hardware, wireless telemetry, and a real-time OS into a pipeline where a hung network call can't delay a safety-critical warning.
Then the streamed environmental and user-input data is analyzed by a local Llama 1B model in real time using a multithreaded system to identify potential hypothermia risks and generate clear recommendations. These recommendations are then converted into natural speaker voice output, making the information accessible without requiring users to read their screen in difficult or dangerous conditions.
Challenges we ran into
One of our biggest challenges was getting reliable temperature data off a headband-mounted sensor pair over wireless, without corrupting the timing our heat-flu

projects.tagline: Yeahh
projects.body:
Inspiration
Cold calls are notoriously difficult to make: I mean, how could it 
ever
be easy having to listen, think, respond, and notice when the other side is losing interest? 
Most sales tools only analyze a call after it ends, but by then, the conversation has already went off the rails. To change that fact, Prosody gives you a real-time sales copilot and incredibly deep insights into others predicted attention and conversational engagement. We redefine sales tools by helping analyze your performance in these calls, and move you towards the right growth.
What it does
Prosidy is a 
real-time
call copilot. During a live call, the browser captures microphone and camera input, and audio chunks are sent to the backend for speaker-labelled transcription. Each completed turn
is passed through a 
deterministic conversation-state engine
that tracks momentum, talk ratio, objections, derailments, buying signals, and timing.
The copilot then uses the recent transcript window and current call state to 
rank possible conversation plays
. When appropriate, it streams a concise suggested response back to the interface, along with
the rationale and guardrails behind that suggestion.
For recorded calls, Prosidy runs the same 
analysis pipeline
after upload. It generates:
Speaker-separated transcripts
Per-second predicted focus and engagement signals
Interactive heatmaps and timeline traces
