A deterministic call scorecard
An AI-generated debrief with weaknesses, actions, and follow-up recommendations
Prospect research is handled through Browserbase Search and Fetch, which retrieves public professional information and returns source-backed context. Prospects are assigned a persistent callee_id, allowing
calls, research, and history to be associated with the same person across sessions.
Call records, transcripts, scores, and prospect records are indexed in Elasticsearch. Authentication and sessions are handled separately through

projects.name: Concerto
projects.tagline: what if we made hack the north into a live orchestra?
projects.body:
Inspiration
At concerts, the audience usually participates by watching, singing, or turning on their phone flashlights. We wanted to take that further and turn every audience member’s phone into part of the sound system.
Concerto transforms a crowd of phones into a distributed orchestra. Each phone is assigned a musical part based on where its owner is sitting, allowing different sections of the audience to play melody, vocals, or percussion together.
What it does
Audience members scan a QR code and open Concerto in their browser. The application automatically connects their phone, synchronizes its clock with the server, and downloads the required audio.
To determine where each phone is located, Concerto displays a timed red-and-blue pattern on every participating screen. Cameras record the audience, and our computer vision pipeline decodes each phone’s unique optical ID and estimates its position in the venue.
The operator can then:
Review a map of the detected phones
Select groups using rectangles, a lasso, or adjustable regions
Assign Melody, Vocals, or Percussion to each group
Control playback from a shared timeline
Adjust gain, mute or solo channels, pause, seek, and stop the performance
Immediately mute every phone using an emergency control
All phones follow the same server-controlled playhead. If optical localization fails, audience members can manually select the left, center, or right section.
How we built it
Concerto is a browser-based distributed system with four interfaces:
The audience experience
The operator console
A projector view with a QR code and live readiness counts
A camera upload interface
The frontends use Next.js, React, and TypeScript. A Bun and Hono backend manages device identities, synchronization, assignments, playback state, media uploads, and operator commands.
For synchronization, each phone performs NTP-style clock exchanges with the server. We estimate the server-to-device clock offset using the lowest-latency samples. Playback co

projects.name: Astra Risk
projects.tagline: Find the asterisk before you underwrite the risk.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Underwriters work through large queues of submissions, gathering information across policies, claims, locations, and buildings. Every submission requires
attention, and the available evidence varies considerably.
Federato’s challenge gave us a practical problem to solve: help an underwriter decide which submissions deserve attention first and explain why.
We approached Astra Risk from the workflow outward. We wanted the reviewer to understand the opportunity, identify the uncertainty, and know the next useful
action.
What it does
Astra Risk helps underwriters prioritize submissions and investigate individual risks.
The Federato triage flow discovers the API schema, retrieves submissions and related evidence, and ranks records against the supplied commercial-property
appetite guidelines. Each result includes a match score, priority score, determining factors, and source evidence.
Review checklists turn findings into actions, including requesting complete loss runs, confirming construction details, or escalating an appetite exception.
The case workflow handles individually entered submissions. It extracts facts, applies the same appetite checks, supports follow-up information and public-
source research, and maintains an activity history through the underwriter’s decision.
Triage and cases currently have separate entry points. Final decisions remain with the underwriter.
How we built it
We started by understanding the carrier guidelines and the relationships in Federato’s data.
Astra authenticates server-side and discovers the available resources, fields, and references. A schema-aware query planner retrieves relevant evidence,
follows relationships, and paginates the queue. Query traces show what was requested and the reason for each request.
Policy evidence supplements a submission only when the link is unique and the insured, insurance line, and effective date agree. Unresolved relationships
remain visible as evidence gaps.

💡 Inspiration
When people dislike something about a product, they usually do not fill out a feedback form. They complain in a YouTube comment, a Reddit thread, or somewhere the company never checks.
There can be thousands of useful comments spread across the internet, but reading them manually is not realistic. Even after finding them, a product manager still has to work out which complaints are repeated and which came from a single popular post.
We built Overheard to do that research for them. It gathers public feedback and turns it into a small set of problems a product team can review and act on.

A user adds a product and starts a research run. Overheard searches the available sources, collects relevant public comments, then runs them through a cleaning and analysis pipeline that removes duplicate or unrelated content and groups the rest by the product problem they describe.
When the run finishes, the dashboard shows the actions that seem most important. Each one links directly to the comments behind it, so a manager can read the recommendation first, then check the evidence before deciding whether it makes sense. projects.name: StoryScape
projects.tagline: Turn any doodle into an explorable 3D world.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Have you ever drawn your dream world as a kid? How about being able to step into it? 
We wanted to build the special thing little Harold drew the other day. Instead of just a picture, an actual 3D world you can fly through, with the castle he placed, and the sky the colour he picked.
What it does
Drawing
draw using a whiteboard. you get a variety of colours, brush sizes, an eraser, fill bucket, shapes, and under/redo; works with mouse, touch, or stylus
Interpreting
a vision model reads the messy drawing, turning it into a world brief
Build
agents build the world by calling tools that edit a JSON scene
full scene is streamed to the browser allowing you to see live edits
mix of library models + generated models
Explore
a low-poly world with unique lighting, terrain, weather, scenery, structures
auto fly through visits at each point of interest, or control the camera yourself
How we built it
The AI only decides what's in the world. It never draws anything or picks a colour. The renderer does all the visuals, and a zod schema is the only thing the two halves share.
The drawing board is a canvas with perfect-freehand for strokes and a wax grain pass on top so it looks like crayon instead of a vector line. Pen, eraser, fill, shapes, undo. Done exports a PNG.
The PNG gets moderated, then a vision model lists what's on the page: what each thing is, where it sits, how big, what colour, and how sure it is. We tell it to take the drawing at face value, so a six-legged purple thing stays a six-legged purple thing.
A second call turns that list into a brief: zones, the important objects, mood, weather, time of day, and a three-colour palette taken from the drawing itself. Each object gets matched to the closest model in our low-poly library.
Then an agent builds the world with tools (create_zone, place_object, scatter, that kind of thing). Each call edits a JSON scene that gets validated before it goes anywhere. If the agent makes a bad call the error comes back to i

Sapling
Sapling is pair research: an interactive frontier autoresearch system that humans guide through conversation, built for machine learning, math, and computational science.
Inspiration
Frontier autoresearch systems can now sustain large research efforts. OpenAI recently ran 10,000 agents on the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem. The AI Scientist-v2 wrote a workshop paper end to end. AIRA(_2) runs experiments asynchronously across a large research tree.
Agents are great at executing research tasks, but not so great at dictating research taste.
Long-horizon research depends on choices that are hard to specify in advance. Which question is worth asking? Whats the end goal? Which result needs to be replicated? When is a promising direction no longer worth pursuing?
Sapling keeps a human inside the research process while it runs. The system handles search, experiments, memory, and coordination. The human provides direction through the same conversation they use to understand the work.
Codex and Claude Code made pair programming a normal way to build software. Sapling applies that interaction model to research. We call it "pair research".

projects.name: FirmWar
projects.tagline: We turned the HackTheNorth badges into a wireless multiplayer first person shooter. We pushed a constrained embedded device to its limits and wrote a lightweight pseudo-3D shooter game from scratch.
projects.body:
Inspiration
The classic hacker rite of passage has always been: "Can it run DOOM?"
When we walked into Hack the North and got our hardware badges we knew we couldn't just leave them as glorified digital nametags. We wanted to push the hardware to its absolute limits. Instead of settling for a simple port or a basic 2D mini-game, we decided to revive the golden age of 90s LAN parties right on our lanyards by turning hacker badges into a real-time, playful 3D battle. Additionally, the games that we can currently play are only single person, but we wanted a way to play against each other.
What it does
FirmWar transforms standard Hack the North badges into a standalone, peer-to-peer 1v1 corridor shooter:
Pseudo-3D Raycasting Engine: Renders textured walls, perspective depth, and player sprites smoothly on the badge’s embedded display.
Low-Latency Wireless Networking: Wirelessly syncs player positions, orientations, and projectile states between two badges in real time for responsive PvP duels.
On-Badge Controls: Maps movement, turning, and shooting directly to the badge’s physical buttons with retro audio/visual hit feedback.
Zero Infrastructure Required: Players can face off anywhere: in line for food, between workshops, or while walking across campus, as long as they are on the same network.
How we built it
Challenges we ran into
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Achieving a rock-solid, playable frame rate on embedded hardware never intended to run 3D perspective graphics.
Pulling off real-time wireless 1v1 gameplay that feels responsive and fair.
What we learned
Embedded Optimization: Writing performant code on low-power hardware is hard and every clock cycle, bit shift, and byte of heap memory counts.
Reverse-Engineering: How to quickly dissect unknown hardware platforms under intense 36-hour hackathon time constraints.

Different games, different game modes.
Map & Weapon Pickups: Adding health packs, armor, shotguns, and multiple labyrinth

projects.name: plus1
projects.tagline: plus1
projects.body:
Inspiration
Meetings move fast, but most assistants only produce a transcript after the useful moment has passed. We built plus1 to be a real-time participant: a visible AI teammate that listens, reasons over messy information, speaks when invited, and gets work done while everyone is still in the room.
Insurance became a natural proving ground. Buyers need an easier, more transparent quoting experience, while underwriting teams need help turning incomplete submissions, appetite rules, and external risk signals into defensible decisions.
What it does
plus1 joins a Google Meet as a suited 3D character with a voice. It transcribes the room with speaker context, stays quiet unless addressed, and can answer questions, draft documents, create PDF artifacts, and safely prepare email actions.
For insurance, plus1 supports two flows:
Conversational car and tenant insurance estimates. It asks only for missing information, explains coverage in plain language, looks up vehicles from a VIN, returns transparent quote ranges, and routes complex cases to a broker.
An underwriting copilot for Federato. It ranks submissions against appetite guidelines, investigates an account, queries a messy schema, enriches an address with FEMA, NFIP, and weather data, and explains the decision, evidence, and next step.
How we built it
The dashboard is built in Next.js and provides a live meeting console, chat interface, quote cards, meeting history, and an underwriting workspace.
A local Playwright meeting runner joins Google Meet, captures remote audio, and streams PCM to Gemini Live for transcription. Gemini also powers structured action decisions and Federato query planning. The agent uses a fast gate to decide whether to ignore, answer, or act on each utterance.
ElevenLabs provides streaming speech in PCM format for plus1's voice and avatar. We implemented barge-in support so human speech interrupts playback immediately.
For the Intact experience, Gemini runs conversational intake while a sep

projects.name: Narvis
projects.tagline: AI-assisted 3D modeling you can reach out and control
projects.body:
Inspiration
3D modeling is still mostly done with a mouse, keyboard, and flat screen, even though the objects themselves exist in three dimensions. We wanted to make the process feel more natural by letting people interact with 3D models directly using their hands. Inspired by futuristic interfaces like JARVIS, we built Narvis to combine hand tracking, AI-assisted modeling, and a holographic-style display into one more intuitive way to create in 3D.
What it does
Narvis lets users create and manipulate 3D objects naturally using their hands and voice, while seeing those objects appear in a holographic-style display in front of them. Users can move, rotate, scale, zoom, extrude, and smooth models in a more spatial and intuitive way, with AI assistance helping with more complex modeling tasks. Beyond 3D creation, Narvis can also act as a holographic visualization tool for complex systems, such as exploring a software project’s file structure, seeing how different components connect, and understanding how an entire codebase works together in three-dimensional space.
How we built it
Narvis combines computer vision, AI, voice interaction, 3D modeling, and a custom physical display. We use a Stereolabs ZED stereo camera for depth perception, while OpenCV and MediaPipe handle hand tracking, gesture recognition, and 6DoF head tracking through a single camera. These inputs are translated into spatial modeling interactions, allowing the system to respond to both the user's hands and viewing position. OpenAI GPT-6 Astra powers the AI assistance through an indirect Blender integration, allowing it to create and edit Blender models while the results are displayed in real time through our Three.js frontend. ElevenLabs provides the voice layer for conversational control, while MongoDB stores model states and versions so users can undo changes and return to earlier iterations. The final visuals are displayed through an angled acrylic setup that creates the holographic-style effect.

projects.name: The Matrix
projects.tagline: We turn AI agents into a coordinated robotic swarm that can explore unknown spaces, avoid obstacles, build a shared map, and make navigation decisions together in real time.
projects.note: Agents as a coordinated swarm building a shared map of unknown space in real time.
projects.body:
Inspiration
AI agents are getting better at reasoning and making decisions, but most of them still exist entirely on a screen.
We wanted to see what would happen if we gave those agents a physical body.
That idea became 
The Matrix
: a swarm of autonomous robots that can explore unfamiliar environments, detect obstacles, make navigation decisions, and work together to understand the space around them.
What it does
The Matrix is a multi-robot exploration system designed to navigate unknown environments autonomously.
Each robot uses its onboard camera and sensors to understand what is around it while moving through the environment. The robots detect obstacles, avoid collisions, and contribute information to a shared view of the space.
The goal is for the swarm to divide exploration between multiple robots instead of having each one move randomly or cover the same area.
As the robots move, the system can continuously update where they are, what they have already explored, and where they should go next.
The robots are designed to keep moving while perception and navigation happen in the background, rather than stopping every time the system needs to process new information.
How we built it
We built The Matrix as a combination of robotics, computer vision, wireless control, and autonomous navigation.
At the hardware level, we use robotic platforms equipped with ESP32-based communication, onboard cameras, ultrasonic sensors, and motor control.
The robots communicate wirelessly with a laptop, where higher-level processing and navigation takes place.
For perception, camera frames are processed using computer vision models such as 
YOLO11n
to detect objects and obstacles in the environment.
We also use ultrasonic sensing as a fast safety layer for anything directly in front of the robot.
The overall control pipeline works like this:
Camera + Sensors → Perception → Navigation Decision → Motion Control → Robot
This lets the system make decisions about where to go while keeping

projects.name: Badge Kart
projects.tagline: Turn your hacker badge into gamepads for super mario kart/super tux kart! Shake to use the nitro and be careful to not get hit!
projects.body:
Inspiration
We looked at our badges and asked the only question that matters: 
can we play mario kart on this
?
The answer was yes. The answer is always yes. We didn't ask if we should.
What it does
Badge Kart turns two Hacker Badges into 
wired game pads
for SuperTuxKart, which runs on a regular computer in split-screen. Plug both badges into the PC, and now your name tag is a steering wheel.
Press Start on a badge to switch it between P1 and P2 (blue or orange, so you know who to blame). - - - Steer, accelerate, brake, drift, and use items with the badge buttons. A is gas, B is reverse.
SHAKE FOR NITRO. Physically shake your badge to go faster. Yes, this is scientifically the correct way to play a racing game. Nitro stays on until 1 second after you stop shaking, so you can vibrate like a maraca in peace.
The LEDs react to how you drive. Steer left and the left side glows brighter. Reverse lights up red. Shake and the whole badge floods neon green. It's basically a tiny rave that only exists to tell your opponent how they're losing.
How we built it
The game itself runs on the computer. The badges just tell it what your thumbs are doing.
Each badge runs our custom Lua app. Every time you press or release a button, the badge prints a line over its USB cable that looks like 
GAME:P1:LEFT:1
.
That's it. That's the protocol. It's a printf.
On the computer, a Python script listens to both badges, reads those lines, and turns them into real keyboard presses that SuperTuxKart understands:
Challenges we ran into
NOT ENOUGH MEMORY. The badge only has so much to work with, and the Lua app already eats a huge chunk of it. We wanted Bluetooth so we could go wireless. We dreamed of Bluetooth. But turning on Bluetooth would have left the badge with roughly the memory of a Tamagotchi, and the whole app would have died on startup.
So we went WIRED.
And since we couldn't send real commands the fancy way, our controller protocol is literally debug print statements. Every button pres

projects.name: Chalk Chain: Proof-of-Presence Pay for Teachers
projects.tagline: Teacher attendance records are written by the people being measured. Chalk Chain makes presence provable: three words from a live Solana block, chalked on the board and photographed with the class.
projects.note: Anchor program rejects a class photo sealed more than 90s after a live block hash; chalked words chain to the previous photo so the blackboard becomes a hash chain. Gasless relayer, USDC vault. Cites a real RCT.
projects.body:
Inspiration
In several sub-Saharan African countries, roughly one in four teachers is absent on a given school day. Paying teachers for each day they can prove they were in class works: a randomized trial in India (Duflo, Hanna & Ryan, 2012) cut absence by 21 percentage points. But the proof gets faked, and photo-attendance apps are gamed with old photos. We wanted proof that's cheap on any phone and hard to fake.
What it does
The app turns a Solana block hash only seconds old into three words.
The teacher chalks them on the board and photographs the class.
Our Solana program rejects the photo if it was sealed more than 90 seconds after the words existed.
A vision service checks the words, the head count and that the photo isn't of a screen. Hashing catches reused photos.
Each verified photo earns a USDC bonus at the end of the day.
Surprise re-checks, timed by future block hashes, make the teacher add new words under the old ones. Each set depends on the previous photo, so the board becomes a hash chain written in chalk. Teachers never see a wallet or pay a fee.
How we built it
Program:
Anchor 1.1.2 (Rust). Checks Solana's recent block hashes on-chain to enforce the time window, and pays USDC from a program-owned vault.
Backend:
Hono relayer that pays transaction fees, but only for our own instructions.
Vision:
FastAPI + Claude, with decoy words to catch misreadings, plus perceptual hashing (PDQ) to catch reused photos.
App:
React + Vite installable web app.
Shared library:
@solana/kit 8. The word derivation matches byte for byte in Rust, TypeScript and Python.
Challenges we ran into
Anchor 1.x and Kit 8 are newer than most tutorials.
The list of recent block hashes is too big to decode normally on-chain, so we parse it by hand.
Reading chalk handwriting is unreliable, so we made it multiple choice with decoys.
A fee-paying relayer is a wallet anyone can call, so we locked it to our instructions.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
The full loop runs on a real Sola

projects.name: Herd
projects.tagline: Privacy-first automated license plate reading. Locking down search logs, revamped data deletion so public safety is prioritized without building a surveillance state.
projects.note: Privacy-first license plate reading that deliberately refuses to become surveillance infrastructure.
projects.body:
Inspiration
There's been a lot of discourse about automated license plate technology used by government contractors. Cases have emerged of misuse by law enforcement, and the public has a deep mistrust of these companies to handle individual privacy. I wholeheartedly agree with individual privacy first, yet wanted to explore automated safety technology.
What it does
Herd is a privacy-first Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) middleware that eliminates mass surveillance while preserving the critical crime-solving benefits of vehicle tracking. Instead of uploading unencrypted video feeds and maintaining searchable location maps of innocent drivers in a cloud database, Herd processes license plate scans locally on edge cameras. Plates that do not match an active hotlist (such as stolen vehicles or Amber Alerts) are dropped from RAM immediately. When a match occurs, Herd logs the query through a cryptographically signed audit, ensuring law enforcement gets actionable leads without exposing everyday citizens to dragnet surveillance in addition to allowing scrutiny into each query made.
How I built it
Python and OpenCV running locally on a Raspberry Pi simulates an edge node (Herd camera) to detect vehicles and parse license plates entirely in RAM. SHA-256 hash chains are used to create zero-knowledge style local hotlist matching. Raw video feeds and non-matching plate data are instantly scrubbed at the edge node. FastAPI backend enforces the privacy policy by only unlocking search queries if it matches details accompanied by a valid case ID or warrant.
I also use an SQLite ledger that signs every query with a private key associated with law enforcement to prevent undocumented searches.
Challenges we ran into
Running real-time character recognition on low-power hardware to simulate real cameras was difficult. Higher scrutiny for privacy also had the risk of increasing latency.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
I'm proud of demonstrating that police can catch suspects w

projects.name: Real-Time Raytraced Pac-Man
projects.tagline: Raytraced Pac-Man running in real time on an FPGA. It works!
projects.body:
Inspiration
Ray-tracing is a computer graphics technique used to produce realistic lighting effects. It's commonly used to render images or videos with realistic lighting ahead of time.
This project is inspired by NVIDIA's RTX GPUs, which have specialised ray-tracing units to enable real-time ray-tracing, meaning you can have those cool lighting effects while playing video games! I've never had an RTX GPU but the concept was interesting enough that I wanted to make a real-time raytracing processor.
What it does
This is a miniature version of Pac-Man running at a 400x240 pixel resolution, so the rules should be pretty familiar: eat all the pellets and don't run into ghosts. 
The map and all the characters are represented as 3D objects, ray-traced on an FPGA and shown on the built-in LCD screen. Despite the pixelation, you can still see Pac-Man and friends cast shadows and reflections on the surrounding surfaces. The Super-Pellets even glow! To add more fun, Pac-Man's movement is determined by tilt controls!
Tricks to make it run smoothly in real-time
Fixed-point arithmetic: For fast calculations compared to floats
Multi-core parallelism: Calculations for multiple pixels run on separate cores in parallel to increase throughput
Double frame buffering: The LCD only starts drawing frames when they have been fully rendered, eliminating screen tearing
Development process
All hardware is my own, including the Tang Mega 138K FPGA. So most of the work was writing a design to run on the FPGA. 
My usual approach (as a student) doing digital design projects is to carefully plan out the architecture before slowly implementing it in SystemVerilog. This hackathon is my first time using agentic AI to do hardware design; it certainly made this project possible by cutting the time spent writing RTL and doing timing analysis, although perhaps at the cost of human-readability.
Challenges we ran into
One big challenge overall was that synthesizing and place-and-routing a design to check

projects.name: SpideyIRL
projects.tagline: The Real Life Peter Tingle
projects.body:
Inspiration
Ever wanted to be Spider-Man? Or maybe you’ve just related a little too much to Peter Parker lately?
Either way, you can’t exactly get bitten by a radioactive spider at Hack the North… so we tried the next best thing.
We built a real-life Spidey Sense.
SpideyIRL is a head worn wearable that lets you feel the world around you. It turns nearby obstacles into directional vibrations, giving you an intuitive sense of where things are without having to see them. It also has a built in, voice activated AI assistant that can see through the onboard camera, understand your surroundings, and answer questions about what is happening around you.
What it does
We’re building a head-worn prototype that translates distance measurements into directional vibrations, with voice access to visual context. The interaction is simple: feel a cue, understand its direction, and ask for more information when you need it.
Our target is eight distance sensors paired with eight vibration motors around an adjustable headband. Each sensor has a fixed relationship with its corresponding motor. An obstacle detected on the right produces feedback on the right; as measured distance decreases, the planned vibration pattern becomes more frequent. The goal is an interaction someone can learn through touch, without repeatedly checking a display.
A forward-facing camera adds another layer of information. Local computer vision detects and tracks objects within the camera view, while an optional multimodal assistant can turn current visual evidence into a short spoken description. Directional touch communicates proximity; speech adds context.
The experience we’re working toward is:
Sense → Feel → Ask → Hear
How we built it
Building that experience requires several systems to cooperate while keeping their responsibilities clear. Our architecture places distance sensing and vibration control on an independent local path, so camera inference and cloud requests cannot hold up proximity feedback. AI i

projects.name: TakeOne
projects.tagline: TakeOne is a mobile robotic film crew that tracks performers, moves the camera, positions lighting, and helps plan shots—so the person behind the camera can step into the story.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We had two SO-101 robotic arms sitting on a desk, each taking more than 48 hours to train a VLA model just to move LEGO bricks. Yet, they were still limited by a fixed base position. At the same time, an old RC truck from a previous project was collecting dust, held back by a flimsy analog receiver and power electronics that could barely support its own microcontrollers.
Then another problem came up. While trying to film with friends, we realized how tedious it was to constantly rely on someone else to hold and position the camera.
That was when the idea clicked: why not combine the two projects?
We could reinforce the RC truck’s drivetrain and power electronics, mount the SO-101 robotic arm on top, and turn the robot arm’s fixed base into a mobile platform. Instead of being confined to one coordinate on a desk, the arm could move freely through the environment.
With a simple UI control, the system could reposition itself, track a subject, and act as an autonomous camera operator, letting us film ourselves without needing an extra person behind the camera.
What it does
TakeOne is an intelligent robotic filmmaking system that helps independent creators plan, film, and edit cinematic content.
It combines a mobile cart, a camera arm, and an independent lighting arm. You describe the shot you want, and an AI Director translates that idea into framing, camera movement, lighting, and performance cues.
Before anything moves, TakeOne rehearses the shot in a 3D simulator, where you can refine paths, preview movements, and check physical limits safely. After filming, the recorded takes flow directly into TakeOne’s built-in editor. There, you can organize clips, trim and split shots, adjust timing, add transitions and visual effects, review the result, and export the finished video.
The vision is simple: instead of programming robots and assembling a complicated production workflow, a filmmaker can focus on the story.
TakeOne turns a creative direction into a rehea

projects.name: Snitch
projects.tagline: Snitch helps recruiters spot suspicious moments in remote interviews by combining behavioral signals, AI-language detection, CV checks, and visual canaries.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Remote interviews have gotten weird.
With AI copilots like Cluely helping candidates answer questions in real time, it's becoming harder for recruiters to know whether they're hearing from the candidate or an AI assisting them in the background. That makes it harder to assess what someone actually knows and how they think under pressure.
However, we do not want to create a soulless black-box system that filters out candidates directly. Rather, we want to create a solution that empowers recruiters to make more accurate and faster decisions.
What it does
Snitch is an end-to-end online interview platform with built-in video calling and interview analytics. It surfaces signs of AI-generated answers from real-time cheating tools, checks how well responses align with the candidate's CV, and tracks speaking rhythm. It is also equipped with signature AI defence that involves planting visual canaries that humans can't see but multimodal AI assistants can, stopping them from interfering with the interview.
How we built it
We built Snitch around a Next.js interview room and recruiter review dashboard, with a Python + FastAPI pipeline handling the analysis and Firebase managing our data and recorded files.
Next.js:
Live interview room and recruiter review dashboard.
Python + FastAPI:
Interview signal processing and analysis pipeline.
AssemblyAI:
Word-level transcription, including pauses.
GPTZero + OpenAI:
AI-shaped language analysis and CV consistency checks.
Firebase:
Firestore and Storage for application data and recordings.
Codex and Claude Code were part of our development workflow throughout the weekend. They helped us move quickly, but we still had to make the architecture decisions, validate the approaches, and figure out what actually worked. 
Codex helped us turn our idea into a working prototype through implementation, debugging, testing, and iteration. It helped build the live interview and screen-sharing workflow, connect recordings to post-interview re

projects.name: Gestura
projects.tagline: Gloves that turn your movements and voice into game controls, so instead of learning the controller, the controller learns you.
projects.note: Gloves replacing keyboard and mouse. Physical and demo-friendly, but a crowded idea.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Our original idea was to build a small device that you could attach to almost any real-world object and turn that object into a game controller. A bottle could become a sword, a broom could become a staff, and basically anything around you could become part of a game.
While experimenting with that idea, we realized our hands are already the most natural controller we have.
That led us to 
Gestura
: wearable motion-control gloves that let you control games using your actual hand movements, finger touches, and voice instead of a traditional keyboard and mouse.
What it does
Gestura turns hand movement, finger touches, and voice commands into game controls.
For our demo, we use Minecraft because its controls are easy to understand and show off physically.
The left glove controls movement, replacing keys like 
WASD
, while the right glove handles camera movement and actions.
The right glove also has 
touch sensors on the fingers
, giving us extra controls without needing physical buttons. Different finger touches can be mapped to actions such as interacting, placing blocks, switching items, or other game commands.
Instead of clicking a mouse button to break a block, you can physically swing your hand. Instead of reaching for a keyboard key, you can tap your fingers together.
We also integrated voice so repetitive controls do not always require physical movement. For example, if you are tired of continuously holding your hand forward, you can simply say:
"Keep moving forward."
Gestura continues the input until you tell it to stop.
Our bigger goal is for Gestura to become a controller that can learn how each person wants to play. Instead of changing complicated keybind settings, a user could eventually say:
"When I do this gesture, make me jump."
Then demonstrate the movement and have Gestura turn it into a new control.
How we built it
We built two wearable controllers using 
ESP32-S3 microcontrollers, IMUs, and touch sensors
mounted onto gloves.

projects.name: Nexus
projects.tagline: NEXUS lets you assign goals to a robot fleet, then automatically selects the best robot, coordinates traffic, and recovers from failures. People set goals. Fleets deliver.
projects.note: Assigns goals to a robot fleet, picks the robot, coordinates traffic and recovers from failure.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Modern warehouses may have many autonomous robots, but coordinating them creates a new problem: 
who should do each job, who should move first, and what happens when something fails?
That inspired me to build 
NEXUS
, a fleet-level coordination system where the operator gives the fleet a goal and NEXUS decides how to accomplish it.
What it does
NEXUS lets users manage a robot fleet without manually controlling individual robots.
From the Fleet Command interface, I can select an item, choose its destination, set its priority or cargo type, and dispatch the task.
NEXUS evaluates available robots based on:
Distance
Battery
Health
Reliability
Workload
Cargo type
Priority
It then selects the best robot and explains why.
Multiple robots can work at the same time. NEXUS predicts route conflicts before they happen, decides which robot gets right-of-way, makes others yield, and automatically resumes them when the path is clear.
If a robot fails mid-delivery, NEXUS creates a recovery point, requeues the job, and assigns another robot to finish it.
How I built it
NEXUS is built on top of the 
Bracket Bot MuJoCo simulation environment
.
Each robot runs independently, while a Python coordination layer maintains a shared warehouse model and handles:
Multi-job scheduling
Explainable task allocation
Traffic conflict prediction
Context-aware right-of-way
Failure recovery
Package reassignment
The live Control Center uses 
FastAPI, WebSockets, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG, MuJoCo, and NumPy
.
Challenges
One major challenge was coordinating robots running in separate MuJoCo simulations. I solved this using a shared logical warehouse coordinate system.
Another challenge was predicting real traffic conflicts. Crossing paths are not enough, the robots also have to arrive at the same place at roughly the same time, so NEXUS predicts future positions using safety thresholds.
Failure recovery was also tricky because a package may already be in transit. NEXUS preserves the package s

projects.name: Kit
projects.tagline: The art of building is disappearing. Kit turns real-world creation into a game, guiding people with 3D holograms and a copilot that helps them build anything, making hands-on creation beat screens.
projects.body:
Inspiration
How did we go from kids who took things apart and made something new, to kids who watch someone else do it on a screen? Around the world, half as many students take shop class as in 2009. The art of building is being lost to screen time.
When Michael was 12, he built a cottage with his dad, and it's still his best memory. That feeling comes from making a real thing with your hands, not from an app.
In The Lego Movie, master builders look at a pile of junk and see a spaceship. Almost nobody can do that. We wanted to hand that ability to any kid with a table full of cans, boxes and tape.
What it does
Put on a Meta Quest 3, look at whatever is on the table, and ask out loud: "What can I build?"
Kit scans the table. Outlines appear around every object, then each one gets a name and its real size. Kit says what it found, and three designs float above the table as holograms.
Point at one and pull the trigger. The holograms fly off the real objects and assemble into the design. The first piece glows, Kit reads the step aloud, and you stand the real can inside its hologram and say "done". The next step lights up.
Ask for "something crazier" and Kit invents new designs from the same objects, live. Ask a question mid-build, like which can holds the roof, and the object you're asking about glows while Kit answers.
How we built it
Scanning.
The headset takes one photo and casts a 128×96 grid of depth rays through it. The server finds the table, groups the points above it into objects, and fits each as a box or an upright cylinder.
Naming.
A vision model names each object from a 13-item vocabulary (cans, pizza boxes, bottles, tape, books, mugs). A known object snaps to its exact real size, because depth is 1 to 3 cm out at 1.5 m.
Designing.
An OpenAI model writes a design in a small placement language: what goes on what, which way up, taped or loose. Our solver turns that into exact positions, then checks it: will it tip, does each support actually span what rests on

projects.name: Pardon Us
projects.tagline: A speech therapy platform that analyzes your speaking patterns, identifies areas for improvement, and delivers personalized coaching to help you communicate with more clarity, confidence, and fluency.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Speech therapy is often limited to a small number of clinical hours each week, while the most important practice happens at home—alone, without immediate feedback. We wanted to make that practice feel less like filling out homework and more like having a calm, encouraging coach in your pocket.
VocalFlow is inspired by the moment a person realizes they have improved. Instead of hiding speech data in a dashboard, we make the change visible and audible right after someone speaks.
What it does
VocalFlow is an AI speech-practice companion built around a 
Speech Mirror
. A user says a target phrase, sees which word or sound needs another try, hears a concise coaching cue, and immediately retries.
Our hero flow is ClearSpeak: the user practises an 
/r/
phrase such as “Red robin runs rapidly.” VocalFlow highlights a weak word, explains one small adjustment, and then shows a Before → After improvement card when the user retries.
We also built Scenario Sprint, a voice roleplay mode for real-world practice. In the Coffee Shop scenario, users can choose a Calm or Busy environment, order a drink, respond to a clarification, and see transparent delivery signals such as pace, fillers, and long pauses.
How we built it
The mobile experience is designed in React Native with Expo and TypeScript. It records a short spoken turn, renders a local waveform, and presents the Speech Mirror, word-level feedback, coach playback, and achievement reveal.
Our FastAPI backend orchestrates the voice pipeline:
Azure Speech Pronunciation Assessment scores scripted drills against the expected phrase at word and phoneme granularity.
OpenAI transcription provides roleplay text for delivery analysis and contextual coaching.
A structured LLM response turns measured signals into one warm, actionable cue.
ElevenLabs streams the coach’s voice back to the user with low latency.
Supabase persists sessions, attempts, feedback, and comparable Before → After snapshots.

projects.name: SubZero
projects.tagline: SubZero is a pick-and-place robot with a swerve drivetrain, 1.5 m elevator, extending arm, and swappable WiFi tools for autonomous AprilTag alignment and object interaction.
projects.note: Swerve drivetrain, 1.5m elevator, swappable WiFi tools, AprilTag alignment. Serious hardware for 36 hours.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to build a robot that could do more than simply drive around a room. We were inspired by industrial robotic systems that can move, position themselves precisely, and use different tools for different tasks. This led us to create SubZero: a mobile robot that can navigate a space, align itself to AprilTags, move an elevator and arm, and switch between different tools for pick-and-place tasks.
What it does
SubZero is an FRC-style swerve robot with a 1.5 m elevator, extending arm, and WiFi-controlled tool system. It can use AprilTags for positioning and alignment, allowing it to approach specific locations with high precision. The robot's modular tool system allows different tools to be connected and controlled remotely, making the robot adaptable to different tasks.
Our simulation currently demonstrates AprilTag alignment to within 3 cm and 2° in under 5 seconds, along with controlled elevator and arm movement. The communication system between the robot, laptop, and tools was also tested for fast responses and link-loss detection.
How we built it
We divided SubZero into several interconnected systems. The main robot code runs on a RoboRIO using WPILib, Phoenix 6, PhotonLib, and AdvantageKit. An ESP32-S3 controls the interchangeable tools, while a laptop-based bridge connects the robot's NetworkTables system to HTTP commands. We also incorporated Jetson and PhotonVision components for vision processing.
We designed software contracts between these systems so that each component could communicate reliably without being tightly dependent on the others. We also created simulation tests to verify robot movement and communication before testing on physical hardware.
Challenges we ran into
One of our biggest challenges was coordinating several independent systems at once. The drivetrain, elevator, arm, vision system, and tool controller all needed to communicate reliably.
We also encountered a bug where the elevator and arm could incorrectly report that

projects.name: Needy
projects.tagline: See what you have, find what you need, and order the rest.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Imagine this: you are out grocery shopping, and you know you need to cook dinner tomorrow, but you are not quite sure what ingredients you already have at home. Do you have enough eggs? Is there still milk in the fridge? Did someone use the last of the butter?
Or maybe you are volunteering at the QNX Makerspace and need to check whether a specific sensor, development board, or cable is available in the back room before buying another one.
In both cases, the problem is the same: you need to know what is already in your inventory, but you are not there to check it yourself.
That inspired us to build Needy, an AI inventory assistant that can see what is available, understand what you are trying to make or build, identify what is missing, compare prices, and create purchase requests for the items you still need.
What it does
Needy combines voice, vision, and procurement into one workflow:
Users say what they want to make, such as pancakes, tacos, or a Raspberry Pi Local Sensor Weather Station.
OMNI converts the goal into a list of required ingredients.
A live camera identifies which items are available and which are missing.
Users can review or skip items before ordering.
For food items, the app compares prices across Loblaws, Metro, Walmart, and Costco.
Each item is routed to the vendor offering the lowest price.
Items outside the catalogue receive a pinned OMNI price estimate.
Zip creates and tracks the purchase requests.
A purchase history page displays orders, vendors, prices, and approval statuses.
How we built it
We built the frontend with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion. It provides the live camera experience, voice and typed input, inventory results, price comparisons, and purchase history.
The backend uses FastAPI and Python. It coordinates:
OMNI for speech understanding, goal decomposition, visual inventory checks, and fallback price estimates.
Zip for vendors, products, vendor items, purchase requests, and approval statuses.

projects.name: PrintDnD
projects.tagline: Print farms are repetitive and labour intensive. We built a robot that automates 3D printing farms.
projects.body:
Inspiration
3D printing is a pivotal part of any engineer's workflow; however, running many jobs back-to-back requires a human in the loop to monitor for completion, remove the old print, and reset the printer for the next job. Some of our group members have personally woken up in the middle of nights, ran a few miles from place to place, and messaged other people for help just to fulfill this task. This problem is magnified in scale when the operator has more than one printer. 
What it does
Introducing 
PrintDND
, a robot that is able to autonomously clear the printers from their previous job and place the print down in a desired location. This allows printing to occur while you can be on Do Not Disturb.
How we built it
This robot was provided by one of the Hack the North sponsors, BracketBot. This robot has a bimanual 7-DOF setup with a mobile 2-wheel base. The robot uses reinforcement learning to balance itself upright.
We took this hardware and software stack provided by BracketBot and evaluated the problem via first principles. We broke down the rudimentary movements required to remove prints from the printer and collected data via teleoperation with the Meta Quest 3S.  We collected over 100 datasets that we stored in BracketBot's cloud service.
This data was then audited for quality and used to fine-tune the Physical Intelligence PI0.5 Vision Language Action (VLA) model. Once the model was trained, we built upon the deployment stack to use the model for inference. 
On top of training the model to reset the 3D Printer, we also implemented voice prompt. The BracketBot will detect "Hey Bracketbot" and it will listen and do the command that we tell it to. Example, "Hey BracketBot, reset the printer". The BracketBot is also able to reply to our command.
Challenges we ran into
Network and connectivity has been a huge issue for us (HTN, eduroam, and even starlink was an issue). This involved us moving our entire setup 3 separate times.

projects.name: Goose Paint
projects.tagline: Draw pixel art on your 2026 Hack the North badge. Better yet, scan a code and now it's published to Solana: no cable, no wallet, no fees. The badge has no Wi-Fi, so the screen itself is the wire.
projects.body:
Inspiration
My inspiration for this project came from a situation many hackers know all too well. I came to Hack the North ready to start running, my brain packed with ideas, only to sit down and realize either they were too large or not at all possible. Nonetheless, I sat in my chair, disappointed, wondering what possibly could make my day go faster.
Then it hit me. Microsoft Paint. Although a relic of ancient times (yes, don't shoot the messenger), its pixelated yet so simple interface peaked and calmed the minds of many through their roughest times, and I found it only right to port it onto a piece of tech every hacker had: the all new 2026 Hack the North badge.
So was born Goose Paint, a spin off of Microsoft Paint.
What it does
Upon opening the app, you are presented with a 12x12 pixel array, in which you can fill however you see fit using any of the provided 17 colors. The controls: D-pad to move around, Start to cycle through colors, B to clear a pixel or set it to white, and A to paint a pixel with the select color. Press A and B together, and A once again, and your given a scannable 172-character code, of which you can use to forever preserve your piece of work on the Solana blockchain using 
https://paintgoose.work
, free of charge! 
How I built it
Badge (Lua): There's no canvas or framebuffer API, so the grid is 144 individual box widgets, built four per tick during a short loading phase to stay inside the callback deadline. Most of the engineering was memory. My first working version held 174 live widget handles, a 144-entry pixel table, a palette table, and three pre-built overlay screens: 45.4 KB of Lua heap. The rewrite finds cells on demand with root:child(n), packs the whole canvas into 24 integers of six 5-bit cells each (a paint is a masked write that allocates nothing), stores the palette as one 48-byte string, builds the menu and code screens only when they're opened, and has on_enter delete itself after it runs. projects.name: Genie Jury
projects.tagline: Genie Jury is a live AI pitch panel that challenges your idea, researches your claims, and turns tough feedback into your next best move.
projects.body:
Inspiration
When I brainstormed project ideas with ordinary AI chatbots, the feedback often felt too agreeable. It would make an idea sound impressive without asking the uncomfortable questions: Does anyone actually need this? Can it be built this weekend? Is the “nobody else does this” claim even true?
I wanted the opposite experience: a pressure test that feels like pitching to real people. That became 
Genie Jury
—four cloud-seated AI jurors with different personalities, priorities, and voices. They can interrupt a pitch, challenge assumptions, research risky claims in a live browser, disagree with each other, and still leave the builder with a constructive recovery plan.
What it does
A builder pitches an idea by voice or typed fallback. Genie Jury brings in four specialists:
Ember, the Builder
challenges feasibility, scope, and what can actually ship.
Gale, the Skeptic
checks factual and competitive claims using a real Browserbase cloud browser.
Tide, the User
focuses on who has the problem, how they solve it now, and why they would switch.
Volt, the Jester
delivers a playful roast that exposes the clearest flaw without being cruel.
The jury does not just give generic opinions. A Bailiff agent breaks the pitch into claims and assigns non-overlapping investigation angles. Gale can gather real evidence, while the other jurors use the shared evidence and each other’s findings to form independent assessments. At the end, the Ally provides a practical “cut, prove, test, build” plan, alongside four scorecards out of 100.
How we built it
We built Genie Jury as a React and TypeScript experience with a full-screen daytime-sky stage, illustrated jurors, speaking states, live captions, voice cues, scorecards, and a Browserbase research dock.
The backend is a local Node API that keeps provider credentials off the client. OpenAI Realtime supports the live microphone experience, while OpenAI Responses powers claim extraction, agent reasoning, jury interruptions, and structure

projects.name: DominIQ
projects.tagline: 4 drones, dropped with no idea where the enemy ship is. Within minutes, it's found - using just camera geometry, and tracked by an algorithm, all while you watch in VR and clarify by voice.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We set out to solve a hard physical AI problem with real-world impact in the defense and maritime surveillance sectors. The challenge: autonomously detect, locate, and continuously track a moving vessel across a large Arctic environment using only drone-mounted cameras and onboard sensors. No GPS on the target, no pre-known position, no human operator in the loop.
What it does
DominIQ autonomously detects, locates, and tracks a moving vessel across a 6.5km Arctic environment using coordinated drones and AI. It fuses YOLO detections with real-time drone telemetry to compute the boat's GPS coordinates purely from camera geometry, with no human in the loop.
How we built it
We built a multi-asset MAVLink controller that flies a quadcopter and fixed-wing plane in coordinated patrol orbits while running a custom-trained YOLO model on their live camera feeds. On top of that we layered a voice interface using Whisper, GPT-4o, and ElevenLabs so operators can ask questions about the mission in plain English and get spoken answers back.
Challenges we ran into
Figuring out how to position and deploy the drones for optimal performance was somewhat difficult. It was unclear at first, but after experimenting over the weekend, we developed a reasonable arrangement.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We're proud that the full pipeline works end-to-end with zero human guidance: the drones take off, find a randomly spawned moving vessel somewhere in the site, and lock onto it using only what the camera sees. The voice assistant accurately answers live mission questions because it reads real telemetry logs, not canned responses.
What we learned
Physical AI is a completely different beast from pure software AI because every sensor has noise, every motor has lag, and the math that looks clean on paper breaks down the moment the drone tilts 5 degrees. We learned that multi-agent coordination over MAVLink requires extremely careful message sequencing since shared state and con

projects.name: PawTrace
projects.tagline: PawTrace is a missing-pet search platform that combines community sightings and available camera footage to determine where a lost pet is most likely to be.
projects.body:
Inspiration
When a pet goes missing, every minute matters, but useful information is often scattered across neighbourhood posts, doorbell cameras, shelter reports, and word of mouth. Owners are left manually sorting through incomplete sightings without knowing where to search next. We built PawTrace to bring those signals together and turn them into a focused, evidence-based search.
What it does
PawTrace combines community sightings with footage from doorbell cameras, home cameras, and local businesses to determine where a missing pet is most likely to be.
It compares descriptions and images while considering when and where each sighting occurred. PawTrace then creates a prioritized search map, identifies nearby cameras that may have captured the pet, analyzes their footage, and follows the pet’s estimated direction of travel. When a possible match is found, the owner sees the camera frame alongside their reference photos and makes the final decision.
How we built it
We built the frontend with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and React Leaflet, with a FastAPI backend connected to Elasticsearch.
Elasticsearch acts as PawTrace’s decision engine. We combine BM25 keyword search, text-vector search, image-vector search, and geographic and time-based scoring through reciprocal rank fusion. Credible sightings are used to update a hexagonal search map based on distance, terrain, movement, and previously searched areas.
Camera fields of view are stored as geographic shapes, allowing us to query which cameras overlap the highest-priority areas. Camera footage is processed using YOLOv8 for detection and tracking, while DINOv2 compares detected animals with the owner’s reference photos. An agent with 13 tools coordinates the search, camera selection, and evidence gathering, with its activity streamed to the interface using Server-Sent Events.
Challenges we ran into
One of our biggest challenges was tuning Elasticsearch to return confident matches without filtering out useful

Scout is a lidar rover that goes in first and measures whether a wheelchair can get through.

projects.name: Otli
projects.tagline: Your surroundings, explained. Otli sees your space and projects guidance right where you need it, from a game of pool to your workbench, and beyond.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Most educational tools either collect data passively for later review or pull you out of your flow with screens and notifications. We wanted something different: a device that teaches in the moment, right where your attention already is, without getting in the way.
What it does
Otli sees the world through its camera and "sheds light" on it, literally. A computer vision framework interprets the scene, then passes that information to a machine learning model that emulates a physics engine. Otli turns the model's output into visuals and projects them directly onto the physical objects in front of you, so explanations appear on the world itself instead of on a screen.
How we built it
A Raspberry Pi ties everything together: it runs the camera and projector and drives a stepper-powered gear train that lets Otli pan to take in more of its surroundings. We designed the gear train in Fusion 360, 3D printed the parts, and combined them with off-the-shelf bearings and stepper motors.
Challenges we ran into
Our 3D printers broke down often, and the print quality wasn't precise enough for parts to fit together cleanly. The printers' small build plates also forced us to split Otli into many smaller subcomponents, which meant more prints, more assembly, and more places for tolerances to add up.
We also ran into a string of hardware shortages. Our kit didn't include a power cable for the Jetson Nano, one of our Arduino Unos broke partway through, and we had no jumper wires or AAA batteries on hand. Each gap forced us to hunt down replacements or find workarounds, which ate into our build time.
On the software side, we couldn't get a depth camera, which limited what our CV model could identify. We also lacked the peripherals needed to set up and program the Raspberry Pi, which slowed down development and integration.
Accomplishments that we're proud of

projects.name: orca-ctl
projects.tagline: Remote, autonomous server recovery directly via hardware I/O
projects.body:
Inspiration
During a major data-center outage, tens to hundreds of servers can end up bricked or unreachable (from every remote tool on an OS level). 
This could be due to a bad firmware/kernel update, and traditionally, troubleshooting may involve technicians many on site.
What it does
orca-ctl is a device that connects to each machine via their hardware: 
reading directly from HDMI and emulating keyboard/mouse input as a USB peripheral
.
This allows orca-ctl to troubleshoot on any machine directly out of the box, 
with no software installed
. You can easily switch between servers by just re-plugging!
On request, orca-ctl will autonomously iterate to solve an issue, capturing display and sending input. This can be 
scaled to diagnose and interpret several connected machines at once
.
How we built it
orca-ctl uses a 
Raspberry Pi 5
running QNX connected by GPIO pins (on UART) to an 
Arduino Leonardo
(Pi TX to Leonardo RX + ground).
The QNX RPi acts as a middle layer between our agent system and the machine, handling input and output. 
As the RPi 5 does not support acting as a USB peripheral, the USB input commands are forwarded to the Leonardo which maps and sends keystrokes and mouse coordinates.
We wrote a C daemon on QNX to convert HDMI frame data (from a Guermok capture card sensor) to images and stream it over HTTP to our webserver. 
On the input side, we forward commands over the RPi's GPIO UART to the Arduino which runs our C++ firmware to map commands to USB as keyboard and mouse. We used NicoHood's HID-project library to also emulate as a boot-protocol device when working on BIOS/UEFI menus (regular USB devices are generally not supported).
Our webserver has a client that run Next.js that hosts the dashboard, while the backend runs Go Gin's framework. We use the OpenAI API which continuously shares screenshots and gathers context on the display. 
On autonomous mode, we have 
a master agent which drafts a plan, and a vision model which iterates over the step

projects.name: BaymaxBot
projects.tagline: A mobile medical device that stays by your side, at all times.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We watched 
Big Hero 6
as children and loved the interactions between Baymax and Hiro. For context, Hiro was a teenage robotics genius and Baymax was his loyal medical assistant! As robotics enter the home, it's inevitable that the relationship that humans have with our digital friends will also become important. We wanted to play around with that concept using BracketBot, and asked what if we make a medical device friendly?
What it does
Baymax Bot turns BracketBot into an interactive companion that can:
Respond to voice commands and hold conversations
Perform gestures such as waving, handshakes, fist bumps, hugs, and dancing
Run multi-step routines like a welcome sequence, calm moment, and dance party
Express itself using lights, sound effects, and music
Detect people and visible facial expressions using a fully local vision pipeline
Be controlled through an accessible web dashboard
Medical event checkers such as rPPG, fall detection, as well as a autonomous medical supplies packer. 
Follow mode, so BaymaxBot never leaves your side.
Stop actions immediately through a global emergency stop control
Every physical action passes through a fixed allowlist and deterministic safety checks. The language model can suggest an action, but it never directly controls the robot's motors.
How we built it
We built Baymax Bot in Python on top of BracketBot OS. We created a local web dashboard that connects to the robot over SSH, bringing gestures, lights, sounds, music, and movement controls into one place.
To give Baymax personality, we used recorded arm movements for gestures like waving, hugging, and fist bumps. We combined these with lights and audio to create routines such as a welcome sequence and a dance party. Before each gesture, the robot checks its balance and movement limits, then smoothly moves into and out of the action.

projects.name: Align
projects.tagline: Hands-free posture coach you can talk to.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Most posture apps show you a number the second you open them, a confidence score from a single photo through a generic pose model, and that number is almost always made up. We wanted to build something that refuses to do that.
Align started from one rule we set before writing any code: never show a measurement we have not actually verified. Everything else in the product follows from that constraint.
What it does
Align turns an iPhone into a guided, hands-free posture and movement capture rig. Prop the phone on a stand, and live device-motion sensing tells you in real time when the camera itself is actually level, because a crooked camera produces a crooked read no matter how good your posture is. Once it is level, Align walks you through four full-body views (front, right, back, left) with a countdown, a framing guide, and haptic confirmation, no screen-tapping required mid-scan.
At any point you can just talk to it. Hold the mic, ask a real question out loud (for example, "I feel stiff after sitting at my desk all day, what should I try?"), and release. Align sends your actual camera frame and your actual recorded voice, together, to OMNI, a live multimodal model that reasons over both at once and answers back in its own generated speech, with synced captions so nothing is lost if audio fails.
Every session saves locally via SQLite, no account needed, and every piece of guidance OMNI gives is checked against a versioned evidence catalog built from WHO, CCOHS, NICE, NHS, and peer-reviewed systematic reviews, so the advice is traceable to a real source, not a hallucination.
And when Align does not have a validated, measured number to show you, it says so, explicitly, on screen. Capture completeness is not posture quality, and we will not blur that line just to look more finished in a demo.
How we built it
Expo / React Native (SDK 57) with Expo Router for a fully native iOS app: camera, navigation, and haptics that feel like a shipped App Store product.

projects.name: fly VS worm
projects.tagline: legal crypto trading
projects.body:
Inspiration
Two animals have nervous systems whose wiring we actually know. C. elegans (or the roundworm) was the first. White, Southgate, Thomson and Brenner spent a decade cutting one hermaphrodite into serial sections and tracing every process by hand, publishing the result in 1986. Drosophila (or the fruit fly) came much later, and its central complex is the part we understand best: a ring of neurons that holds the fly's heading like a compass needle.
Both are small enough to simulate completely. Neither is a model of a brain. They are the brain, every cell without sampling.
So the question was not whether we could put AI on a blockchain. It was narrower and more interesting. 
Can a blockchain execute a nervous system?
Almost everything on-chain that calls itself intelligent keeps a hash of a model that ran somewhere else. We wanted the arithmetic itself, every membrane equation and every synapse, inside the VM, with a signature you can open in a block explorer.
That only works if the chain is fast enough. And Thru is.
What it does
The worm runs on Thru. All 302 neurons of the C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous system, one on-chain account each. A timestep is a program instruction that reads all 302 accounts, integrates the membrane equation in Q16.16 fixed point, and writes them back. Gap-junction current settles as real tsys_account_transfer calls between neuron accounts, so electrical coupling between two cells is a balance transfer between two addresses. A classifier reads the five command interneurons and writes one byte of behaviour. A browser renders that byte as a crawling animal, with the real traced anatomy lighting up as voltages move.
The fly trades. A 134-neuron heading circuit taken from the Janelia hemibrain connectome reads price momentum as push-pull turning drive. The heading bump rotates, counterclockwise for long and clockwise for short, with size proportional to turning speed and scaled by bump strength as a confidence signal. No single bump m

projects.name: Neuro North
projects.tagline: Typing is hard. What if you could do it with your brain?
projects.note: Typing with your brain. High ceiling if the signal actually works on the floor.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Companies like Neuralink have achieved the impossible when it comes to making computers accessible to everyone. The last frontier of this problem is making the solution open source and cost efficient.
What it does
NeuroNorth lets users accomplish text-based tasks, without moving their fingers, or opening their mouth. We've integrated with AI agents so you can launch tasks and ask questions entirely with your brain.
How we built it
BrainFlow
Decoding part:
English lexicon, using prefix trie to search
using GPT-2 as a way to decode ranges based on the past context (GPT-2 is not post-trained, so it acts as a general autocomplete rather than a traditional AI assistant). The range decoder produces a constrained shortlist, then a locally hosted GPT-2 ranks only those valid candidates
beam search over the entire sentence. we keep the 8 strongest sentence hypotheses, allowing later words to repair earlier mistakes
Challenges we ran into
Non-invasive headsets have severe limitations for collecting data
Biggest: collecting a reliable signal
many words share the same ranges, so relying on the EEG range collection alone cannot produce the correct reconstructed/decoded words. We ran into lots of cases where different words have the same sequence of ranges (nice -> ride, tacos -> years, what -> that). Greedy decoding is not enough to recover the intended words. This led us to sentence-wide beam decoding that can rely on future context to decode current word
Accuracy versus latency and interaction cost
The stronger language processing was meaningfully slower:
Bigram: 51 ms/action
GPT-2: 153 ms/action
Greedy GPT-2: 31.76 seconds for the autonomous probe
Sentence-beam GPT-2: 44.92 seconds, about 41% slower
Galvanic isolation
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Given the unreliability of non-invasive EEG headsets, our results are quite good
What we learned
Non-invasive EEG headsets produce really noisy outputs
What's next for Neuro North
Try with a better headset

projects.name: SurgePrep
projects.tagline: Built by future engineers for future surgeons
projects.body:
Inspiration
We began with a simple question: why should meaningful surgical-skills practice depend so heavily on a student’s school, location, or financial situation?
Advanced simulators and specialized software can be expensive. Simulation labs have limited availability, and students cannot always access supervised clinical observation or cadaver-based anatomy education as often as they would like.
These experiences are important, but they are difficult to repeat regularly—especially for learners from lower-income communities and under-resourced institutions.
As future engineers, we wanted to explore whether familiar technology could make safe practice more accessible to future surgeons.
That idea became 
SurgePrep
.
What it does
SurgePrep is a physical–digital surgical-skills training prototype designed around hardware that students may already own or can access more easily.
In simple terms, it works like a flight simulator for foundational surgical skills.
The learner holds a realistic, scalpel-shaped blunt training instrument and practises on a reusable synthetic surface. A normal Logitech USB webcam observes how the tool moves, while an ESP32 measures contact and pressure.
Those physical movements control a virtual instrument interacting with a 3D model on the computer screen.
The learner can see whether they followed the intended path, maintained consistent pressure, positioned the tool correctly, and completed the exercise accurately. At the end, SurgePrep provides a score, replay, and understandable feedback.
The goal is to let trainees safely repeat instructor-assigned exercises from home or through a shared community kit instead of depending entirely on expensive institutional equipment and limited lab hours.
SurgePrep does not replace instructors, clinical observation, simulation centers, or cadaver-based education. It helps learners practise beforehand, reinforce skills between supervised sessions, and arrive better prepared.
