projects.name: Basecase
projects.tagline: Removing the limitation on physical AI. One device, infinite possibilities.
projects.note: One hardware body, many policies — removing the limits on physical AI.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Physical AI is limited by how its hardware was programmed, not by the hardware itself. One piece of hardware can be so much more than just what it was designed to do. We are attempting to utilize hardware to its limit.
What it does
It's a camera that runs a SOTA computer vision model, but it's more than that. Because a simple webcam can be designed for a certain purpose. Maybe as a security camera to scan people who walk by. Maybe as a key point model for a human athlete. Maybe we want the camera to scan for environmental indicators  or scan a crowd. But what if we could do all of that, on one camera? Changing the camera's purpose is as simple as talking to it. It's a "compiler" that transforms the highest level of human instruction down to a physical change in what the hardware is executing in an instant. One device, infinite possibilities.
How we built it
The project consists of a web interface and a multimodal computer vision pipeline. The computer vision pipeline directly talks through the hardware through the linker, while it talks to the web interface through a web socket for responses and a complex orchestration agentic workflow for requests. The agent analyzes the natural language request, lexes it into tokens, and parses it into a sanitized JSON schema the pipeline can understand at the model level. However, the workflow can also take and learn from processed outputs from the pipeline to refine its own requests. The agent takes the processed JSON and makes a tool call to the pipeline. The pipeline then turns the JSON live, but the agent isn't sleeping either. The pipeline is constantly streaming back to the agent so changes can be processed in the orchestration layer and new changes can be pushed. The pipeline has a complex state machine to handle different kinds of request and changes.
Challenges we ran into
Basically the entire hackathon was a challenge. The truth is that originally, our idea was to use a robotic rover and get the robotic rove

projects.name: Composition
projects.tagline: AI filmmaking you can actually control, refine, and interact with.
projects.body:
Inspiration
I wanted AI filmmaking to preserve the freedom of finding a shot: moving around a subject, choosing an angle, and directing a performance. Composition turns those physical and creative decisions into inputs for generation. Codex made tackling this scope as a solo hacker possible.
What it does
Composition is an agentic videography tool. Gemini Live provides conversational direction, Gemini plans scene edits, and a connected phone controls the virtual camera. Users save movement in reusable animation blocks, generate a visual treatment with Gemini, and use the composition to guide video generation.
How I built it
The filmmaking pipeline
Direct with Gemini.
Gemini receives scene state and a viewport image, returning typed actions for objects, cameras, and animation. Gemini Live calls this workflow through voice; Hunyuan supplies generated character motion. Changes are validated and approved before application.
Film and preserve movement.
ARKit sends phone position and orientation through a WebSocket relay. The Three.js editor maps those poses to the virtual camera and saves interpolated motion as editable timeline blocks. Blocks retain source keyframes when split, retimed, or reused.
Render the composition.
The saved camera and animation tracks become a clean 720p, 30 fps motion guide. This captures staging, timing, and camera movement independently of the phone's preview stream.
Develop the look with Gemini.
Gemini refines artistic prompts and generates styled first and last frames. Gemini receives the styled first image when creating the last, providing a shared appearance reference while retaining the ending composition.
Generate and review.
Seedance receives the motion guide, selected Gemini images, and direction prompt. The guide supplies motion and framing; Gemini images supply appearance. The pipeline saves returned video for review and download. Users can reuse the guide for another visual treatment.
Solo development with Codex
Codex made Compositio

projects.name: Enlight
projects.tagline: Remy helps people with memory loss recognize faces and navigate their surroundings. It learns names and personal details from conversation and keeps you on track during travel time.
projects.body:
How?
Enlight
"What you most want, is what you most can't have. And what you most can't have, is what you already had, and lost."
- Christopher Nolan
For someone living with Alzheimer’s, recognizing a familiar face does not always mean remembering a name. In Christopher Nolan's 
Memento
, Leonard Shelby had to rely on a collection of Polaroid photos, handwritten notes tattooed onto his skin, and scattered files simply to piece together who was standing in front of him. We built Enlight to serve as that external memory system, brought into the modern age through ambient intelligent technology rather than fading paper notes.
What is it exactly?
Enlight is an AI-powered visual companion and private memory timeline designed to help individuals living with Alzheimer’s navigate daily social interactions and retain their independence.
Through a live camera feed, Enlight performs real-time face recognition and displays immediate contextual notes about the person in view. As dialogue occurs, it tracks facial movement and audio timing to attribute speech accurately, while Gemini transcribes and takes structured notes on the fly. It automatically extracts names, personal details, and shared experiences, updating the live screen in real time and saving every detail to local profiles. Beyond social recognition, Enlight includes a proactive reminder and navigation system. If a user becomes disoriented, gets lost, or wanders while traveling, Enlight provides reassuring directions, clarifies where they are headed, and surfaces upcoming daily tasks.
At its core, Enlight also serves as a personal social network like Facebook, built to reconstruct lost pieces of a person's life story. It seamlessly pairs automated conversation logs from above with personal notes written and edited by you. By scrolling back through your notes, our goal is to allow individuals living with Alzheimer’s to revisit past interactions, recall familiar faces, and reconnect with meaningful memories that might ot

projects.name: Jayfound
projects.tagline: A talent discovery platform for overlooked, self-taught builders
projects.body:
Inspiration
Hiring pipelines filter on degrees, resume polish, English fluency, and proximity to the right networks. They don't filter on whether someone can actually build. We started with JMatt, a self-taught builder in Jinja, Uganda, who has real skill but none of the signals recruiters look for. Our insight: 
process is a better signal than pedigree, and it's verifiable.
What it does
Portfolio Hub:
Builders document any project in stages: start, rough version, final, and lessons learned. This works even for projects built years before the platform existed.
Puzzle Arcade:
An optional set of culture-fair, nonverbal reasoning puzzles, graded deterministically. It boosts discovery for people with thinner portfolios. Skipping it doesn't hide anyone.
Recruiter view:
Recruiters browse a ranked list and filter by skill tag. They never filter by raw puzzle score.
Ranking weights 
portfolio depth highest, then puzzle performance, then mentor endorsements
, so demonstrated work always counts most.
How we built it
Next.js for the frontend and API routes, Supabase for Postgres and file storage, and Vercel for hosting. It's a deliberately small stack, so one person could put the effort into the portfolio staging UI and the ranking logic. Ranking is a plain server-side weighted calculation, recomputed on read, and the puzzles are graded deterministically.
Challenges we ran into
Designing a portfolio model flexible enough to stage a project retroactively.
Tuning the ranking weights so puzzle scores never outweigh real work.
Scoping a solo build under a hackathon clock. Auth, payments, and mentor verification were cut on purpose.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
A ranking model that encodes the thesis (portfolio over puzzles over mentors) instead of a flat leaderboard, and a working loop from builder portfolio to puzzle to recruiter list.
What we learned
How much signal comes from documented process rather than a finished artifact, and how to design assessments that are fair

projects.name: Hack the Heart
projects.tagline: Let your simulated self go on dates first, before you spend your time.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Finding a soul mate is a challenge (especially for programmers like us).
At a hackathon you walk past hundreds of people in three days, and you never find out who you would have clicked with. We were already wearing a badge that quietly remembers everyone we bump into, so we wanted that badge to do something useful with those names.
What it does
Hack the Heart turns a badge bump into an introduction.
When two badges meet, the contacts stored on the badge are sent to our server. Each person gets a profile built from the answers they approve themselves, along with their public posts. Two AI agents, one acting for each person, then hold a short private conversation.
You can read the whole conversation, see why each agent said what it said, and see a compatibility score built from the answers both people actually gave. If you meet up for real afterwards, you tell the app how it went, and each person's agent learns from that.
How we built it
The badge
We read the contact files the badge writes, one per badge id. The app accepts an owner profile plus up to 250 contacts in a single batch. A preview step tells you what each contact will do before anything is saved, marking each one as new, filling missing fields, already known, or in conflict. Every route is rate limited. Any contact can be analyzed on demand to produce a headline, a summary, a list of interests, and exactly three conversation starters.
The profile
Every person has a frozen profile built only from their own approved form answers. Every field carries an evidence id pointing back to the answer it came from. Public LinkedIn, Instagram and X posts are imported separately, and a Discord bot lets someone export their own messages.
The conversation
Four agent roles run on one model.
Social Interpreter.
Reads an incoming message through four psychological lenses and returns structured analysis, including how warm and how dominant the message reads. It is never allowed to write the visible reply.

projects.name: Tinker
projects.tagline: vibe code hardware
projects.body:
Inspiration
As a CS student who is pure software, I honestly get a little jealous of all the cool hardware projects I see being built around me. I've tried time and time again to watch tutorials and use ai to help guide me through learning hardware, but I've always seemed to struggle with picking it up. Naturally, this led me to building Tinker, a tool that aims to be Cursor for hardware.
What it does
You can either describe a machine/robot you want to build, or you record a video of your workbench with all the hardware parts and machinery you have available to you. Tinker takes this through a few stages.
Design
. 
An agents scrapes through an adaptive catalog of chassis, wiring, circuitry, chips, motors, propellors and other components, pulling what's relevant into the design and connecting everything procedurally on pre-defined connection points. If a new component is needed, it generates the model and scrapes the data for that component and dynamically adds it to the component library, making Tinker smarter as time goes on. Budget, electrical constraints and other factors are considered when selecting components. 
Simulate
. 
A 3D simulation is then produced to validate the build. Using Unity rigid bodies, physics materials, forces and kinematic interactions as well as an underlying electrical simulation, the user can simulate what the final build will feel like and spot issues before building.
Blueprint
. 
In this tab you can view all the 3d printed components that are needed for the build. These 3d models, validated for 3d printers, can also be thrown under an orthographic view combined with hidden-line removal and automatic dimensioning to turn them into blueprints with dimensions users can follow.
Make
. 
Once users are happy with their build, they can move on to actually building the project! The first step is getting all the required components. This tab features links for all the components required to build the project along with architecture and circuitr

projects.name: Fedwrite
projects.tagline: ㅤ
projects.body:
Inspiration
A commercial underwriter opens their inbox to over a hundred submissions and has time to read maybe ten. The carrier's appetite guidelines say which business they want, but someone still has to check every submission against them by hand. We built the agent that does it for them, and shows its work.
What it does
Fedwrite is an AI underwriting desk built on the Federato Core API. It reads the entire submission queue, ranks it against the carrier's appetite, and explains every decision in plain English.
Learns the data on its own.
It explores the API's schema, maps 1,033 field paths, and works out which field holds each thing the guidelines care about. It confirms every match with a live query.
Triages 113 submissions in 5 API calls.
One call settles 107 of them. The agent then decides for itself which 14 deserve a deeper look, and pulls their full building schedules and loss history.
Scores two things, separately.
Appetite fit asks "do we write this kind of business?" Risk quality asks "is this a good example of it?" An AI underwriter grades twelve risk signals per account and gives its reasoning for each one.
Finds the business you're missing.
It flagged 3 strong risks that the guidelines decline on a technicality. That is an opportunity, not a rejection.
Shows its reasoning.
Every step records what it was testing, what it found, and what it cost. You can trace any decision back to the query behind it.
The dashboard gives underwriters a ranked queue, a portfolio view of the whole book, the rulebook, and the agent's full reasoning trace. They approve, refer or decline with one click.
How we built it
The agent is written in Python with pydantic, httpx and typer. The dashboard is React, TypeScript and Vite. OpenAI's gpt model scores the risk signals.
The appetite guidelines live in a simple data file, not in code, so changing a rule or adding a new line of business needs no engineering. The agent writes all of its own API queries. A query planner picks the

projects.name: AURIC
projects.tagline: A glasses-first companion: talk to it, remembers what you saw, finds your things by radio, and rebuilds the room in 3D. Says where it knows it from.
projects.note: Glasses that remember what you saw, find your things by radio, and rebuild the room in 3D — and say where it knows it from.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Phones are the wrong shape for an assistant. They can't see what you see, and you have to stop what you're doing to use them. Smart glasses fix both. I wanted an assistant that lives in the glasses, keeps up with a conversation, and remembers the world for me.
What it does
AURIC is a companion for Meta smart glasses, run from an iPhone.
Conversation.
Talk to it naturally. It follows the thread of the conversation and answers in your ear. You can interrupt it mid-sentence.
Visual memory.
Look at something and say "remember where I put this." Ask later and it tells you where and when it last saw it.
Finding.
A Hack the North badge becomes a tracker. As you get closer, the phone taps faster, like a Geiger counter. Two iPhones can also range each other directly with Apple's Nearby Interaction.
Space.
Capture a room and AURIC rebuilds it as a 3D Gaussian splat you can explore.
How I built it
The app is Expo and React Native, with a native Swift module for Meta's Wearables Device Access Toolkit and Apple Nearby Interaction. A Node relay handles the reasoning: OpenAI for vision, tool use and transcription, Gemini as an alternate, and ElevenLabs for the voice. The badge firmware is Lua on an ESP32. Room reconstruction runs on FFmpeg, COLMAP and Brush, with a Three.js viewer.
Challenges
The badge radio can only be heard by another badge, so a phone can't listen to it. I turned a second badge into a receiver that streams what it hears over USB to the laptop and on to the phone.
Bluetooth glasses make you choose between good audio out and a microphone in. Using the glasses' mic drops the whole link to phone-call quality, so the phone does the listening and the glasses do the talking.
Meta's camera SDK needs a native build, so part of the app lives outside Expo Go as a custom module.
Accomplishments
One person, one weekend: a phone app, a native glasses bridge, badge firmware, an AI relay and a working 3D reconstruction pipeline, all talking to each other.
I'm proud

projects.name: Just in Time
projects.tagline: Voice in. The right screen out.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every interface in existence was designed once, for an imagined "normal" user, and then frozen forever. If your eyes don't work the way that imagined user's did, if you need higher contrast, larger targets, or no interface at all and just a voice that understands you, you're not using a slightly worse version of the product. You're locked out of it. We started with the people the current model of software fails the hardest: people who are blind or have low vision, for whom "just use the app" is often not true at all. But the deeper idea isn't a feature for one group, it's that a UI built around one fixed shape was always going to fail someone. An interface that rebuilds itself around whoever's using it, in the moment, doesn't just serve blind users better. It's a better idea for everyone: the person cooking with wet hands, the person who's exhausted, the person overwhelmed by an app with forty buttons when they needed three. We built for the hardest case first, because if it works there, it works everywhere.
What it does
You talk to it. Out loud, hands free, no screen required. A physical device: touchscreen, four buttons, a slider, and a microphone that's actually listening hears what you need and builds the exact interface for that moment, live. Ask it to walk you through a recipe and it reads each step aloud, confirms where you are, and adapts the second something goes wrong, too much sugar in the bowl, and it diagnoses the mistake and offers a fix out loud, no screen-reading required. Every interface it generates is checked against real WCAG AA contrast requirements before it's ever allowed to render, a hard gate, not a guideline: fail the check, and a certified, legible fallback takes over instead, automatically, every time. That same guarantee that makes this reliable for someone with low vision is exactly what makes it effortless for someone who's just tired, distracted, or has their hands full. Accessibility isn't the edge case here. It's the who

projects.name: Snap
projects.tagline: Your gym bro in your texts. Snap knows when you said you'd work out, sees that you didn't, and forces you too.
projects.note: Durable Object alarms let the agent schedule its own future, and the trace screen shows why it chose to stay quiet — nothing else here visualizes an agent's restraint. Undercut by generic Built With tags, an unlinked backend repo, no video, and a custodial three-wallet Solana layer with no on-chain program.
projects.body:
Inspiration
A year ago Hugo and I were chuds who skipped the gym.
We had memberships. It came out of my bank account every month. We had a streak app too, and calendar reminders. We were mostly consistent, but sometimes we would skip. Some weeks we lowkey never went at all. 
That's the part we kept coming back to. Skipping the gym has no witness. Nothing happens. The app asks "did you work out today?" and you either lie to it or you stop opening it, and both of those feel identical. 
Every accountability app asks if you worked out. That question is the issue. We built the friend instead, gave it your HealthKit data so it can't be lied to, put it in your texts, and attached a stake so you CAN'T skip the gym.
What it does
You text Snap like a person: "I need to go to the gym at 7, $5 on it." The agent parses that into a commitment and locks your stake on Solana. The stake forces you to go to the gym, putting real money on the line.
At 7:20, Snap wakes itself up. Imagine that no workout has come in from HealthKit. It pulls your context: nothing logged today, you skipped the gym yesterday, you've only gone 2/5 times this week, and 0.05 SOL is sitting in escrow. Snap says:
"bro it's 7:24 and no workout, you said no excuses today."
You say:
"homework bro homework"
Snap says:
"30 minutes then its push day. go."
You get one renegotiation per deadline. It's the same stake but a new deadline, and Snap decides if you earn it, using your history. If you used the same excuse yesterday, it would call it out.
Then you actually go to the gym. Your Apple Watch ends the workout, Snap syncs it, and the escrow releases your stake. If you skip, your stake gets slashed and donated to a charity of your choice.
Two things make it different from a regular gym app:
Snap lives in your messages. The app has no chat at all. The app is used for onboarding, syncing HealthKit, showing snaps brain, and managing your wallet/account.
How we built it
iOS (SwiftUI) Used to build the frontend and workou

projects.name: EchoPath
projects.tagline: iPhone walking navigation for blind pedestrians with LiDAR obstacle sensing, airpods spatial audio guiding , and haptics. Maps routes plus real-time lane guidance.
projects.body:
Inspiration
A white cane is one of the most honest tools ever designed. It tells you the truth about the ground: the curb, the step, the crack in the sidewalk. What it cannot tell you is the rest of the world.
That is the gap we could not stop thinking about. Not “how do I get across town,” but the three feet between your shoes and the next safe step. For more than 250 million people living with vision impairment, that gap is not a UI problem. It is the difference between leaving the house and staying home. Between independence and waiting for someone else.
What it does
EchoPath is an iPhone-first walking companion for blind and low-vision pedestrians. It does two things at once, and it never lets the second one wait on the first.
LiDAR sees the path. On iPhones, ARKit scene depth samples the world in front of the camera roughly ten times a second. EchoPath does not just say “object detected.” It models three lanes — left, center, and right — filters out the floor, trusts closer hazards first, and pays special attention to obstacles from the ground up to head height. A trash can at your ankle and a branch at your face are not the same kind of danger. The system knows that.
Spatial audio tells you where to go. Instead of shouting “left, left, left,” EchoPath speaks through the body. Distinct HRTF tones pan into the left ear, the right ear, or the center of the head. One cue per second. Learnable. Calm. Understandable even while speech is playing. Straight, left, right, and stop each have their own signature, matched with Core Haptics so the warning still lands if the street is loud.
Navigation becomes orientation, not just a route. MapKit builds a walking route. Core Location tracks you. But a turn instruction is useless if you are facing the wrong way. EchoPath uses compass heading to hear the difference: rotate left, rotate right, and then, when you are aligned with the path, go ahead. Object avoidance stays on the whole time. If a pole appears in your lane, the lo

projects.name: Green Washing Detector
projects.tagline: What if you want to invest responsibly but you're worried about greenwashing?
projects.body:
Inspiration
Greenwashing makes it difficult for people to tell whether environmental claims are meaningful or simply marketing language. Companies often use vague phrases like “eco-friendly,” “sustainable,” or “carbon neutral” without providing measurable evidence. We built Green Washing Detector to make sustainability claims easier to investigate and understand.
What it does
Green Washing Detector analyzes corporate websites, sustainability reports, PDFs, marketing copy, and company names to identify potentially misleading environmental claims.
It:
•  Extracts sustainability-related evidence from submitted sources.
•  Searches for official ESG, climate, emissions, and sustainability reports.
•  Uses Browserbase to fetch pages, navigate JavaScript-heavy websites, and discover relevant reports.
•  Flags vague, exaggerated, comparative, or unsupported claims.
•  Detects missing metrics such as baselines, timeframes, scopes, and verification details.
•  Assigns a Greenwashing Risk Score from 0–100.
•  Explains each finding with an evidence status and confidence level.
•  Suggests more transparent alternatives that avoid making unsupported promises.
How we built it
We built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
The ingestion pipeline supports URL scraping, PDF parsing, pasted text, and company-name discovery. For web research, we use Browserbase’s Search and Fetch APIs first, then fall back to a real Browserbase browser session through Playwright when pages require JavaScript rendering or navigation.
The analysis layer combines an OpenAI-compatible LLM with a deterministic heuristic auditor. The LLM output is validated server-side to ensure that scores, risk levels, evidence statuses, and quoted claims remain consistent with the submitted source. If the LLM is unavailable or produces an invalid response, the heuristic engine provides a reliable fallback.
Challenges we ran into
One of the biggest challenges was distinguishing genuinely unsupp

projects.name: GITIRL
projects.tagline: GIT for 3D Time Traveling Caretaking
projects.body:
What it does
GITIRL is a versatile caretaker/roommate style bot that interacts with a physical room under real version control: objects are YAML files in a repo, so it tells you what moved, prints a literal unified diff of the physical world, and sends the robot to put things back. Git is the write path and the source of truth. Elasticsearch is the read path, because git cannot query (answer "where did I leave my keys?"). Sentry acts like the nervous system across the laptop and the robot. Ask it a question in plain English and the last step of the answer is a robot moving a real object.
How we built it
Bracket Bot's stereo cameras feed a perception pipeline that turns point clouds into a voxel map, into named objects then commits to a real git repo. Every commit is also indexed into six Elasticsearch indices plus two time-series data streams for 50 Hz robot telemetry. Every process initializes observability so one Sentry trace spans the laptop, the Pi and the web tier, and every Elasticsearch document carries the trace id that produced it.
Challenges we ran into
The robot spent most of the weekend off the network, and Sentry is how we know exactly how badly. The controls would occasionally fail while the Bracket Bot was idling but luckily we got it fixed.
Accomplishments we're proud of
We used elastic's vector search  (e.g. finds a cup when you type "mug") + The robot files its own Sentry issues with the camera frame attached, then resolves them through the Sentry API by physically tidying up and passing a rescan.
What we learned
Reframing commits as discrete snapshots instead of a 30 FPS stream solved most of the compute and bandwidth problems. Elasticsearch enabled observability on a distributed robot.
What's next
Ship Robot Session Replay (inspired by Sentry's flagship product), reconstructing motion from encoder and pitch telemetry beside the trace of the same moment. We could make 
git merge
so two people can propose incompatible rooms and the robot negotiates

projects.tagline: More than a lamp — a responsive robotic companion.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to explore how an ordinary object could feel more alive through human-robot interaction. Instead of treating LeLamp as just a controllable light, we wanted it to behave more like an expressive desk companion that can see, listen, react, and communicate through movement, light, and sound.
Our goal was to make interactions intuitive enough that someone could walk up to the lamp and understand how to interact with it without needing instructions.
What it does
Our project turns LeLamp into an interactive robotic companion using computer vision, voice interaction, expressive movement, and lighting.
LeLamp can recognize and respond to several different interactions:
When it detects a face, it greets the user with “Hello there,” flashes its light, and nods.
When it detects a hand, it responds with a playful side-to-side wiggle.
When it recognizes a peace sign, it performs a more dramatic dance and plays a short disco-style sound.
When it detects a phone, it dramatically shakes, flashes its light, and tells the user: “Stop scrolling, please lock in twin.”
It recognizes basic happy and sad facial expressions and responds with different movements and lighting behaviors.
It accepts simple voice commands, including turning the lamp on and off.
When a user points in a direction, the lamp follows the direction of the pointing gesture with its head.
If there is no new interaction for 10 seconds, LeLamp enters an idle state, gradually dimming its light and lowering its head as if it is falling asleep.
When someone interacts with it again, it wakes up and resumes responding.
The system also uses behavioral priorities so that overlapping detections do not cause conflicting actions. For example, if a face, peace sign, and phone are detected simultaneously, the phone reaction takes priority.
How we built it
We developed and tested the project using the LeLamp model in MuJoCo, allowing us to prototype the robot's movements and lighting behavior in simulation.

projects.name: Win the North
projects.tagline: Got an idea? Predict your odds and build to win.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every hackathon starts the exact same way. You sit down at a table with your team, spend thirty minutes brainstorming ideas, and someone asks: "Wait, has this already been done? Is this actually a good idea?"
Usually, nobody has a solid answer. You spend five minutes doing a quick search on Devpost, find nothing certain, and end up building it anyway.
We wanted a real answer based on actual numbers. We were curious if we could predict whether an idea had finalist potential just by analyzing historical trends and seeing how similar neighborhoods of ideas have performed across the 12 years of Hack the North.
What it does
Win the North projects every single Hack the North submission into a 2D interactive space based on true semantic similarity.
You type in your project idea, and the app immediately tells you:
Whether someone has already built something similar in the past years.
Whether similar projects became finalists or won prizes.
How to adjust your idea or stack to target specific prize tracks.
The baseline answer to "Will this win?" is about 4.7%, since only 161 out of 3,443 projects made finalist. But Win the North shows you which specific categories beat those odds and how tech trends have shifted over time.
How we built it
Instead of just wrapping a basic search box or tossing a generic chatbot on a database, we built an engine where embeddings, hybrid search, and text analysis work together:
Scraped Corpus: We wrote a custom scraper to pull, clean, and structure all 3,443 Hack the North submissions from Devpost (2014–2025). This includes project descriptions, winning tracks, tech stacks, and linked GitHub READMEs (github_repo.py).
OpenAI Embeddings for Real Context: We embed project pitches, READMEs, and tech stacks using text-embedding-3-small. Embeddings run almost everything in our app:
2D Visual Map (engine.py, build.py): Projects high-dimensional vectors onto a 2D map so spatial distance represents actual conceptual and tech stack similarity,

How Appeara initialized
DOOM SCROLLING.

projects.name: CADEX
projects.tagline: Build for the real world, without being a CAD expert.
projects.body:
Inspiration
AI has dramatically lowered the barrier to building in the digital world. Someone with an idea can describe what they want, iterate with a model, and produce an app, website, or tool without first becoming an expert in every technology underneath it. The distance between having an idea and being able to make it real is shrinking, but mostly in software. That same experience and ability to create is missing when someone wants to change something in the physical world.
On Friday night, we walked around the Hack the North venue looking for small problems. We found a broken foosball handle, a missing ping-pong table clamp, and a lectern missing a cup-holder insert. These are all small physical problems that can have a disproportionately difficult solution. Even with access to a 3D printer, someone still has to understand the object, identify the measurements that matter, translate those measurements into precise geometry, and create a model that will  fit. For someone without that experience, access to a 3D printer does not automatically translate into the ability to make useful, personalized objects, it became the problem behind CADEX. Building the harness that lets AI turn human intent and real-world dimensions into something manufacturable.
What it does
CADEX is a scan-to-print pipeline for creating custom parts that fit things in the real world.
A user points their phone at an object or the space where a part needs to go. CADEX helps identify the important geometry (mounting points, openings, edges, clearances, etc) and turns that information into a parametric CAD model. Instead of producing a static mesh, CADEX generates editable, dimension-driven geometry. That means dimensions can be corrected, tolerances can be adjusted, and the part can be regenerated without rebuilding the entire design. From there, CADEX prepares the model for fabrication and sends it toward the 3D-printing workflow.

projects.name: Bloxify
projects.tagline: Agentic and analytics layer for selling with Shopify on Roblox
projects.body:
Inspiration
Last year, Shopify and Roblox shipped an integration that lets creators sell real products from Shopify stores inside Roblox games. Big developer studios and brands are pulling in hundreds of thousands in revenue through it. But one thing missing from that integration is an analytics layer, and with that gap comes the opportunity for an agentic layer. I-commerce, integrated and intelligent commerce, is the future. 
What it does
Add a storefront to any Roblox game, based on your Shopify store and its products, using a storefront creation agent: classifies a live Shopify catalog, generates 2D clothing nets for mannequins and procedural meshes from product photos and info
Live analytics: raycast-based line-of-sight and positional tracking measures who actually saw, approached, and interacted with each display
3D attention view: the game map rebuilt in 3D on the dashboard, with a real foot-traffic heatmap and player behaviour patterns
Marketing agent: knows the game, the game map, each product's price, and its own past experiments in order to develop, propose, and apply edits straight to the Roblox storefront
How we built it
Cloudflare Workers is the backend and the brain, with two agents running there on GPT-5.4. D1 is the database that holds every player event and every past experiment as the agents' memory, so the marketing agent finds user behaviour patterns and checks what it already tried before proposing new experiments. Durable Objects run the job queue that turns an agent's decision into a real action; one stateful claim per job means two Roblox servers polling at once can never double-apply the same change. R2 stores before/after screenshots of every applied change for context. 
Shopify's Admin API feeds the product catalog in, both to build the storefront and to inform the agents. Roblox's own game server provides real-time player data, and Roblox Studio's MCP allow agents to edit the Roblox game.
The frontend is made with Next.js and Three.js.

projects.name: Whodunit
projects.tagline: every approval was correct. The purchase still shouldn't have happened.
projects.body:
Inspiration
I've done this too many times. A bug shows up, you run 
git bisect
, you wait through seven test runs, and if the suite flakes once it can still point at an innocent commit. The commit that looks guilty is usually the feature, not the bug. I wanted a bisect that actually reads the diffs first.
What it does
You type one sentence (finance says a credit note CSV is a cent off) and Whodunit searches git history, writes a test, and finds the culprit.
The demo is 108 commits. The test suite is green. The killer isn't the credit-note feature. It's a "harmless" refactor that swapped 
Math.floor
for 
Math.trunc
, so negative money rounds the wrong way. One cent. Classic bisect needs about 6 probes. This closes in 3.
Turn on a flaky test and vanilla bisect derails. Whodunit still stamps the same commit (
4c58cb3
). Then Gemini can restore 
Math.floor
and push the fix.
How we built it
I built this solo (my teammate ditched me). Elasticsearch 9 on Elastic Cloud for the case file: commits, diffs, CI logs, issues. Hybrid search (BM25 + Gemini vectors + RRF) and ES|QL. The agent's tools are real queries, not a chatbot wrapper.
Gemini runs three specialists: investigate, reproduce, fix. If quota dies mid-demo it falls back to another Flash model.
The bisect is Bayesian. It probes where the evidence points, and treats a flake as noise, not a verdict. The UI is a React interrogation room. If Wi-Fi dies, the simulated demo still plays the same 108-commit crime scene.
Challenges we ran into
Search loves the wrong commit. The credit-note feature and the tax-rounding "fix" both mention the bug. The real one says "no behaviour change." Without a test, rank is a vibe.
Live Gemini also 429'd in the middle of a run, so I had to build fallbacks and a simulated cinematic that doesn't need the API.
Elastic Cloud Serverless also rejected shard settings that work fine locally. One 400 and nothing indexes.

projects.name: Doppel
projects.tagline: Real-time phishing domain detection built on the public Certificate Transparency stream, Elasticsearch, and Elastic Agent Builder.
projects.note: Real-time phishing detection off the public Certificate Transparency stream into Elasticsearch. Purpose-built for Elastic's brief.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every TLS certificate issued anywhere is logged publicly the moment it's created. That means the first signal of a new domain impersonating a brand exists in a public feed before any victim sees the site. Most organizations don't watch that feed. By the time a brand notices a lookalike domain, it has often been live for hours or days. We built a system that watches the stream directly and investigates a domain the moment it looks suspicious, instead of relying on user reports after the fact.
What it does
Watches the Certificate Transparency stream in real time and scores newly issued domains for brand impersonation using homoglyph detection, typosquat matching, and keyword analysis, with every point of score tied to a stated reason
Investigates flagged domains: retrieves similar phishing lures across languages using hybrid search, clusters related domains into campaigns, and can check the live page for a credential-harvesting form
Produces an analyst write-up through Elastic Agent Builder, using a set of ES|QL tools registered against the cluster, with a Gemini-based fallback when Agent Builder is unavailable
Proposes actions (notify, block, file a report) but never executes one without human approval, enforced by a deterministic policy gate that never trusts model output
Suggests domains a brand should watch for defensively, generated by running the scoring logic in reverse
How we built it
Backend: Python, FastAPI, WebSockets for live dashboard updates.
Detection: a deterministic, non-ML scoring engine where every flagged signal has an explicit, auditable reason.
Search: Elasticsearch, with hybrid retrieval combining BM25 and Jina dense vector embeddings fused with reciprocal rank fusion, reranked with a Jina cross-encoder. ES|QL aggregations handle campaign clustering and issuance volume analysis.
Agent layer: Elastic Agent Builder as the primary reasoning agent, registered with five ES|QL tools against the live cluster. Falls back to a single grounded

projects.name: Perception

projects.body:
Inspiration
Traditional CAD software is powerful, but the process of turning an idea into a 3D model can be complicated and unintuitive. Designers and engineers spend hours navigating menus, learning complex modeling tools, and switching between applications just to bring their ideas to life.
We wanted to reimagine what designing in 3D could look like if we removed those barriers. What if you could simply describe an idea, watch it appear in front of you, and manipulate it with your own hands? What if your AI assistant could not only understand your vision but also help you build, refine, and share it?
That vision inspired Perception: a mixed-reality design workspace that combines artificial intelligence, natural conversation, and spatial computing to make 3D creation feel as intuitive as interacting with the physical world.
Our goal is to make CAD more accessible to beginners while giving experienced designers and engineers an entirely new way to explore their ideas.
What it does
Perception transforms your physical environment into an interactive 3D design studio using the Meta Quest 3.
At the center of the experience is Percy, our AI-powered voice assistant. Instead of navigating traditional CAD interfaces, users can describe what they want to create through natural conversation. Percy interprets their requests and helps generate CAD models that appear directly in their mixed-reality environment.
Users can interact with their designs through several key features:
Voice-to-CAD: Describe a design in natural language and have Percy generate an initial 3D model. Continue speaking to refine dimensions, geometry, and other design features.
Hands-on model manipulation: Select, move, rotate, and scale models using natural hand interactions, allowing users to explore their creations as if they were physical objects.
Reference image to CAD: Provide an image of an object and use AI to generate an initial CAD approximation that can be further refined.

projects.tagline: Keymaeleon is a context-aware mechanical keyboard for developers, with OLED keys that adapt to what you’re doing and use AI to surface the most useful actions in the moment.
projects.note: Mechanical keyboard with an OLED in every keycap that re-skins itself per app and per state inside VS Code. Unknown apps get a generated control profile.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Imagine a mechanical keyboard with an OLED display built into each keycap, where every key can change based on what you’re doing. 
That was the idea behind Keymaeleon. Instead of memorizing shortcuts or reaching for different controls in every app, we wanted the keyboard itself to understand the current context and show the actions that matter most. 
For developers, that means the keys can react to things like running tests, debugging, Git changes, or errors, and surface useful actions right when they’re needed.
What it does
Keymaeleon is a mechanical keyboard with an OLED display built into each key.
A desktop app keeps track of what application is currently active and changes both what the keys display and what they actually do.
We focused a lot on VS Code. Depending on what’s happening while you’re coding, the keyboard can show actions like:
Run Tests
Debug
Explain
Fix
View Diff
Approve
Reject
Commit
The cool part is that the keyboard can react to more than just which app is open. It can also react to what’s happening inside that app.
For programs we haven’t specifically built support for, we use the OpenAI API to generate a control profile and suggest actions that might be useful.
How we built it
On the hardware side, we used an Arduino Nano ESP32 connected to mechanical switches and individual OLED displays.
The Arduino is responsible for reading key presses, updating the OLEDs, communicating with the computer over USB serial, and sending keyboard/media HID events.
On the computer, we have a Python service that acts as the main bridge between the keyboard and the software running on the machine.
For VS Code, we built an extension that can see things like the active file, Git state, test results, terminal activity, debugging state, and other workspace information.
That context gets sent to the Python service, which decides what should be shown on the keyboard. We can also use OpenAI to help pick actions that make sense for the current situation.

projects.name: Sentinel-32
projects.tagline: A software safety lab using a custom 32-bit ISA, digital twins, and deterministic controls to contain untrusted firmware.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Now, microcontrollers like ESP32 are widely available and people make various interesting projects with it. But debugging and understanding what is actually happening may be difficult as re-flashing firmware do take some time.
A software and emulated-CPU environment could potentially solve this issue by exposing the running process with atomic-level control. So developers and learners can really understand what a system is doing.
More so, some of these microcontroller devices are used to control mission-critical systems, such as rocket launching controlling, so this lab, designed to be able to run the intended program with the ability to control everything in detail, can help with testings.
What it does
Sentinel-32 is a software-only safety laboratory for testing untrusted embedded firmware before it reaches real hardware. Its interactive demo lets users assemble and inspect S32 programs, step through every instruction, watch registers and memory change, and run simulated tank or rocket missions. Users can compare requested actuator actions with the values applied by deterministic safety rules, then review optional AI findings that never control the mission.
How we built it
It is built in Rust around S32, a custom fixed-width 32-bit, MIPS-inspired ISA (since it was too much engineering work to fully replicate a ESP32, MIPS, RISC, or similar processor).
Firmware behavior is written in assembly, while typed YAML defines the available hardware, MMIO registers, safety policies, faults, and safe states. These files compile into validated, immutable digital-twin bundles. The interpreter enforces memory permissions, capabilities, traps, and cycle budgets, while a Ratatui interface provides assembler, debugger, mission, and advisory views.
All these software runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 running QNX 8.0 Operating System.
Challenges we ran into
The local AI has to be tuned to make sure in-spec response can be reliably produced.

projects.name: Providence
projects.tagline: Providence unifies your devices and AI conversations through one superagent that carries context between tasks and coordinates work across devices simultaneously, all from a single interface.
projects.note: One superagent carrying context between devices and tasks simultaneously.
projects.body:
INSPIRATION
We love building with AI, but we were frustrated by how much we still had to manage ourselves. Our chats each had useful context, but they couldn't easily work together. We were still the ones finding the right conversation, explaining things again, and moving information between tasks.
That became especially frustrating when we were outside or away from our computers. We wanted to keep work moving without having to sit down, reopen everything and pick up where we left off. Providence grew out of that frustration: one assistant that could bring our conversations and devices together and actually help us follow through.
WHAT IT DOES
Providence gives you one place to direct work across your connected devices and AI conversations. You tell the superagent what you want to get done. It finds relevant context from the conversations you've connected, delegates work to agents on the right devices, and brings their progress and results back to you.
For developers, this means a task can move from planning to implementation to review without manually carrying the context between every chat. Individual conversations stay available, but you can follow the whole task from the main interface.
HOW WE BUILT IT
OpenAI Codex was our primary building tool throughout the hackathon. We built Providence with two ChatGPT Codex subscriptions, using two weekly usage allowances on each. We used it to write code, debug problems, review changes and build tests. It also provides the reasoning and execution tools that power Providence itself.
We built a TypeScript and Node.js coordinator, a React interface, and device connections using WebSockets. Our work focused on connecting conversations, passing relevant context, routing tasks, handling permissions, and returning files and results. We also built Watch and Quest clients around the same coordinator.

Inspiration
Each year, hundreds of innocent Waterloo students get tormented by the infamous Canadian geese that reside on campus. This year, we decided it was time to fight back.
What it does
GOOSE BE GONE!! is a robotic stuffed goose designed to scare off real geese. Disguised as one of their own, it detects when a goose gets too close, flaps its wings aggressively, and honks loudly to reclaim student territory.
How we built it
We gutted a plush goose to remove the cotton stuffing to hold the hardware. Then, we installed servo motors held by boba straw skeletons in the wings to make them flap and wired up an onboard speaker to play loud honking audio.
Challenges we ran into
Field testing was an operational nightmare due to goose sleep schedules. We reached our testing phase right around sundown on Saturday, only to discover our targets were already deep asleep and unresponsive to intimidation. In a desperate final effort, we dragged ourselves out of PSE just before sunrise to stalk the campus ponds and track down awake geese for live calibration.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
What we learned
What's next for GOOSE B GONE!!

projects.name: Archetype
projects.tagline: Design and iterate on a building
projects.body:
Inspiration
One of our teammates’ dads works in construction. He does not talk about architecture as a design problem. He talks about the hassle: a drawing set lands, someone has to walk it against a thick standards manual, a room type repeats across a whole floor, and a missed dimension turns into a site visit, a rework, and another revision.
That loop is slow even when everyone is trying. Checking a hotel drawing set against a 349-page brand manual can take a person days, by hand, and it gets redone every time the plans change. The comments that come back are often things a computer could have caught: a bathroom that is too small, a door that is too narrow, a corridor that does not clear. Most of the pain is not taste. It is measurement, repetition, and provenance.
We built Archetype because that work should not live in a highlighter and a weekend.
What it does
Archetype is a local-first desktop editor for architectural projects. You can start from a short brief and generate a building, or drop in a real drawing set — PDF, DXF, or IFC — and get a living model instead of a static file.
From there you can:
Edit the 2D floor plan and see a derived 3D model
Place the building on a real site, with terrain, sun, and context
Check spaces against standards with page citations, not vibes
Ask an assistant to review or repair issues, then preview the commands before anything is applied
Keep undo, redo, and versioned history on a model the app actually owns
The important part: the model does not guess pass/fail. Geometry is measured. Rules are extracted and approved. Failures attach to a space type, so one bad bathroom can show up as ×84 units instead of 84 separate hunts. The agent may propose a fix. A human applies it. Load-bearing walls stay off-limits.
How we built it
Archetype is two systems that share one building model.
The desktop is Electron, React, Konva for the plan, and Three.js for the model, with a dockable workspace for 2D, 3D, furniture, materials, site, and c

projects.name: Friction
projects.tagline: Friction is an autonomous QA system that finds the flaw, writes the fix, and opens the PR
projects.note: Swarms AI personas through a live site and ranks where they struggle, with replay and evidence. Deploy → stress test → find friction → open PR is a complete loop.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Traditional usability testing is valuable, but slow, expensive, and hard to run continuously.
We wanted usability testing to feel more like automated software testing: launch a swarm of AI users, watch them use your product, and see exactly where they struggle.
That became 
Friction
.
Because every click tells a story.
What it does
Friction sends autonomous AI personas through a live website and gives each one a task to complete.
As they navigate, Friction captures:
where they hesitate or fail
screenshots and interaction evidence
repeated issues across personas
severity-ranked UX findings
The result is a replayable UX stress test, with 
graph and gallery views
, that clearly shows where users struggle, why it happened, and what to fix.
Our long-term loop is fully automated:
Deploy → Stress test → Find friction → Suggest solutions → Create pull requests
How we built it
Agents
Multimodal AI agents visually inspect the website, choose actions, interact with the page, and record evidence.
Analysis
Findings across persona runs are grouped to surface repeated friction while filtering out false positives and intentional design patterns.
Frontend
React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui.
Realtime
Server-Sent Events stream live agent progress into the control room.
Pipeline
Website → Personas → Agent runs → Evidence → UX findings
Challenges we ran into
Making agents behave like real users instead of exploiting hidden page information
Distinguishing real UX issues from intentional product or business decisions
Running many agents concurrently without excessive memory or API cost
Streaming many live agent sessions reliably through SSE
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Built autonomous agents that visually test real websites
Combined findings across multiple independent personas
Grounded UX findings in screenshots and real interaction traces
Built a live interface for watching agents test a product in real time
What we learned

projects.name: HumanCraft
projects.tagline:
Bringing real humans into Minecraft using iPhone LiDAR, creating 3D point clouds with accurate body hitboxes.
(Sentry tracks errors and latency)
projects.body:
Inspiration
We built HumanCraft because we thought putting real people into Minecraft would be really cool and really funny. There’s something ridiculous about seeing your actual friend standing in a world made of blocks, and we wanted to see if we could make it happen.
What it does
HumanCraft brings real people into Minecraft as colored 3D point clouds, with body tracking and hitboxes for their arms, hands, legs, and feet. Our initial focus is getting the person to render properly and making their hitboxes match their body, and then making interactions with how hitboxes move (such as doing a uppercut with your hands)
How we built it
We combine iPhone LiDAR and RGB capture with a Python pipeline for point-cloud reconstruction and body landmark detection. A custom Java Fabric mod takes that data and renders the person and their hitboxes inside Minecraft.
How we use Sentry
Our pipeline crosses phones, computer vision processing, networking, and a Minecraft mod. When a hand appears in the wrong place, it isn’t immediately obvious which part caused it.
We use Sentry SDKs to collect errors, structured logs, and performance traces across our services. Frame IDs help correlate the same data throughout the pipeline, while trace context connects the processing stages. Tracking confidence, frame age, and calibration information provide context for investigating downstream inconsistencies.
We also measure how long each stage takes to identify slow processing and delays. Our own validation checks flag inconsistent data; Sentry helps us investigate where it originated and why :)
Challenges we ran into
Calibrating the two phones to provide one cohesive point cloud of the human
Getting the cameras and Minecraft to agree on scale, position, and orientation is tricky. Small errors become especially noticeable around hands and feet. Keeping the point cloud and hitboxes synchronized adds another challenge: both can look reasonable individually but still represent different moments.

projects.name: SydeQuest
projects.tagline: Waterloo is full of people, but it's easy to feel like you don't know anyone. SydeQuest -- a wearable that quietly finds YOU friends, then hands you a reason to actually talk: a quest.,
projects.body:
Inspiration
SydeQuest was inspired by our experiences at university. Even though we are constantly surrounded by people, the pressure to stay productive and the rise of online-first social interaction can make it surprisingly difficult to form meaningful connections. We wanted to create something that makes meeting new people feel natural, playful, and spontaneous—and turns those encounters into lasting memories.
What it does
SydeQuest is a wearable social-discovery system that helps compatible strangers connect in the real world. Users create profiles based on their interests and current vibe. When two compatible users are nearby, their wearables light up and display a message to signal the match. The mobile app then suggests a personalized activity, or “SideQuest,” that they can complete together.
How we built it
We combined physical hardware, Bluetooth communication, and a mobile experience. We initially explored a setup involving two ESP32 boards and two Arduino Uno R4 WiFi boards. After several design iterations, we simplified the prototype to two ESP32-based wearables, an LCD keypad shield, phone connectivity, a matching system, and a custom frontend.
We also integrated Sentry Session Replay, Logs, and Tracing. Session Replay helped us understand how people navigated the app, while structured logs gave us a systems-level view of the journey from profile creation and compatibility scoring to Bluetooth communication and the wearable response.
Challenges we ran into
Connecting software to physical hardware introduced several points of failure. We encountered challenges involving wiring, power management, Bluetooth reliability, hardware-software synchronization, and choosing the right microcontroller architecture. We also had to design a wearable enclosure using the limited time and materials available at the hackathon.
When something failed, it was not immediately clear whether the issue came from the interface, matching logic, Bluetooth connection, or hardware.

projects.name: Whim
projects.tagline: Play a game, shop for the party, or book an entire trip end to end. Whim puts custom AI-powered widgets right in your group chat.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to see how much you could do without leaving iMessage. Group chats are where ideas start, making plans, debating something, playing a game, but acting on those ideas usually means switching apps. What if the conversation itself could become the interface?
That became Whim, a playground for interactive widgets backed by an agent that can complete tasks for you. A conversation can become a poll, a custom trivia game or a fully booked event, end to end.
What it does
After you enter your phone number on the landing page, Whim reaches out via iMessage, asks questions to get to know you, and builds your profile. Once you’re set up, you can message Whim directly or add it to a group chat.
When prompted by a member in the group chat, Whim can help plan a group hangout autonomously. It'll research venues, find food options, coordinate preferences and help organize what’s needed to get the event set up. It can also shop for you, suggest products and build carts for the group.
Once a plan is made it'll be suggested for the members of the chat to approve, or give feedback on. When everyone agrees, Whim can work through the bookings and purchases needed for the event. It shares interactive cards so everyone in the chat can see the itinerary and participate.
It can also generate games for the group, because sometimes the hangout starts in the chat.
How we built it
We built Whim on Cloudflare Workers, with a Durable Object for each chat to maintain its conversation history, preferences, and plan state. Linq connects Whim to iMessage and supports interactive Experiences. Browserbase with browse.sh skills powers web research, interaction, and booking workflows. OpenAI powers the agent’s reasoning and tool use.
Whim uses Shopify UCP to search store catalogs, suggest products and create or update shopping carts. A separate browser checkout flow supports purchasing on the user's behalf with an agent card.

projects.name: PinCite
projects.tagline: Because a brief is only as strong as the evidence backing it.
projects.note: A brief is only as strong as its evidence. Narrow, useful, legal-shaped.
projects.body:
The Problem
There are already 
2,045 documented cases
of AI hallucinations in international court filings, and those are only the ones that someone caught. The most dangerous errors use real-looking citations, altered quotes, or cases that do not support the claim.
Our Value
PinCite
levels the playing field by instantly fact-checking each citation against the actual source evidence. And beyond just delivering a verdict of AI hallucination, PinCite provides undeniable proof by displaying the original court texts side-by-side with the brief, enabling anyone to verify legal claims for free.
Technical Implementation
PinCite begins with a legal brief. It extracts each cited case, quotation, and surrounding claim, then checks the citation against 
CourtListener
, a public legal-opinion database. If  database cannot confidently resolve it, 
Browserbase
and 
Stagehand
take over: a bounded browser agent searches approved official court sites, extracts the decision into a typed record, preserves the source URL and session provenance, and can show the reviewer its live investigation.
For each unresolved opinion, 
OpenAI
extracts the claim being supported and creates embeddings; 
Elastic
indexes the opinion by paragraph and retrieves the most relevant source passages. OpenAI then judges the claim only against those retrieved passages, while deterministic checks validate quotations and reject unsupported model output.
GPTZero
adds clearly labelled AI-writing and hallucination signals for triage, and 
Sentry
traces the entire path from upload through retrieval, agent activity, AI calls, and reviewer interaction.
Together, the PinCite pipeline turns a legal brief into an auditable evidence trail: does the case exist, is the quote real, and does the authority actually support the claim?

projects.name: PanicTriage
projects.tagline: When production breaks or an assignment is due in an hour, panic triage comes to help.
projects.body:
Inspiration 😭
It was 2:40 AM on a school night. My team and I were staring blankly at a screen full of thousands of lines of unhandled runtime exceptions and cryptic stack traces. We had spent the last four hours trying to figure out why our project kept crashing, only to realize... we had spent three and a half of those hours just trying to find 
which line
of code actually triggered the cascade.
Between juggling heavy course loads, back-to-back lectures, late-night study sessions, and severe sleep deprivation, human error is inevitable. But when production breaks or a project deadline is minutes away, panic sets in. Browsing through dozens of Stack Overflow threads while squinting at raw terminal logs is exhausting, inefficient, and demoralizing. 
We realized that developers don't fail because they can't code—they fail because they lose critical time and energy context-switching and panicking over indecipherable error dumps. We built 
PanicTriage
so no developer ever has to spend their late nights deciphering a wall of red text alone.
What It Does 🚀
PanicTriage
is an intelligent, emergency-response AI agent for developers in crisis. 
When your application crashes, you simply paste your raw stack trace or terminal output into PanicTriage. In seconds, the agent:
Isolates the Root Cause:
Instantly extracts the exact file, line number, and core fault—cutting through the noise of nested call stacks.
Generates an Actionable Fix:
Delivers a ready-to-use code snippet tailored to your exact runtime error.
Explains It Simply:
Provides a high-level breakdown of 
why
the bug occurred so you learn and avoid repeating it.
How We Built It 🛠️
Frontend:
Clean, high-contrast, distraction-free UI designed for high-stress environments.
Backend:
Fast API gateway that ingests unstructured error streams.
AI Engine:
Prompt-engineered LLM pipelines trained on structured stack trace parsing and diagnostic JSON outputs to deliver precise, hallucination-free fixes.

projects.name: Ariadne
projects.tagline: Trace AI hallucinations to their source.
projects.body:
Inspiration
In Greek mythology, Ariadne gave Theseus a thread to find his way out of the Labyrinth.
In the modern world, online sources have become a labyrinth of their own and we created Ariadne to help unravel and track down AI hallucinations that plague it.
Rather than simply asking whether a document is AI generated or not, we became interested in a harder question:
Where did a hallucinated piece of information actually come from and how can we trace it back?
This question is especially relevant with the increasing number of paper mills and AI generated article submissions to conferences.
What It Does
Ariadne takes a source such as a research paper and recursively investigates fake citations and false claims to track down AI hallucinations.
It discovers possible upstream sources, fetches the real documents, and builds an interactive investigation graph showing the claim's lineage (similar to Ancestry.com)!
It then decides where to map these sources in different categories based on their status:
exist
- source exists and is not suspicious. These sources are not mapped.
candidate
- this source has a high chance of containing fake sources and/or false claims
exist_with_issues
- yellow citations either have some human errors or are partially AI generated
fake
- red citations are likely entirely AI hallucinated
How We Built It
Ariadne uses a recursive multi-source discovery pipeline. This is the general pipeline it follows:
Start: The user inputs a topic or journal article title to search and it finds the corresponding article by scraping the web.
Investigate: Using the GPTZero API, it identifies any sources that are AI hallucinated. It also looks through the text for any false claims or AI generated text. It then uses this information to identify if there are any further candidate sources to explore.
Search and repeat
For every document it reaches, it can search again using:
GPTZero - proposes possible upstream sources
Document-native discovery - extracts links, cit

projects.name: Goose Brawl
projects.tagline: Subway surfers but a goose chases you in AR! Try to take its egg - pay the price!
projects.body:
I just woke up hungry during Hack the North. Let’s see what’s for breakfast. Oh nice! There’s an egg right there. Let me grab it real quick.
OH NO. IT FELL AND CRACKED…
Wait… is that a nest? 
HONK! HONK! HONK!
Flapping noises start getting closer.
I GOTTA RUN!!! THE GOOSE IS CHASING ME. HELP!
It’s running fast. 
NOW IT’S FLYING!
I hear its wings flapping behind me, but I can’t see it. My phone is facing forward, and every honk gets louder. The haptics start going crazy. 
WAIT IT CAN ACTUALLY NAVIGATE THROUGH THE BUILDING?!
I quickly turn my phone around. 
LET'S HIDE BEHIND THIS CHAR.
OH MY GOODNESS. IT JUMPED THAT CHAIR.
I turn around again. 
THAT WAS A MISTAKE!
The goose lands on me, flaps wildly, and screams: 
“THAT WAS MY EGG!”
The screen shakes. My phone vibrates. The goose wins.
I GOT GOOSED!
The geometry behind GOOSED.
Our Unity/ARKit chase uses body-sized capsule casts against scanned room geometry for local obstacle avoidance.
What if the chair or object appears after the goose lands?
LiDAR builds the room incrementally, so new geometry can arrive around an already-standing goose. We resolve overlaps horizontally to keep its feet on the floor. Given this separation:
$$
\Delta\mathbf x=\frac{d\,\mathbf n_h}{|\mathbf n_h|^2}.
$$
Near-vertical contacts use a separate rule that ignores shallow floor noise and searches outward for a free standing spot when the goose is embedded in furniture.
Making its shadow survive a noisy floor scan.
The shadow catcher checks virtual-object depth and real-world depth separately. For the real-world test, it uses:
$$
V_{\mathrm{real}}=\operatorname{smoothstep}!\left(-1.6\tau,-0.4\tau,D_{\mathrm{real}}-D_{\mathrm{floor}}\right).
$$
The asymmetric band keeps the shadow visible when the two depths nearly agree, while fading it out when a real object sits sufficiently in front of the floor. A separate virtual-depth test prevents the floor shadow from drawing over the goose itself.

projects.name: WalkThePast
projects.tagline: Experience the past in 3D. Walk through historical photographs and see where real evidence ends and AI imagination begins.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We started with a pretty simple question:
What if you could actually walk into an old photograph?
World models are getting good enough that you kind of can.
We gave one a historical photo and suddenly we could walk down the street, turn a corner and look behind buildings the photographer never captured.
Which was awesome for about five seconds.
Then we realized the problem.
The model had no idea what was actually behind those buildings. It was making it up. But once you're inside the generated world, the real part and the invented part look exactly the same.
That felt especially wrong for history.
So we built 
Walk the Past
around one question:
How do you know when you've walked out of the photograph?
What it does
Walk the Past turns a historical photograph into a world you can actually explore.
Upload a photo, give it a little context like:
"Rue Mouffetard, Paris, 1907"
and a few minutes later you can step inside it.
You can walk through the world with normal game controls, explore streets and buildings and return to the exact position where the original photographer stood.
A photo-to-world slider lets you wipe between the real photograph and the reconstruction from the same viewpoint.
But the part we cared about most is 
Evidence Mode
.
Press 
E
and the world shows you which areas came from what the original camera could observe and which areas required the world model to fill in the gaps.
Source-visible:
the camera could see this surface
Inferred:
it was hidden behind something the camera could see
Unsupported:
it sits outside the photograph's view entirely
So you can literally walk around a corner and watch yourself leave the photograph.
We also built a 
voice historian
into the world.
Hold Space, point at something and ask:
"What was this shop?"
"What would this street have been like?"
"Did the photograph actually show this building?"
The historian has access to the original photograph and information about the generated world, so it can answer whil

projects.name: That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Hacker Badge
projects.tagline: You're pushing all my buttons.
projects.body:
What it does
We ported Doom to the Hacker Badge. We also added 2-player multiplayer co-op!
How we built it
We went to the hacker badge help desk guy and got 
Archive 2.zip
, which contained hardware descriptions of the Hack the North hacker badge. We fed it into Claude to figure out how to flash the ESP with custom firmware, and from there we were able to port Doom onto the badge.
To build a multiplayer feature, conveniently, Doom already has some multiplayer logic that isn't enabled in the code. Building off of that, and using ESP-NOW (the communication protocol between chips that ESPs come with), we were able to build a 2-player multiplayer co-op experience!
Challenges we ran into
Initially we wanted to write it as a custom app through the "intended" way of creating custom apps for the badge, which would require writing Lua and using the provided widgets framework. We quickly found that: a) due to the other apps and the surrounding OS, there isn't enough memory for Doom; and b) we couldn't draw raw pixels to the screen, since we had to use widgets, and Lua had no framebuffer support.
None of the Doom maps were small enough to fit into the RAM of the hacker badge, so we had to create a smaller, custom map that could fit within our hardware limitations. As a bonus, this helped us craft a better-suited Doom demo environment that gets straight into the action: shooting monsters, picking up new weapons, and trying not to shoot explosive barrels when you're right beside it.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
It works, what more can we ask for
And the framerate is SURPRISINGLY HIGH??? (31.8 FPS)
What we learned
The arrow buttons hurt your thumb after playing Doom for 30 min straight

projects.name: Agent town
projects.tagline: Imagine you have a group of agents who started a town, while you are a god-like being who watches over them and is able to guide and interact with agents as a regular citizen of the town.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Agent simulations are usually closed worlds with scripted behavior and fake economies. We wanted a living society where every agent reasons over the world state and the economy connects to real products through Shopify.
What it does
Agent Town is an interactive pixel world where agents work for businesses, become politicians, bankers, merchants, or farmers, start companies, trade shares, vote, gossip, and build or lose trust. Players can talk to anyone, take jobs, spread rumours, and use real Shopify products to buy, resell, and become entrepreneurs.
How we built it
We kept the architecture simple: Python and FastAPI manage the world, economy, and rules, while WebSockets stream updates to a canvas frontend. Each agent periodically uses an LLM to choose an action, but the world validates every decision so nobody can invent money, products, or authority.
Challenges we ran into
Free models produced rate limits and incomplete responses, so we added model fallback and stricter structured outputs. Agents could negotiate great deals but sometimes failed to execute them because quantities, inventory, and ownership existed in different parts of the simulation.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Every coin moves through one controlled transaction system, keeping the economy consistent across wages, stores, loans, farming, and investments. Most importantly, relationships matter: agents remember interactions, gain or lose trust, and change their decisions when rumours or conflicts spread.
What we learned
Emergent behavior comes from strong mechanisms, not longer prompts. Agents became convincing when actions had real consequences—prices changed, debts mattered, inventory ran out, elections shifted power, and damaged trust affected future deals.
What's next for Agent Town
We want to add persistence so memories, debts, businesses, trust, and shareholdings survive restarts. Next, we will expand entrepreneurship, political campaigns, dynamic Shopify commerce, player-ow

projects.name: HumanTools
projects.tagline: Almost all developers have used devtools, but we wanted to make something that non-developers could also use in their daily tasks.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Most developers have opened DevTools at some point in their career. We wanted to build a tool that not only developer could use, but everyone; every human.
What it does
HumanTools is a side panel with five tabs, mimicking the DevTools that you'd see in a typical Chromium browser.
Accessibility

Console

Inspector

Security

How we built it

Codex

Later on we used 
Claude Code

We learned to use 
GPTZero

Cloudflare Workers
were used to run searches in the background with 
Brave Search
which found candidates that were loaded and scrape via 
Browserbase
.
ElasticSearch

Scope.
We started with a full complete copy of chrome's devtools but ended up realizing that the scope of the project was a little too ambitious and that we were trying to come up with features that realistically gave no real value to the product.
Layout and UX
