projects.name: SOLD!
projects.tagline: You take a picture of the thing you want to get rid of. AI agents figure out what it is, what people actually pay for it, write the listing, post it, and negotiate with buyers for you.
projects.note: Photograph junk, it prices it, writes the listing, posts it and talks to buyers.
projects.body:
What it does
Identify:
a vision agent uses vision/OCR to pull the brand, model, category, condition, visible text, and flaws from your photos.
Find comps:
it searches eBay, Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, Mercari, Google Shopping, and the web for real listings to figure out what the item actually sells for.
Write the listing:
it generates the title, description, suggested platforms, price reasoning, and a private minimum price. You can edit all of it before approving.
Post:
an operator agent uses your existing Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, and eBay accounts through the browser. You log in yourself, and Sold doesn't store your marketplace passwords.
Verify:
a listing isn't "live" just because the form was submitted. Sold needs to capture the actual public listing URL first. If Facebook says it's in review, it's still in review.
Monitor and negotiate:
once the listing is up, Sold watches your inboxes for buyer messages. The negotiator can answer questions, counter offers, hold on low offers, accept, or escalate anything that looks suspicious. It knows your private floor price and never shows it to the buyer.
How I built it
The interesting part of Sold wasn't generating a listing. I wanted to see if I could build an agentic system that carries out a multi-step task in the real world instead of just giving me an answer.
Photo → Identify → Find comps → Write listing → Review → Post → Verify → Monitor → Negotiate
The 
lister
is a LangGraph graph (
vision_extract → comp_search → generate_listing
) running on GPT-5.4. Negotiation is a separate loop, since it repeats for the whole life of a listing.
The 
operator
is the agent that actually uses the marketplace sites. Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, and eBay don't give me a clean API for what I needed, so it drives a real browser with Playwright:
look at the page → decide the next action → click / type / open editor → look again → ...
It's not following one hardcoded sequence of clicks. It looks at the current page an

projects.name: AndroidRelay
projects.tagline: Android Relay gives AI agents fast, safe control of Android apps. Instead of slow, chat-by-chat ADB connections and fragile scripts, it provides an interface for agents to interact with devices.
projects.body:
Android Relay
Agent Dashboard
Agent interacting with alarms
About the project
Android Relay gives AI agents a bounded, evidence-first way to interact with real Android devices.
The project grew out of Android development work I was doing at Square. As AI became more capable at writing and reasoning about code, one bottleneck became especially obvious: testing Android changes. Agents could help build features, but they struggled to efficiently interact with physical devices and emulators to validate the result. Existing approaches were often slow, brittle, app-specific, or unable to prove that an action actually produced the intended user-visible outcome. I wanted to build a tool that allows for us to interact with Android devices efficiently, to help to allow AI to test and identify issues in our software.
Android Relay is a local Android controller that connects to one explicitly selected, ADB-authorized device. It captures screenshots and UI hierarchy data, then exposes generic MCP tools for observing the device, finding UI elements, clicking, typing, launching apps, waiting for state changes, and verifying outcomes. It is not built around hardcoded flows for Discord, Clock, or another individual app; it works from accessibility metadata such as visible text, descriptions, resource IDs, hierarchy context, and editable fields.
The core principle is that command dispatch is not proof. Before an action, Android Relay refreshes and validates the UI target, rejecting ambiguous selectors. Before text entry, it proves the exact destination field. After an action, it looks for independent evidence in the resulting UI whenever possible. If the screen is ambiguous or the intended result cannot be verified, it stops and records the uncertainty instead of continuing to guess.

projects.name: NO BUMP INTENDED
projects.tagline: NO BUMP INTENDED: An AI Mobility Companion That Helps You Understand What’s Ahead
projects.body:
Inspiration
Visual impairment can affect people at any stage of life, whether from birth, injury, illness, or age related vision loss. Everyday environments are often designed around the assumption that people can easily see obstacles, changes in elevation, or objects placed in their path.
We believe that having a visual impairment should not mean having less access to safety, independence, or confidence while moving through everyday spaces. That belief inspired 
NO BUMP INTENDED
, our attempt to use intelligent, real time environmental awareness to provide an additional layer of support for visually impaired users.
What it Does
NO BUMP INTENDED
is a real time mobility companion designed to help visually impaired users better understand the environment directly around them.
A chest mounted iPhone continuously analyzes the space ahead and determines whether nearby obstacles interfere with the user's walking path. The environment is divided into left, centre, and right regions so the system can understand where an obstacle is located and provide concise feedback when something enters the user's path.
We also added computer vision to give those obstacles meaning. Instead of only knowing that something is ahead, the system can analyze the camera view and identify surrounding objects such as chairs, people, doors, boxes, and stairs.
For example, the system can turn:
"Obstacle ahead."
into more useful information such as:
"Chair ahead."
or:
"Stairs detected in front of you."
Immediate obstacle warnings are handled locally and always take priority over longer AI generated responses, allowing the system to remain responsive even if the online AI component is unavailable.
How we built it
We built 
NO BUMP INTENDED
as an iOS first application using 
Expo, React Native, TypeScript, Swift, ARKit, and Baseten

projects.name: Octavius
projects.tagline: Extra DIY arm, made with cardboard, code, and love.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We were inspired by Doctor Octopus and wanted to build our own low-budget, wearable version of one of his robotic arms. We also wanted to challenge ourselves to turn simple materials like popsicle sticks, cardboard, and small servos into something that feels like a real robotic device.
What it does
Octavius is a backpack-mounted robotic arm controlled through a Raspberry Pi and Arduino Nano. An iPhone connects to the Pi’s private Wi-Fi network and can send commands using voice shortcuts, photos, or a web controller. The arm can move horizontally and vertically, control a claw, and perform preset motions such as waving.
How we built it
We built the arm around a lightweight popsicle-stick frame with cardboard panels for the exterior. The shoulder is fixed to the backpack, while two micro servos control the arm’s horizontal and vertical movement. A third servo operates the claw using a cable mechanism. The Raspberry Pi processes commands from the iPhone and sends them to the Arduino Nano through USB. The Arduino controls the servo signals while a separate power supply powers the servos.
Challenges we ran into
Our biggest challenge was working within the limitations of micro servos. They are small and affordable, but they cannot lift much weight, so we had to keep the arm short and lightweight. Power was another challenge because the Raspberry Pi and servos need different power arrangements. We also had to figure out how to make the Pi communicate with the Arduino and create a private Wi-Fi network without relying on venue internet.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We are proud that we turned a fun idea into a working physical system using inexpensive and accessible materials. We successfully set up the Raspberry Pi as its own Wi-Fi network, created communication between the Pi and Arduino, and designed an arm structure that can be worn in a backpack. We are also proud of the cardboard and popsicle-stick aesthetic because it makes the project look intenti

projects.name: YourCall
projects.tagline: turn a message into enterprise action.
projects.body:
Enterprise software is supposed to make work easier. But somewhere along the way, doing the work became navigating the software.
Want to approve a purchase? Open the platform, find the request, inspect the vendor, check the amount, verify policy, approve it, move to the next one, and repeat.
That's manageable for one request. It's a lot less manageable when you're boarding a flight with eleven of them waiting.
What if you could just tell your company what you want done?
In short, we built YourCall — because the decision should be your call, not the workflow.
YourCall is an iMessage-powered enterprise agent that turns natural-language instructions into real actions across company software.
Instead of navigating through procurement workflows, a manager can simply text:
“I'm boarding. Handle everything under $5k from vendors we already use. Don't touch new AI vendors, and tell me what actually needs me.”
From that one message, YourCall interprets the manager's intent and constraints, retrieves live procurement requests from Zip, evaluates them against those instructions, and separates routine work from decisions that actually deserve human attention.
Maybe Figma, Adobe, and AWS are existing vendors below the manager's limit. Those can be prepared for approval. But a $7,200 Datadog request? That gets surfaced. A new AI vendor? Surfaced. Six individually small purchases from the same vendor that collectively cross the manager's threshold? Also surfaced.
And before anything consequential happens, YourCall asks for confirmation.
The manager says “yes,” and only then are the approved actions written back to Zip.
The idea is simple: you make the call. YourCall handles everything between intent and execution.
Your call, minus all the calls

Inspiration
If you want to access a a premium service, you usually need to pay a monthly subscription for it. But what if you only wanted to use that service once, or a couple times, without committing to an expensive plan? You should be able to pay just for what you need.
Fluere is what happens when AI can access paid models, data, and services at the moment it (and you!) needs them. Instead of managing separate API keys and subscriptions for every capability, Fluere uses x402 and Solana to make paid access part of a conversational workflow.
What it does
Fluere is an AI workspace for chat and voice interactions. Users can choose between multiple AI providers, request fresh information from paid tools, and view the activity and payment receipts generated during each request.
Available tools include Exa semantic web search, Wolfram computational queries, Birdeye Solana token prices, and trending-token data. Fluere can also suggest tools based on a prompt, transcribe microphone input, generate spoken responses, and receive, display, send USDC through Solana.
How we built it
Fluere is built with Next.js, React, Solana web3.js, SPL Token, Solana Kit, and the x402 SDK. Server-side API routes coordinate model requests, external tools, speech recognition, text-to-speech, wallet operations, and payment handling
When a paid endpoint returns 402 Payment Required, Fluere creates and signs the required Solana payment payload, retries the request, and surfaces the resulting receipt and provider activity in the interface. Responses from Gemini-style, OpenAI-compatible, and x402engine providers are normalized into one chat experience.
Challenges we ran into
The hardest part was coordinating several systems with different protocols, response formats, pricing models, and failure modes. A single request can involve tool selection, a payment challenge, Solana signing, external API data, model inference, and audio generation.

projects.name: Bricked
projects.tagline: Turn any idea into a Lego design.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We love building Legos, but oftentimes our builds end up collecting dust on top of the shelf. What if we could use our existing pieces and switch up our own designs?
What it does
Bricked turns a sentence into a 3D lego model. You watch a team of AI agents plan, execute and validate the design. A planner slices it into layers, a builder fills it with different lego shapes, and an inspector physics check each step. The model stream it's building process live, with an option to jump in and steer the AI towards your vision. You can also use natural language to tweak and modify existing models. 
How we built it
Multi-agent orchestrator (agents.py). Planner -> per-layer Builder -> deterministic Inspector -> Vision Critic, building bottom-up one layer at a time.
BrickGPT grammar (hxw (x,y,z)) on a 20×20×20 grid, with every placement is lintable.
Claude as the reasoning engine (planner + builders on Sonnet, vision critic on Opus), driven via the CLI.
Deterministic verification with linting (bounds/collision), connectivity, and a real force/torque physics model + a lenient "will it stand" check.
Live web app (Next.js + Three.js). SSE streams the agent tape and the geometry, an LDraw renderer assembles the model brick-by-brick, a joints overlay, and a steer bar.

An LLM doesn't generate well in 3D. Bricks start floating, pieces don't mesh together perfectly. We solved this by backing them with BrickGPT grammar that we can lint and deterministically check.
Creating a strong physics model used to verify if our designs will sstand

projects.name: Bricky
projects.tagline: Turn a photo of an object into a buildable LEGO model
projects.note: Photo of an object becomes a buildable LEGO model. Instantly legible, instantly delightful.
projects.body:
Inspiration
LEGO is one of those rare mediums where almost anything can become something you can build. But there is a huge gap between looking at an object and figuring out how to recreate it with LEGO bricks.
Ivwanted to explore a simple question:
What if you could take a picture of something in the real world and have a computer figure out how to build it out of LEGO?
That idea became 
Brickify
, a system designed to transform a photograph into a buildable LEGO representation.
What We Built
Brickify is built around a multi-stage pipeline:
Photo → 3D Model → Voxels → LEGO Bricks → Parts List → Building Guide
Instead of trying to directly generate a LEGO model from pixels, we break the problem into smaller, more controllable stages.
First, an image is converted into a 3D mesh using AI-powered 3D reconstruction. The mesh is then normalized and converted into a voxel representation. From there, a procedural decomposition algorithm determines how the voxel volume can be covered using LEGO bricks.
Our current LEGO decomposition system supports multiple brick sizes, including 2×4, 2×3, 2×2, 1×4, 1×3, 1×2, and 1×1 bricks.
This approach gives us an intermediate representation that we can inspect, modify, and eventually use to generate the final LEGO model and construction instructions.
How We Built It
Brickify uses a 
React + Three.js frontend
and a 
Python + FastAPI backend
.
The backend handles the computational pipeline:
3D mesh loading and validation
mesh normalization
voxelization
LEGO brick decomposition
LEGO model data generation
The frontend is responsible for presenting the result interactively and will eventually allow users to upload an image, inspect the generated 3D model, view the LEGO reconstruction, and explore the generated building process.
We deliberately built the system incrementally rather than attempting to create the entire pipeline at once.

Inspiration
Donations are invisible by design, so we built a planet where they aren't. Every environmental cause we support gets its own tile of land, and as funding comes in, the land visibly changes, and giving finally has something to look at.
Solana's speed and low fees made it possible to imagine thousands of small, real transactions (buying a tile, donating a few cents, ad-revenue microtransactions) without the friction or gas costs that would kill the idea on most other chains. And because it isn't tied to any single currency, anyone anywhere in the world can take part without worrying about exchange rates or banking access.
What it does
SolTerra generates fictional planets made of up to hexagonal tiles, each rendered on an interactive 3D globe. Every tile belongs to one of twelve biomes (ice cap, tundra, plains, savannah, temperate forest, boreal forest, rainforest, warm desert, cool desert, highlands, cool mountain, and warm mountain) and represents a specific environmental issue related to the biome. 
SolTerra turns the globe into a living map of real environmental causes. It's made up of thousands of hexagonal tiles, and each one represents a specific issue. Some are barren land that needs reforesting, some are oceans choked with litter, some are forests still smoldering from wildfire.
Each tile can be purchased with SOL. Once owned, it comes with a fundraiser goal tied to its cause, and anyone can donate SOL toward that goal, not just the owner. As the fundraiser fills up, the owner unlocks more ways to physically restore the land. Early funding unlocks simple actions, like planting a first handful of trees, clearing some litter, or putting out early flames. More funding unlocks bigger features, like generating custom tree canopies from an uploaded photo, so every tree an owner plants can look different. Full funding brings the tile to life on its own. projects.name: Parity
projects.tagline: Specialized AI agents divide tasks, share knowledge, and migrate code across languages through parallel implementation and collaboration
projects.body:
The problem
Code migrations are hard. Companies want them for speed, for safety, or to get onto one stack, but one AI agent can't do it alone since a big library codebase doesn't fit in its context. The AI forgets the delicate code structure and its own decisions halfway through, which is not acceptable because the result has to be right. Everything downstream depends on this code and a rewrite that just looks right isn't enough. You need strict proof that the code functions the same way.
What Parity does
Point Parity at a file and it tells you which functions it can migrate, and why it can't do the rest. You choose the ones you want, and a team of agents rewrites them. A checker then runs the old and new versions on the same inputs and compares every output. The checker is plain code and it keeps a function only when the two versions produce results that match exactly.
/check file      which functions can be migrated, and why not for the rest
/migrate file    build the tests, then let the team rewrite the functions you tick
/export          the new code, plus a report of what was checked
How a run works
Scan.
Before any AI runs, a plain-code scanner reads every function. It keeps the ones whose answer depends only on their inputs: no files, network, clock, randomness or shared state. In C it also turns away anything that writes through a pointer. Every function it turns away comes with the reason.
Build the tests.
Nobody writes them. Parity generates inputs for each function and gets the expected answers by running the original. A function that crashes, or answers the same input two different ways, is dropped here. Each function gets 40 visible tests and 100 hidden ones. The hidden ones are locked away and no agent ever sees them.
Split.
The library is cut into one task per function. Each task holds that function, the helpers it uses, and nothing else. The planner orders the tasks so a function comes after the ones it calls.
Rewrite in isolation.

projects.name: Waypoint
projects.tagline: When a new building is proposed, people usually see a flat rendering and have to imagine how it fits. Waypoint lets you delete a real building, drop in a 3D model, and see it from any angle.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We live in areas where the surroundings keep changing. When a new building is proposed, most people only see a flat rendering and have to imagine how tall it is, how it sits on the street and what it replaces. We wanted a way to see a proposal in place, at street level, before anything is built.
What it does
Waypoint is a 3D explorer where you pick any spot on a map and choose a radius of 100m. The real buildings, roads, trees and terrain of that area appear in 3D, and you can walk or fly through them.
Select a building, delete it, and replace it with your own 3D model, which fits itself to the original footprint. Every change goes into an edit history. You can jump the camera to any change, revert the scene to that point, or hit Replay and watch the whole design fly past in order.
How we built it
3D scene:
Three.js. Buildings are extruded from OpenStreetMap footprints, with pitched roofs, real 3D windows, doors and trim.
Map data:
the Overpass API for buildings, roads, parks and trees. Mapbox provides the satellite ground imagery and the elevation data for the terrain.
Custom model:
we generated a 3D model of the Dana Porter Library in code as a GLB file, to show the swap.
Edit log:
an Express server stores every edit in Tiger Data (a Postgres/TimescaleDB database). Each edit is saved with a snapshot of the scene, which powers revert and replay. If the server is offline, the log falls back to the browser.
Picker:
a Mapbox map restricted to Kitchener-Waterloo.
Challenges we ran into
Rate-limited map data:
the public Overpass servers kept returning 504 and rate-limit errors. We added several mirror servers, cooldowns, retries and a local cache.
Performance:
detailed windows and doors on every building were too heavy. We added a triangle budget, so only the nearest buildings get full detail.
Camera bug:
the view would suddenly jump sideways. It came from a bad mouse event in Chrome's pointer lock, and we filtered those events out.

projects.name: Alive Internet Theory
projects.tagline: Dead Internet Theory: 60% of the web is bots. Know what's human.
projects.body:
Inspiration
This project was heavily inspired by the GPTZero mission, to scan and identify AI slop in the upcoming era. 
Scrolling down YouTube, half of videos use a generic avatar, text-to-speech audio, and no creativity. Frequent AI-generated sloppy uploading has become the new norm, clouding our feed from the quality YouTubers we used to hold dear. We made this extension to keep people informed of the information they consume on YouTube.
What it does
A Chrome extension that overlays on a YT video/short and evaluates whether it is likely AI, mixed, or likely human, based on various automated scoring factors. It displays the evaluation as "Likely human", "Possibly AI", or "AI slop," and lists the factors it took into consideration.
The factors it takes into consideration:
Scan video transcript for AI-generated text (using GPTZero API)
Filler words/stutters (perfect speech = red flag)
Upload cadence (very frequent uploads of long videos are suspicious)
Account age (long-standing channels are not as suspicious)
Channel history (whether the author's other videos were marked "AI slop" from the criteria above)
How we built it
For each scoring criteria:
Scan video transcript:
Pull YT subtitles and metadata using yt-dlp, or if not available, uses local speech-to-text. Feeds it into GPTZero's document classifier and use its probabilities. Stronger confidence = more it affects the evaluation.
Filler words and stutters:
Analyse the transcript locally for common stutters ("um", "uh", "like",...), filler words ("you know", "i mean"...) and repeating a word twice in a row. The presence of these indicates higher likelihood of human video.
**ElevenLabs AI detection:" make a request the ElevenLabs AI classifier to check if the audio was generated with ElevenLabs.
Upload cadence, Account age:
Pulls metadata from yt-dlp to evaluate.
Channel history:
Queries other videos by same author and finds existing ratings.
Performance:

projects.name: Provenance
projects.tagline: The why behind your code
projects.body:
Inspiration
The most expensive bugs are often not caused by bad code. They happen when someone makes a reasonable change without knowing the reason the system looks the way it does.
Picture a developer cleaning up an old checkout flow. They find an awkward confirmation step that slows the request down, so they remove it. What they cannot see is the conversation from a year ago: the payment provider sometimes processed a charge but timed out before responding. That extra step was added after customers were charged twice.
The decision was never lost on purpose. It was spread across a Slack thread, an incident review, and a PR that only explained the immediate fix. By the time someone touches the code again, nobody knows where to look.
This happens constantly in growing teams. The code survives, but the lessons behind it do not.
Provenance connects code to those lessons, so teams can build on what they have already learned instead of learning it again the hard way.
What It Does
Provenance is a VS Code extension that gives developers the context behind the code they are changing.
A developer highlights a block of code in VS Code and asks Provenance to explain it. Provenance reads the selected code, nearby function context, and Git history to identify the commits and pull requests that shaped it. From there, it finds the Slack conversations, tickets, and, when available, Sentry incidents connected to those changes.
Provenance does more than search for similar words. If a Slack thread directly mentions the relevant pull request, commit, or file, it is returned as direct evidence. It also finds related conversations that may use completely different language than the code, such as a design debate, a customer requirement, or a production incident.
The result is a short, cited explanation inside VS Code, along with links to the original sources and a visual timeline showing how the code evolved. Developers can see the PR that introduced a change, the Slack discussion where t

projects.name: Cue

projects.body:
Inspiration
Networking events are chaotic, high-pressure environments.
We wanted to build a networking superpower: an assistant that quietly understands who the user is speaking with and provides useful context without interrupting the conversation.
Cue combines computer vision, real-time speech transcription, web research, and generative AI into a discreet heads-up display for professional networking.
What it does
Cue acts as a personal heads-up display for conversations.
Through the Meta Quest headset, Cue captures the wearer’s field of view, and the networking assistant is begins through a trigger phrase activated by the user. Cue then captures an image through the Meta Quest headset, segments the visible faces, and identifies the person the user is speaking with.
Simultaneously, a companion Raspberry Pi equipped with Bluetooth mics captures the conversation. This audio is transcribed in real-time, pulling out key entities and topics. Cue then uses the visual identity with the transcribed context to instantly search the web for relevant background information - such as recent projects, mutual interests, or professional history - and displays those insights directly in your AR view.
How we built it
The project was built using the following hardware : 
Meta Quest : Mixed-reality visualization and camera input
Raspberry Pi : Speech-to-text transcription

projects.name: Vanguard
projects.tagline: A sovereign AI security mesh that detects threats, coordinates autonomous agents, and enforces safe actions in real time.
projects.body:
Main Page visualizing the seven ai agents
Hacker-made Art for the 7 Agents
AI agents are becoming capable of investigating incidents, operating infrastructure, and making decisions. But intelligence does not automatically equal authority. We built Vanguard to address the gap between what an AI agent can recommend and what it should be allowed to do.
Vanguard is a zero-trust, multi-agent security control plane. Specialized agents investigate incidents from different perspectives, challenge one another’s conclusions, and produce evidence-backed recommendations. Before any high-impact action reaches production, Vanguard checks the agent’s identity, permissions, evidence confidence, policy, risk, human approval, and signed execution capability.
We were inspired by real concerns around autonomous systems: a hallucinating, compromised, or prompt-injected agent should not be able to isolate a production system, disable an account, or cut power on its own. Our goal was to demonstrate that AI agents can be useful without being given unrestricted authority.
We built the project as a full-stack application with a React and Vite frontend, a Node.js backend, and optional Cloudflare Workers deployment. The local runtime uses QVAC for on-device inference with deterministic fallbacks, while the agent architecture supports Huawei openJiuwen for multi-agent task decomposition and OpenAI for evidence adjudication. Pear/Tether provides a path toward sovereign, peer-to-peer deployment, and a Raspberry Pi edge service demonstrates signed-capability enforcement using low-voltage hardware.
The core experience is organized around three questions:
What is happening? Specialist agents investigate telemetry, authentication, network activity, and system changes.
What does the evidence support? An independent verifier compares findings, challenges assumptions, and evaluates counterfactuals.
Are we allowed to act? Vanguard’s policy gate enforces least privilege, risk thresholds, human approval, a

projects.name: NAVI
projects.tagline: The Alfred for your indoor spaces
projects.body:
About the project
Large buildings are hard to navigate, and phone GPS does not work indoors. At Hack the North, visitors, sponsors, and judges all need to find the right room fast, while organizers still need to keep people out of restricted areas. A teammate who had worked at a security company kept coming back to one idea: what if a robot solved both problems at once, guiding people while also enforcing access rules? At least two sponsors told us this would genuinely help them run large event buildings, which is what pushed us to build 
NAVI
, an embodied, identity aware indoor guide on the newest 
Bracket Bot
platform. A user taps an NFC card (read by a Freenove ESP32-WROVER-E with a PN532 module over USB serial), asks for a destination, and the Jetson checks that specific card against that specific destination's clearance before agreeing to guide anyone, so a card allowed into the judging area can still be denied from hardware storage. If access is granted, NAVI leads the way; if denied, it explains why and offers somewhere it can actually take you. NAVI also runs audio only walking meetings, using Gemini to transcribe, summarize, and extract action items to a dashboard and mobile app, all backed by two RGB cameras for 3D SLAM, a Jetson driven face monitor for live robot state, Google Speech to Text and Text to Speech for voice, and a Meta Quest headset for teleoperated arm demonstrations.
The hardest part was treating identity and permission correctly. It would have been easy to treat an NFC read as "this person is authorized," full stop, but real buildings do not work that way: clearance had to be a function of 
card ID plus destination
, never card ID alone. Getting SLAM to behave reliably in a space full of moving people, and keeping the Jetson, ESP32, and face monitor cleanly separated so each only does its own job, took real discipline under hackathon time pressure. We were also careful to keep the NFC demo honest: it shows a working prototype badge check,

projects.name: Craftpilot
projects.tagline: AI that makes minecraft builds
projects.body:
Inspiration
Someone put Git inside Minecraft and we couldn't stop thinking about what else you could cram into the game. Big builds take forever by hand, so we wanted a copilot: you say what you want, it shows up in front of you.
What it does
Type /build a cozy cottage with a stone chimney (or a skyscraper, or a dragon statue) and CraftPilot builds it in your world, layer by layer, right where you're standing. Don't like it? Say "make it three floors" or "make the roof red" and it fixes it. You can also just save it as a Litematica schematic.
How we built it
Two different agents, because buildings and statues are totally different problems. For buildings, an LLM writes a structured "build program" (shape, roof, windows, palette) and a Python engine turns that into actual blocks using real Minecraft builder tricks like gradients, depth and texturing. For statues and organic stuff, we generate an image from the prompt first and have an LLM turn that into a voxel model. A small Fabric mod connects the game to the Python service and places the blocks one layer per tick. We built basically all of it with Claude Code.
Challenges we ran into
Making the builds not look bad. Early versions had floating blocks, windows on corners and rooms you couldn't walk into. We ended up writing a lot of very specific rules to fix that: flood-filling rooms to make sure they're reachable, only putting windows where they'd actually be visible, checking palettes against a 60-30-10 colour rule, filling roofs so the corners don't have gaps, and checking every block against what the game will actually accept.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
The two-agent setup really works. The text → image → LLM pipeline handles the weird organic builds, the procedural generation + LLM agent handles anything architectural, and between them we can cover a lot of prompts. And it's all live in-game with one chat command, which still feels a bit like magic.
What we learned
LLMs are great at deciding what a bui

projects.name: Palace
projects.tagline: You forget. AI remembers with spatial memory.
projects.note: Spatial memory as the retrieval interface. Nice idea, needs the demo to land.
projects.body:
Inspiration
As two experienced hackathon-goers, we have experienced many a messy table, where papers, junk, and laptops, obscure important parts, technology and flyers, causing increased friction. During the development of a hackathon project, everyone's time spent searching for lost things can mean the difference between a successful project and a hardcoded presentation.
This problem isn't just unique to hackathons though. At home, you would be lying if you say you haven't spent hours searching for something small only to find that it was right under your nose, barely obscured by a stray notebook.
To help solve this problem, we built 
Palace
.
What it does
Made possible only by modern, multimodal AI models like Qwen3.5-Flash, Palace uses an overhead camera to scan the visible desk area whenever it detects some form of movement. It then catalogues every item that it sees in its spacial memory. When an object is placed such that another object is obscured, Palace doesn't forget about it like a newborn playing peek-a-boo, but rather demonstrates the object permanence skills of an 8-month old!
Later, when the user calls the wake word "Palace", it uses Qwen's audio and natural language processing to understand what the user is looking for, matches it to its catalogue, and accurately words its position so that it can be found by the user.
How we built it
Palace is built using the Qwen3.5-Flash model through yibuAPI credits provided by Huawei for the OMNI Live multimodal AI prize track. It also uses DynoV3 as a local ML model in order to detect object movement whilst avoiding the high latency of a cloud model, only using it when required.
Challenges we ran into
One challenge that we ran into was the lack of documentation in the yibuAPI service, which made building our own software around it more difficult. Apart from that, the integration of all the independent systems such as the video and audio processing, as well as the front end system was difficult as unsuspected pro

projects.name: Rainforest
projects.tagline: Rainforest turns product inspiration into shoppable collections while helping independent merchants discover collaboration opportunities and analyze product markets.
projects.note: Shoppable collections plus privacy-safe merchant collaboration. Reads Shopify's brief well.
projects.body:
What it does
Retail Therapy has two sides.
Shoppers: upload an inspiration photo of an outfit or a room/desk setup. We break it into items, and you fix anything we got wrong and confirm your size, dimensions and budget. Then we find real products across Shopify stores and build you a collection, with real prices, links, and honest notes on what didn't match.
Merchants: if shoppers opt in (separate, off by default), their confirmed picks become aggregate demand evidence. A store, even a brand-new one, can see which other stores its catalog pairs with, and get an editable collaboration brief backed by real product proof.
How we built it
TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces): Hono server, React + Vite frontend, Zod contracts shared everywhere. Vision and reasoning go through OpenAI structured outputs, and Stagehand on Browserbase handles catalog collection. Package boundaries are enforced so each lane (catalog, matching, intent, platform) could be built in parallel. Everything is tested offline with fakes and recorded fixtures, so nothing hits a live API from tests.
Challenges we ran into
Keeping merchant data honest. Merchants only see aggregates, never raw uploads, and model suggestions never count as real demand.
Not guessing body sizes or room dimensions from pixels. We ask instead.
Splitting work across four people without stepping on each other's code.
Matching a whole collection is harder than matching one item.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Outfits and room setups are both first-class, with matching fixtures and test cases.
Consent is separate from matching, so declining doesn't make results worse.
Clear split between observed demand and inferred fit. We never claim demand we didn't see.
A clean, typed foundation with schema-validated fixtures.
What we learned
Two-sided products are mostly a trust problem. Being upfront about sample size and provenance matters more than a flashy number. We also learned strict schemas early save a lot of pain when several

projects.name: ContROLL
projects.tagline: ContROLL turns the HTN x Solana badge into an FPV racing experience. A QNX-powered Raspberry Pi streams live video from a custom car to the badge, letting you drive from its point of view.
projects.note: QNX Raspberry Pi streaming FPV video to the badge so you drive a real car from its point of view. Doubles into the QNX track.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted the feeling of driving a scouting drone in Rainbow Six Siege: sending it around a corner and seeing the world through its camera. We wanted to bring that experience into real life with the HTN x Solana badge.
What it does
ContROLL lets you drive a custom car using the badge. Our goal is to show the car’s live camera feed on the badge screen, so you can navigate from the car’s point of view.
How we built it
We adapted the badge’s ESP32 to send driving commands to the car. Our video setup uses a QNX-powered Raspberry Pi on the car to capture and compress footage, with a second Pi at the controller end to help get frames onto the badge’s screen.
Challenges we ran into
We started with a drone, then found out drones weren’t allowed at the event. Switching to a car meant rethinking the build quickly. Video is the other big challenge: the feed has to be small enough for the badge to display while staying responsive enough to drive by.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We turned the sponsor badge into a controller for something we built ourselves and kept the project going after a major last-minute pivot. Seeing a physical vehicle respond to a hackathon badge is already a great moment.
What we learned
Getting controls to a vehicle is one problem; getting useful video back is another. Compression, wireless transfer, screen size, and delay all matter when you’re trying to drive from a live feed.
What's next for ContROLL
Get the camera feed running reliably on the badge, reduce delay, and build a small course that people can drive using only the screen.

projects.name: Wildfire Atlas | Team FlickrFlow
projects.tagline: Accessible, offline-ready wildfire simulations for more resilient communities
projects.body:
Inspiration
Wildfires constantly ravage Canada and the United States every year; a low cost offline simulation model can help prevent property loss or loss of life.
What it does
Tracks wildfires from both FIRMS and allows users to place custom fires, and creates a simulation of how the fire might spread.
How we built it
We spent a great deal of time collecting data ranging from terrain elevations to weather and wind speeds to road and city infrastructure in order to make the fire behave as realistic as possible. For a tech stack, we used traditional ML models such as histgradientboostingclassifier from scikit-learn, FastAPI with Uvicorn for a webpage, and Pyside6 for the desktop app.
Challenges we ran into
It was difficult to optimize the model; a lot of data needs to be fetched real time. To account for this, we pre-fetch some data during the simulation time, while the app is loading, once we know where the user has placed or the FIRMS locations. We were able to pull simulation down over 10x from the first iteration of the model.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We were able to get a model with over 70% accuracy to historical wildfires, and create an efficient, lightweight, and portable app with offline capability.
What's next for Wildfire Atlas
Support for responses (dropping water on fires, allowing the user to simulate weather such as rain, drought), and allowing an interactive environment (i.e. the user can interact with and set variables in the map).

projects.name: FinRet
projects.tagline: An evidence-first finance research harness that uses AI to deliver fully auditable, citation-backed financial insights.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Financial research is full of signal - but buried in filings, earnings transcripts, and reports that are too large and inconsistent for a single AI context window. We built 
Finance Research Harness
to make AI-assisted research evidence-first: every answer should be traceable to the exact source material behind it.
What it does
The harness ingests financial research from MCP data source, structures the corpus into searchable evidence, and answers research questions with verified citations. It is designed to handle noisy or conflicting data honestly rather than confidently inventing an answer.
How we built it
We built a Python service with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and pgvector, plus a React research chat interface. Our pipeline:
Snapshots raw documents immutably and creates versioned datasets
Extracts documents, source spans, chunks, tables, facts, and findings
Combines lexical and semantic retrieval with structured fact lookup
Uses a bounded OpenAI tool loop and deterministic calculations
Records every answer, citation, tool call, and dataset version for auditability
The system can refresh a complete MCP corpus, reuse unchanged versions by hash, and immediately ingest a new dataset - making it suitable for the surprise-data challenge.
What we learned
The hard part of reliable AI research is not generating polished prose; it is building the evidence infrastructure around the model. We learned that source-level citations, versioned data, read-only evidence access, evaluation suites, and explicit conflict detection are what turn an LLM response into a research result someone can trust.
Challenges we faced
The biggest challenge was designing for ambiguity. Financial documents can restate values, use inconsistent labels or currencies, and contradict one another. We addressed this with structured extraction, validation findings, citation verification, and an audit trace that lets users inspect how each answer was produced.

projects.name: Shadow Stalker
projects.tagline: Shadow Stalker is a secure program that commands an aerial fleet and multiple ground assets to search for, detect, and report shadow vessels.
projects.body:
What it does
Shadow Stalker is a program that searches for and detects "shadow vessels"
Shadow vessels are sea craft that do not emit any Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. 
These vessels are deliberately silenced in order to commit sabotage, conduct covert operations, and transport high-risk cargo.
How we built it
Developed a custom computer vision model that outperforms YOLO in speed and versatility
Plotted and optimized paths for our aerial fleet using Python in order to track the shadow fleet as fast as possible, grounded in lifeguarding patterns
Handled edge casess and emergencies by utilising a secure and local Ollama instance
Challenges we ran into
Collaborating with Linux, Apple, and Windows was difficult, so one of our team members had to migrate from Windows to WSL so that all operating systems would be based on UNIX
We had to plan ahead and minimize brute force due to high latency on the cloud version of the simulator
Simulation was returning incorrect data, we eventually had to switch from the cloud to the local version of the software
Had to delegate different responsibilities to various assets while keeping the entire system connected and communicative
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Developed a multilayered computer vision engine that incorporates color sensing, image detection, and temporal dependencies
What we learned
What's next for Shadow Stalker

projects.name: Fetch
projects.tagline: Lets anyone find the best prices on food with just one text
projects.note: An iMessage grocery agent whose every section still says TODO.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Some people don't have time to order food or groceries, and even if they do, it's hard to tell if you are paying a good price.
What it does
Our project, Fetch, lets anyone find the best prices on food with just one text.
Fetch utilizes Linq to allow anyone to send a food request. As a first-time user, when you send a request, it will ask for your info. Once a request goes through, it goes to a ChatGPT API to standardize the request. That request then goes to Browserbase so it can look for the products across different sites and return the cheapest option.
Fetch also has memory—every request you send gets sent to a MongoDB database and then gets sent to the ChatGPT API, so you can just text things like "get me the same as last" or ask "what were my previous orders?"
How we built it
Linq to receive and parse incoming SMS/text requests from users.
ChatGPT API to process natural language, standardize order requests, and maintain conversational context.
Browserbase to run headless web browsing across multiple sites to scrape and compare product prices in real-time.
MongoDB to store user order history and session state for long-term memory.
Challenges we ran into
Standardizing unstructured user text messages into clean, actionable search queries using the ChatGPT API.
Automating real-time web navigation across multiple different e-commerce and food delivery sites using Browserbase to reliably extract and compare prices.
Managing state and context history across SMS interactions by syncing MongoDB database records with prompt contexts for OpenAI.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Built a fully functional end-to-end SMS bot that allows users to compare food prices seamlessly using a single text message.
Integrated automated browser execution to pull real-time pricing data directly from web storefronts.
Implemented persistent memory so users can easily query or repeat past orders conversationally.
What we learned
How to integrate headless browser automation too

projects.name: Supadrive
projects.tagline: Infinite cloud storage and "instant" access
projects.body:
Inspiration
A couple weeks ago, I came across a post on X about giving your computer
infinite storage through this product called 
SkyGlass
(Now called Space).
The original post can be found
here
by
@byjasonz
.
The demo video looked like complete magic to me and I also ran into this
problem when I had to transfer a giant folder from macOS to Windows which
took a painful amount of time so I challenged myself to rebuild it to use it myself and to learn how the tech works.
What it does
Supadrive is a clone of 
Space
, a cloud storage solution
that lets you upload files to the cloud, and open or edit them on
another machine (Depends on how good your WiFi is) "instantly".
How I built it
The desktop app is Electron and React. The API is Hono on Node, with
PostgreSQL for accounts and the file list, and Cloudflare R2 for object
storage. iOS has a native app. I would have other parts to the system
if I were serving a lot of users but out of scale for my (also not p0) goals.  
Challenges I ran into
The hardest part about this entire process was finding a way to show a
file on your computer without saving it to your hard drive first.
Normal cloud storage options (like Dropbox or Google Drive) don't do this.
If you were trying to download a 10 GB file to check a 60-second clip, the
machine you're using will download all 10 GB in the background.
I had two plausible ideas that could achieve this behaviour:
Empty placeholder files but on open, it would open the original file,
not the placeholder taking up 0 bytes but claiming to be the
original file size
A known file-extension provider for each operating system
My first attempt using the empty placeholder files didn't work. While
you can create a file that claims to be 10 GB while using zero storage,
clicking play just feeds blank empty data to your video player. A normal
placeholder file has no way to pause the player and pull the missing data
from the internet.
The file-extension method worked and the results passed my requireme

projects.name: ScratchPad
projects.tagline: Scratch, but on paper!
projects.body:
Inspiration
Everyone started coding with a simple interface and language, such as the popular block-based platform Scratch. I wondered, what if I took scratch and put it on paper? How could I simplify it and ensure everyone could approach this new programming language easily?
What it does
ScratchPad allows you to write pseudocode using words and symbols, and then run your program on your computer with AI-powered sprite generation, speech, and sound effects! It also supports variables, loops, and user-defined functions and can make a sprite speak, generate its costume, make a sprite move, and create all kinds of interactive experiences!
How we built it
ScratchPad was built primarily with Python and Pygame, with OpenAI and ElevenLabs APIs handling the AI-powered parts of the project.
When the user presses R (for Run), a photo of their handwritten code is captured, it is sent to OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Luna, which identifies the handwritten commands and converts them into a structured JSON format. ScratchPad then parses this JSON and executes each command using its own interpreter. 
I also used OpenAI's GPT-Image-2.5 Flare to generate costumes for sprites, integrated ElevenLabs' Eleven Flash v2.5 for text-to-speech, and Eleven Text to Sound v2 for generating sound effects.
Challenges I ran into
The main challenge I encountered while building ScratchPad was that Luna could not consistently extract the correct commands from the photo due to minor differences in lighting, positioning of the paper, and angle of the camera. Despite my best efforts to minimize inaccuracy by using a thick Sharpie that was easy to read and positioning the camera on a high stand, ScratchPad would still sometimes make errors.
What's next for ScratchPad
Obviously the inconsistency of the Luna command extraction is still one of the biggest limitations of the program. In the future, I would like to experiment with different cameras and create a designated rectangle or frame for the paper to ensure that it

projects.name: WATsForLunch
projects.tagline: The intelligent decision layer between you and your next meal
projects.body:
Inspiration
Eating well around the UWaterloo campus is surprisingly hard. You have to balance distance, price, nutrition, and whatever food happens to be available that day, as residence cafeterias have rotating menus. We wanted one place to answer a simple question: “What should I eat right now?”
What it does
WATsForLunch recommends available meals based on a student's building, travel time, dietary restrictions, and allergies. It combines menu data with walking routes to surface a short list of options that accurately fits the user's needs.
How we built it
Built as a cross-platform Expo app that runs on Android, iOS, and web
Structured with a clear 
app -> services -> domain/data
architecture
Used Google Routes to calculate travel times from campus buildings to restaurants
Added menu filtering for dietary restrictions, allergens, health preferences, and daily availability
Used an LLM to construct complete meal combinations from eligible cafeteria menu items
-Added a lightweight backend to securely handle OpenAI API requests rather than exposing the API key in the client
Challenges we ran into
Modelling rotating cafeteria menus while keeping recommendations tied to today's availability
Combining menu eligibility, restaurant diversity, and travel-time limits into one recommendation

Added cafeteria meal composition so users can see complete meal suggestions, not only individual menu items

Successfully integrated a backend server with OpenAI's API to generate meal combinations from real cafeteria inventory
What we learned
Separating the UI, services, domain logic, and data made it easier to evolve the recommendation flow
Combining deterministic filtering with LLM-based meal composition lets each approach handle what

projects.name: Hackamon
projects.tagline: A Pokemon-style game for the Hack the North 2026 hacker badge. Scan NFC stickers to meet wild Pokemon, battle them Game Boy style, and build your team.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Our inspiration came from 
Pokémon GO
and Hack the North’s NFC stickers. We loved the idea of turning the physical space around us into part of the game, where players have to actually walk around and discover things. We wanted to bring that same feeling to a Pokémon battle game, so we created 
Hackamon
.
What it does
You start the game with Pikachu and explore to find hidden Pokémon NFC tags. When you scan one, the Pokémon appears and challenges you to a battle. If you defeat it, you can capture it and add it to your party.
The goal was to make the whole experience feel like discovering Pokémon in the real world rather than just playing another game on a screen.
How we built it
We programmed each NFC sticker with a unique Pokémon code that tells the game which Pokémon was scanned. For example, 
PKM02
maps to Squirtle.
When the game reads the tag, it uses that code to load the Pokémon's information, including its name, health, and attacks. From there, the player can battle and, if they win, add that Pokémon to their party.
We also added visual feedback to make the battles feel more interactive, including lights flashing when attacks land.
Challenges we ran into
One of our biggest challenges was working with a 
64 KB memory limit
. We originally wanted features like four attacks per Pokémon, items, running from battles, and detailed sprites for around twenty Pokémon. Trying to fit all of that into such a small amount of memory quickly became a problem.
We had to make some tough decisions and simplify the game. We reduced each Pokémon to two attacks, limited the party to four Pokémon, removed items, and simplified our sprites. These changes let us keep the core gameplay while making sure everything could run smoothly on the hardware.
Accomplishments we're proud of
We're really proud of how well Hackamon captures the feeling of discovering and playing Pokémon for the first time. Instead of just tapping through menus, you physically walk around, find hidden

projects.name: Are You Done Yet?
projects.tagline: gf
projects.body:
Why Should I Care?
Everyone eats, and most of us cook badly without ever finding out why.
Cooking has a broken feedback loop, because you follow a recipe, taste the result, and find it somehow flat or soggy or just not what the picture looked like, yet across the forty small decisions you made along the way, nothing tells you which one actually cost you the dish.
There are many things people regret not knowing at 18, and this is one of them, though it has far less to do with knife skills than with the unglamorous fundamentals nobody ever says out loud. None of that is difficult to learn, but all of it is invisible, and a video tutorial can explain it a hundred times without ever being able to watch you.
What Does It Do?
Counter Scan: Looks at your ingredients before you begin, then counts and categorizes everything it can see so the rest of the session has something real to work from.
Recipe Library: Lets you search by name, ingredient, or tag, and shows on every dish both what you already have and what you are still short of.
Recommend a Dish: The AI model customizes a personal recipe for you and only ever suggests a dish you can genuinely make then and there.
Guided Walkthrough: The interface is able to guide you through the recipe step by step in AR, creating guidelines and recommendations for the actions you perform on food such as cutting, mixing, saucing, etc.
Ask the Chef: LLM answers what you are missing at the press of a controller button, reasoning entirely from what you actually did based on a trained dataset of fundamental cooking mistakes 
Session Debrief: Summarizes your score, what you can improve better with your cooking performance, and logs it to analyze your cooking history long-term.
How We Built It
The app runs on a Meta Quest 3S in WebXR through IWSDK with a MongoDB database to maintain a personal dynamic catalog of recipes and ingredients each user favors.
Everything you do is recorded as an action, and the state of the bowl is derived from th

projects.name: Offside
projects.tagline: Stop pushing slop! Soccer-style VAR for coding!
projects.body:
Inspiration
Engineers, we can be honest. Code review is where excitement goes to die. At the same time, GenAI is making it easier than ever to generate and push code to critical codebases, especially without even understanding what it does.
Making Offside, we wanted to help interns and newer developers slow down and ensure they're pushing strong code. Instead of throwing a wall of feedback which they're unlikely to read (and more likely to paste into another AI to fix it for them), we turned code review into a game that teaches them about the risks of change.
So our question was: What if reviewing code felt less like a burden and more like a soccer match?
What it does
Offside is a Git pre-push referee that helps developers push code they actually understand. When a user runs git push and we spot something suspicious, it pauses the push and sends the play to VAR.
The developer sees the code replayed line by line. Offside explains the problem in plain language, then gives the code a card and deducts HP. Intern mode provides more teaching and only gives red cards for serious problems.
Think the referee got it wrong? Contest the call. Developers have 60 seconds to either type or speak out their justification, and then Offside investigates their argument, rechecks the codebase, and may overturn the decision.
Each finding includes a suggested fix, so developers have a clear next step. If the issues are resolved, the referee signals “play on,” and the push continues: all within the Git workflow they already use.
How we built it
The flow starts inside Git. We wrote a Python CLI that installs a pre-push hook into a repository. When someone runs git push, the hook pauses the command. The CLI finds the exact commits being pushed and creates a diff for Offside to review.
That diff is sent to a FastAPI backend. The backend first runs a quick review to look for risky changes. If a finding needs more proof, Offside searches the local repository for related code and checks the Git

projects.name: Awhile
projects.tagline: Before they were your grandparents, they were your age. Awhile turns their stories into living storybooks—with their own voices preserved.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Few months ago, my grandfather passed away.
Afterwards, I found myself thinking about the questions I still wanted to ask him.
What were you like when you were my age? How did you and Grandma meet? Were you happy?
They were simple questions. But I could no longer hear him answer them.
That made me think about what it means to preserve a person’s story. A photograph can capture a face. Written words can record an experience. But there is also the way someone tells a story: their familiar expressions, the pauses, the laughter, the sound of their voice.
I wanted to help families leave room for those conversations—and keep more of them when they happen.
That is where Awhile began. Not as a way to recreate someone who is gone, but as an invitation to sit with someone, ask a question, and stay awhile.
What it does
Awhile is an iOS prototype designed to turn family conversations into interactive storybooks.
AI Interviewer helps someone share their memories through guided conversation. Listening Mode quietly records family chats, with permission, without interrupting.
Stories, photographs, and original recordings come together in a personal book that families can revisit and keep adding to.
How we built it
I chose SwiftUI for the native iOS interface and OpenAI for voice interviews. The design connects recordings to editable story cards, presented through a warm, minimal interface inspired by family albums. Gemini for pic-vid feature.
Challenges we ran into
The hardest design challenge was helping AI guide a conversation without taking it over—or inventing details.
I learned that preserving memories is not about generating a more impressive story. It is about keeping someone’s own words, perspective, and voice intact. Sometimes, the most useful thing AI can do is simply listen.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
The demo video and the presentation

I plan to test with families and explore multilingual interviews, printed keepsake books, an

projects.name: TaskPilot
projects.tagline: The all-in-one AI browser agent that helps you lock in, stay focused, and get real work done. TaskPilot turns goals into manageable steps, organizes your tabs, and guides you when you’re stuck.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We've all opened one tab to get something done, only to look up 30 minutes later with 47 tabs open and somehow be watching NBA highlights.
We realized the problem isn't that browsers lack information — they lack 
intent
. Your browser knows what pages you have open, but it doesn't know 
why
you opened them or what you're actually trying to accomplish.
That inspired 
TaskPilot
: an AI copilot that understands your goal and turns the chaos of the internet into a guided workspace.
What it does
Tell TaskPilot what you want to accomplish, such as applying for an internship, researching a topic, or completing an online form.
TaskPilot can:
Understand your goal and break it into steps
Analyze webpages and guide you toward what to click next
Suggest useful inputs while keeping you in control
Organize messy tabs based on the tasks they belong to
Track your progress across pages and tabs
Detect when your browsing drifts away from your goal
Save your task and tabs so you can pick up where you left off
Instead of blocking websites outright, TaskPilot understands 
context
. A YouTube React tutorial might be useful when you're programming, while NBA highlights probably aren't — no matter how important Game 7 suddenly feels.
Think of it as 
GPS for the internet, with a little judgment.
How we built it
TaskPilot is built as a 
Chrome extension
that observes the user's active browsing context and maintains a representation of their current goal.
Rather than sending an entire webpage to an AI model, we extract useful information from the DOM — buttons, links, inputs, labels, and other interactive elements — and give them identifiable references.
The AI can then reason about the user's current task and determine the most relevant next action. TaskPilot maps that response back to the real DOM element and visually guides the user directly on the page.
We also built 
task-aware tab management
. Instead of simply grouping tabs by website, TaskPilot considers 
why
the tab is op

projects.name: ARDB: AR Debugger
projects.tagline: Augmented Reality debugging tool. Spatial diagnostics for embedded systems.
projects.body:
What It Does
ARDB allows you to view sensor data values 
simultaneously
, in 
augmented reality
.
The result?
Rapidly view log messages, find faulty sensors, and fine tune parameters in 
real-time
.
Data Formats
5 visualization formats are supported:
serial monitor (for text based outputs)
line graph
multi-line graph
camera stream
polar coordinate graph
Developer Experience
This is not a prototype.
We took developer experience 
very seriously
.
We created a custom client library for logging. Simply import it, pass in some metadata, sprinkle some print statements around, and your data is now being tracked.
Technicals
Graphics
WebXR and Three.js is used to render the 3D graphics. Our AR platform is the Meta Quest Pro.
Networking
The networking is extremely technically complex.
We leverage MQTT as the main form of data transfer within our project. Information from all our clients is sent to a single TinyMQTT broker under different topics.
Any radio-enabled IoT device is technically able to act as the MQTT broker and head node of the network. 
Any radio-enabled IoT client device (ESP32, RPi, Arduino Uno R4+) can connect to the broker.
Since TCP isn't supported over the web, our head node creates HTTPS streams to transmit data over self-signed SSL certificates to allow our data to be received by the Quest Pro.
Custom networking is intentionally open to users to allow for MQTT brokers to host offline access points for off-the-grid debugging.
To prevent excessive resource use, clients have exponential backoff until a maximum of 30 or 60 seconds (set by the user), and no packets are sent or collected unless the client has made a connection with the MQTT broker. 
The Quest Pro accesses the same server and reads the data.

projects.name: WaveLens
projects.tagline: Turn the world around you into music. DeskBand sees objects through your camera, gives each one a melody, and layers them together into a complete song.
projects.body:
Inspiration
WaveLens started with Qiyuan's idea of using body movement to modify music in real time, such as moving up and down to control volume. After several iterations, we expanded the idea: what if the objects around us could become part of the music?
That became WaveLens. Users can capture an everyday object, give it a unique musical identity, and gradually build an ensemble as more objects are added.
What It Does
WaveLens turns the physical world into a musical interface. The user takes a snapshot of an object, WaveLens recognizes it, assigns it an instrument, and generates a unique musical motif.
Capturing more objects adds more instruments to the ensemble. Users can then modify each instrument's properties, such as volume and musical complexity.
How We Built It
One of our biggest challenges was figuring out how to modify music dynamically. Since two of us are interested in music composition and production, we decided to represent the music using MIDI-style notes and instruments instead of manipulating finished audio.
This lets us render music in real time and change patterns, density, and complexity while keeping all instruments musically compatible.
We also combined computer vision, object tracking, real-time audio, and hardware components to connect the physical environment directly to music.
Challenges
We faced challenges with real-time music modification, object detection and tracking, dependency management, project planning, and hardware adaptation.
Many of these problems required repeated brainstorming and redesign. ChatGPT from OpenAI also helped us debug, research unfamiliar technologies, and iterate on our architecture throughout the hackathon.
What We Learned
WaveLens taught us how computer vision, music production, real-time audio, and hardware can work together in one creative system.
We also learned that generating music is not just about producing notes. The music needs structure and constraints so that independently generated instruments stil

projects.name: Dex
projects.tagline: TLDR: We hacked into the Macbook's sensors to help bring a tangible and physical occupational therapy exercise experience for kids at home.
projects.body:
TLDR
We hacked into the Macbook's sensors to help bring a tangible and physical occupational therapy exercise experience for kids at home.
Dex Brings Occupational Therapy To Your Child's Home
Meet Harry, a grade three student who’s teacher’s think his dexterity skills are well below average. Even with weekly OT sessions, Harry faces 6 days without active support. And not to mention, getting the materials required for these exercises can be expensive and running them can be tiresome for busy parents.
This is why we built Dex, an occupational therapy tool that uses sensors built into MacBooks to make guided motor-skill exercises more accessible and engaging at home.
The Science
Dex presents a short, fun, and daily “Wordle-Like” experience to practice common OT exercises at home. We took common Occupational Therapy exercises and mapped them to physical aspects of the macbook.
The Pincer Grasp
Strengthening Finger Grip Using the Laptop Hinge.
Developing Hand Strength
Applying a varying amount of pressure to the trackpad.
Coordination + Motor Planning
Understanding how spatial movement works with rotating the laptop.
Annunciation Development
Blowing into the mic of the laptop working mouth muscles.
We then take these interactions and create daily stories around them to keep Harry’s attention throughout. And of course, these lessons are all replayable.

projects.name: SolarPay
projects.tagline: Tap badges, send SOL, instantly.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to turn conference badges into simple, real-world payment devices.
What it does
SolarPay lets a sender badge tap a merchant badge to approve a SOL payment on Solana.
How we built it
We built Lua badge apps, a radio-based payment protocol, a web dashboard, badge-linked wallets, and a Solana Devnet backend.
Challenges we ran into
The badges have very limited memory, so we continuously reduced allocations, radio traffic, and UI updates. We also had to design separate merchant and sender payment identities.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We connected a physical badge tap to an on-chain payment while keeping the experience fast and simple.
What we learned
We learned how to optimize embedded Lua applications and connect constrained hardware to Solana securely.
What's next for SolarPay
We want to add receipts, merchant analytics, easier onboarding, and support for stablecoin payments.

projects.name: S.L.O.P.
projects.tagline: Similarity Lookup for Originality Prediction
projects.body:
Inspiration
We struggled to find an original hackathon idea. Existing tools gave us ideas without evidence, so we built S.L.O.P. to show what exists and help us find what’s different.
What it does
S.L.O.P. searches thousands of projects and companies and the web. A multi agent swarm of AI agents debate similarities, verifies citations, and maps related projects as islands around your idea. An evidence-based score measures originality, while a conversational coach helps you improve it.
How we built it
We used Elasticsearch for hybrid search, Baseten for model inference, openJiuwen for multi-agent orchestration, and GPTZero for citation and writing checks. Exa and Browserbase support web research and FastAPI streams results to a Next.js and three.js interface.
Challenges We Ran Into
Short pitches confused rerankers, duplicate sources distorted our metrics, and models produced unreliable outputs. We added relevance checks, entity resolution, and code-enforced verification and rebuilt our cluttered dashboard around an interactive map.
Accomplishments that We're Proud of
Spelling out Similarity Lookup for Originality Prediction using comments.
What we Learned
Building Multi-Agent Swarms to solve real world problems.
Machine Learning Infrastructure
