projects.name: My Pet Goose
projects.tagline: My Pet Goose is a conversational robotic guide goose that guides visually impaired users, avoids obstacles, autonomously navigates, reads signs aloud, and responds naturally through voice.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Globally, at least 2.2 billion people live with near or distance vision impairment. We wanted to explore how robotics and conversational AI could help make independent mobility more accessible.
Traditional mobility tools can help users detect obstacles, but we wanted to create something that could provide more support. We asked ourselves:
What if a mobility aid could guide you, speak with you, understand where you want to go, and read your surroundings aloud?
That idea became My Pet Goose, a conversational robotic guide designed to help lead visually impaired users while providing information about the environment around them.
What it does
MyPetGoose combines robotics, computer vision, navigation, obstacle detection, and conversational AI into one system.
A user can speak naturally to the robot and give commands such as:
“Take me to Room 204.”
MyPetGoose can understand the request, begin guiding the user, provide spoken directions, detect obstacles in its path, and stop when it identifies a possible hazard.
The camera can also recognize text in the environment to read room numbers, door labels, and other visible text aloud.
Our goal was to make the system simple to use. The user does not need a joystick, complicated controls, or a screen to interact with the robot.
How we built it
We divided MyPetGoose into two main systems: an Android-based software system and an ESP32-based robotics system.
The Android application acts as the main interface and handles:
Conversational AI
Text-to-speech
Camera-based text recognition
GPS Navigation
Communication with the robot
The physical robot uses an ESP32 microcontroller, 2 motor drivers, 4 drive motors, and a Samsung S21 mounted at the head. The ESP32 receives movement commands from the phone and controls the motors.
Challenges we faced
One of our biggest challenges was connecting the software and hardware into one reliable system.
Many of the individual components could work on their own, but connecting voice recog

projects.name: Funderwrito
projects.tagline: A multi-agent setup that makes underwriting simpler
projects.body:
Inspiration
We went to Federato's workshop at the start of the hackathon and their goal stuck with us. They build software that helps insurance carriers get to the right risks faster, so underwriters can spend their time on the submissions that actually matter instead of grinding through a queue one record at a time. That is a real problem for their clients, and it is the kind of problem an AI agent should be good at.
So we built one that does that specific job against their API.
What it does
Federato Agentic reads a carrier's open submission queue, figures out what each account actually looks like, scores every submission against the carrier's appetite guidelines, and gives back a ranked list with a written reason for each position.
It runs on three agents with separate contexts:
a planner that decides what to query and says up front what it expects to find
an executor that runs the query and adapts when the API returns something unexpected
a critic that only sees the hypothesis, the query and the result, and rules on whether the data actually supported it
Because the critic never sees the planner's reasoning, it cannot just agree with it. That is what makes the read on an account's claim history and exposure worth trusting.
You can also click into any figure in the report and the agent explains it: why a submission scored what it did, which queries produced the number, and which parts came from a fixed rule versus a model.
How we built it
Python and FastAPI on the backend for the schema discovery, the scorer, the three agent loop and the reasoning trace. React and JavaScript for the dashboard, with CSS built on Federato's own design tokens. Anthropic's API powers the planner, the critic and the written explanations.
One rule shaped everything: the models decide what to ask, and a deterministic scorer decides what a submission is worth. The agents only get two tools, run a query or hand submissions to the scorer. So the same submission gets the same score on every

projects.name: GPdeTox
projects.tagline: Have you ever wondered how your LLM feels? GPdeTox is the reverse of vibecoding: GPT tells you what to do, grills you while you code, then grades your performance. Make sure to make no mistakes.
projects.note: Reverse vibecoding: the model prompts and heckles you while you code, then grades you. Funny and mean.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We were inspired by the opposite side of the bet on "detecting AI-generated content." Instead of policing AI use, we wanted to make an AI that forces you to actually do the work. The idea started as "Claude Code or Cursor but reversed". Instead of an AI that writes code while you steer, you write code while the AI steers. Vibecoding lets GPT carry you through a problem without you understanding it, and GPdeTox is the withdrawal from that. 
What it does
GPdeTox runs a mock technical interview/work session where the AI is the one applying pressure instead of doing work. It hands you a real development challenge, not a LeetCode problem, watches you work in a live editor, and reacts in real time as an escalating, in-character persona. It keeps track of how long you sit idle, how many times you rewrite the same line, whether you just pasted in a suspiciously large chunk of code, and whether your tests pass or fail. Reactions come in two forms: spoken heckling and a private "notes" that shows the boss's under-the-breath commentary next to the transcript. A live impatience meter tracks the mood of the AI throughout the session, climbing from green to red.
How we built it
Keystrokes never talk to our model directly. A deterministic Java TriggerEngine watches editor telemetry and decides when the interviewer should speak. Idle too long, a suspicious paste, a submit. Only then does a model call happen. That keeps cost bounded and makes OpenAI's prompt caching pay off: every call shares a stable prefix (the interviewer's voice, the problem, the rubric) with just a small volatile tail changing. 
Stack:
Spring Boot on Java 25, SQLite, the OpenAI Java SDK for structured-output calls, React + Typescript + Vite with Monaco as the editor. One Maven build, one runnable jar. 
Challenges we ran into
Lack of diversity in AI responses. 
Accomplishments that we're proud of
What we learned
What's next for GPdeTox

projects.name: BlindSpot
projects.tagline: The cane has guided people for a century, but only reaches a meter and can't say what's there. Blindspot extends that sense, feel obstacles through vibration, understand them through voice.
projects.note: Extends the cane's one-metre reach with vibration and voice. Clear, humane framing.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Millions of people live with visual impairment to a certain degree. The cane has been the primary mobility aid for over a century, and it's a brilliant invention, but lacks in reach and tells you nothing about what is there. We wanted to build something that gives back a sense of the space and provides a layer of awareness. So impaired people can really sense their surroundings.
What it does
A chest camera splits the view into left, center, and right. As obstacles get closer, a vibration pad on that side buzzes harder so you can feel where things are. Ask it a question and it describes the scene out loud. 
How we built it
A Raspberry Pi and camera on the chest, battery at the waist. Python and OpenCV compare each frame to the last one to tell how close things are, For the voice part, we send a photo to an AI model and use ElevenLabs to speak the answer. We 3D printed the cases. 
The buzzing runs on the Pi itself (it can compute on its own) so it's instant. The AI voice only runs when you ask.
Challenges we ran into
Using the proper dev board, since we had defective dev boards, another significant challenge was finding where to put the vibrating sensors
Accomplishments that we're proud of
It feels like you have a sense around you
What we learned
What's next for BlindSpot
We plan on expanding this project, since this can be used to give a surrounding sense for people.

projects.name: Outset
projects.tagline: Airbnb for Activities
projects.body:
Inspiration
Booking a place to stay takes a few taps on Airbnb, but booking a jet ski, a skydive or an escape room still usually means a phone call, a contact form, or waiting on an email reply. We kept losing weekend plans to "we'll get back to you." We wanted booking an activity to feel as easy as booking a stay: pick a time, pay, done.
What it does
Outset is Airbnb for activities. Guests browse local experiences like jet skis, skydiving, karting, escape rooms and fishing charters, see real photos, prices and open times, and book instantly. Every listing has an AI assistant that answers questions about that activity and says it will check with the host when it doesn't know, instead of guessing. Hosts get a dashboard to accept bookings, block off days, edit their services and prices, and track payouts.
How we built it
The guest app and host dashboard are built with Vite, React and TypeScript, with a Node and Hono API on Render and Neon Postgres for bookings and host profiles. The desktop site follows Airbnb's browsing patterns, and on a phone the same app runs full screen like a native app. Bookings lock each time slot as they are made, so two guests can never take the last spot. The listing assistant uses Claude and is limited to the facts on that listing.
Challenges we ran into
The hardest part was trust: if the price or open time a guest sees is wrong even once, instant booking stops meaning anything. Getting the AI assistant to say "I'll have the host confirm" instead of making up an answer took a lot of iteration. We also had to make host sign-in links secure, replacing links that never expired with signed ones that do. Fitting a full host dashboard into both a desktop layout and a phone screen was a design challenge of its own.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Guests can browse about 59,000 activities across the US and Canada. Booking takes a couple of taps, from picking a time to confirmation. Hosts get a complete dashboard covering bookings, calendar, se

projects.name: bingbong
projects.tagline: A multiplayer rhythm party game using the Hack the North hacker badge as a unique controller
projects.body:
Inspiration
Our inspiration for this project was exciting rhythm games that uniquely integrates the controller into the gameplay. We wanted to use the opportunity of having the hacker badge to make something cool and out of the box with it.
What it does
The project is a series of midi badge remotes that players can use to play a 4-person rhythm party game. They must click the correct button to the music beat to gain scores. Players can play with and against each other. 
How we built it
We built this project by altering the Hacker Badge and creating our own custom rhythm game to go hand in hand with. All assets are also original and created using a digital drawing software.
Challenges we ran into
The main challenge that we ran into was figuring out how to use the Hacker Badge in our project. We had to understand what components it had, and what it was capable of, before we could begin our project.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We are mainly proud of creating this project as something that can create an exciting experience for players. We wanted to create something that would be memorable and original.
What we learned
We learned more about adapting to different constraints, as well as gaining more hardware experience and coding the firmware. 
What's next for bing bong ping pong
Bing bong ping pong is currently in it's initial stage of development. There will be more levels and features to come!

projects.name: Poddle
projects.tagline: Play ping pong with friends using AirPod motion tracking!
projects.body:
Inspiration
Poddle was inspired by the nostalgia of playing Wii Sports and discovering that AirPods could be used for much more than listening to music. After seeing someone attach an AirPod to a frisbee to track its motion, we wondered whether the same sensors could turn an everyday object—or even your hand—into a game controller.
What it does
Poddle transforms an AirPod into a motion controller for a Wii-style pickleball game. Players connect their AirPods to a computer, hold one in their hand, and swing as if they were holding a real paddle. The game interprets their movement and translates it into an on-screen shot, making it possible to play without a traditional controller.
How we built it
Challenges we ran into
Our first challenge was deciding what to build. AirPods provide many creative possibilities, so we explored ideas ranging from posture tracking to handwriting recognition before landing on something fun, interactive, and easy to demonstrate.
We also had to determine how to translate imperfect real-world motion data into responsive in-game actions. A natural swing can vary significantly between players, making it challenging to consistently distinguish deliberate shots from ordinary movement.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We are proud that we transformed a device people use every day into an unconventional game controller. Poddle started as a playful idea, but we were able to turn it into an interactive experience that brings the feeling of Wii Sports to hardware people already own.
Most importantly, we built something that is genuinely fun to use and easy for someone to understand within seconds of trying it.
What we learned
We learned how motion-sensor data can be used to create interactions beyond a traditional keyboard, mouse, or game controller. We also learned the importance of testing with different users because everyone holds, moves, and swings an AirPod differently.
The project showed us that familiar technology can become much more inte

projects.name: Living NPCs
projects.tagline: Hard-coded NPCs can only handle a finite number of situations, and every gap breaks the player's immersion. Living NPCs gives each NPC its own AI agent, alongside real-time facial animation and voice.
projects.body:
Living NPCs
In most games, a key pillar of immersion and realism comes from the NPCs: non-player characters. How they act, what they say are all tools that a developer can use. However, there are only so many dialogue options, side quests, and reactions you can hard-code in. Inevitably, there are situations that it can't account for: the NPC fails to act or react in a appropriate manner, and the illusion for the player breaks.
For NPCs to feel 
real
, they need to be able to handle all types of situations: be adaptable, have their own personalities, and their own memory too. There are two parts to this project that when combined, improves believability: Game Agents will make sure the NPCs talk and act real, and Facial Animations will make sure they look and feel real. 
Part I - Game Agents
An NPC that remembers your last conversation and acts on its own changes the feel of a game more than any amount of hand written dialogue. Effectively, we have created an sandbox game environment, where every NPC has is represented by an AI agent that has the ability to perceive, speak, and act.
We built a custom agent hardness that takes in queries alongside with NPC personality, recent actions, memory, among other environmental variables, and generate an output: either dialogue or action. It interacts directly with simulated game environment: and that information is communicated to the 3D models, which we will touch on later.
The biggest challenge we had, which is a fairly common one for projects that relies on LLMs, is consistency and reliability. Robust harness and orchestration often requires repeated verifications, complicated prompts and diverse sets of tools, but with that comes with latency. In a video game, the few seconds of inference time makes a huge difference, so finding that balance between speed and reliability is very necessary, and something we need to improve upon.
Part II - Facial Animations
Game developers can't code every dialogue and action, and actors can'

projects.name: TraceMind
projects.tagline: TraceMind - On Call engineering partner
projects.body:
Inspiration
When production breaks, engineers have to jump between logs, metrics, deployments, code, and infrastructure to figure out what went wrong. We wanted to build an AI team that could do that investigation alongside them.
What it does
TraceMind lets an engineer talk to one Incident Agent that coordinates specialized agents for logs, metrics, deployments, code, databases, and infrastructure. The agents investigate in parallel, challenge hypotheses, verify the root cause, and recommend or execute approved fixes.
How we Built it
TraceMind uses a persistent SQLite investigation state, concurrent specialist agents for metrics, logs, deployments, code, databases, and infrastructure, plus a Skeptic Agent that creates verification tasks dynamically. OpenAI provides evidence-constrained synthesis, Gemini independently reviews the same evidence, and the UI streams the investigation while enforcing approval-gated remediation.
Challenges
The biggest challenge was avoiding “confident chatbot RCA.” We had to model evidence provenance, uncertainty, competing hypotheses, tool permissions, source failures, and agent disagreement so the system can continue investigating without presenting correlation as causation.
Accomplishments
We built an end-to-end, evidence-first multi-agent system—not a mocked dashboard—with persisted tasks, findings, hypotheses, approvals, and an auditable trace. TraceMind can distinguish six incident types, dynamically rule out plausible alternatives, and only execute a simulated rollback after explicit human approval.

projects.name: Apex Jevends
projects.tagline: a first-person shooter where you command your teammates—5 jev-powered agents—with just your voice and hand gestures. battle against other commanders and win!
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to build some cool AI agents with Jev, a new type of model that acts as a decision model for software, as opposed to outputting text. 
Because of this, it's able to make decisions much more quickly than traditional LLMs (and thus allows us to do some pretty cool stuff, like create a video game where you command a real-time team of AI agents)! 
What it does
Apex Jevends is a multiplayer first-person shooter where you command your teammates—5 Jev-powered agents— with just your voice and hand gestures. 
You can switch between a map mode and a first-person mode, giving your team comms on how to claim site and plant the spike. You control with voice commands, and point your team where to go, armed with guns, grenades, smokes, flashes, knives, and spikes. Choose to play against either easy bots, stronger bots with an OpenAI-powered brain, or against your friends in a multiplayer room.
No more bum teammates to blame your 1v9 on. Everything is up to you and your Jev underlings :)
How we built it
We built this with Jev for the brains of the AI agents, OpenAI models for the stronger bots, Deepgram for audio transcription, and MediaPipe for handling gestures. We host multiplayer games using Cloudflare Tunnels. Our graphics are handled with Three.js. 
Challenges we ran into
The Jev models get distracted at times and forget the main mission, so it's almost like you're wrangling up some unruly teammates. But some are more obedient and others, and sometimes their mistakes are what make them endearing. By the end of the game, you might find yourself being emotionally bonded to "Bravo" or "Foxtrot."
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We made a really fun game, while making something really cool! We combined many moving parts and tested it with a number of people (our poor roommates, who came out as we were yelling at 3am) who really enjoyed it. It's fun to control. and the constraints honestly make the game even more fun. We found ourselves playtesting the gam

projects.name: HyperDrive-badge
projects.tagline: HyperDrive Badge powers a hacker badge with a $3 rechargeable flashlight and 3D printed AA inserts. Charge while using it, skip battery swaps, and reduce disposable battery waste.
projects.body:
Last year, I was walking home from E7 in the dark and wished I had a flashlight. This year, I brought a $3 Dollarama flashlight and attached it to my hacker badge for the walk home. But the flashlight needed charging, and the badge needed fresh AA batteries every few hours. That got me thinking: could I use the flashlight’s rechargeable battery to power the badge?
HyperDrive Badge replaces the badge’s disposable AA batteries with power from a rechargeable flashlight. Instead of swapping batteries every few hours, I can recharge the flashlight, including while using the badge. It makes the badge more convenient to use and reduces disposable battery waste.
I removed the flashlight’s bulb and wired its power source to the badge. I then 3D printed two AA-shaped inserts with space for wires. These fit into the badge’s existing battery compartment as drop-in replacements, connecting it to the flashlight’s rechargeable power source.
The main challenge was connecting the flashlight’s power source through the badge’s existing AA battery compartment. The printed inserts needed to fit properly and leave enough room for the wires.
I turned a $3 flashlight into a reusable power source for my hacker badge. The 3D printed inserts let me use the existing battery compartment, and I no longer need to keep replacing disposable batteries.
This project taught me how repurposing everyday electronics and designing simple 3D printed parts can solve a practical problem. A useful hardware hack does not have to start with expensive components; it can start with something you already have.
I’d like to refine the printed inserts, make the wiring more secure, and test how long the badge runs on a full charge. I’d also like to explore bringing back the flashlight function, so it can power my badge and light my walk home.

projects.name: Aftermath — From Crash to Fix
projects.tagline: An AI debugging agent that connects Sentry errors, logs, and traces to reconstruct what went wrong, suggest a code fix, and generate a regression test.
projects.body:
Inspiration
An error alert tells you something broke, but figuring out why often means jumping between stack traces, logs, and requests. We wanted to shorten that investigation and help developers move from a crash to a fix they can actually verify.
What it does
Aftermath is an AI debugging assistant designed to connect Sentry errors, logs, and traces into a clear incident timeline. It helps developers investigate the likely cause, inspect the supporting evidence, and draft a code fix with a regression test.
The goal is simple: show what happened, explain why it might have happened, and give developers a concrete next step.
How we're building it
Our planned stack combines a React and TypeScript interface with a Python backend. Sentry provides error monitoring, Logs, and Tracing, while the OpenAI API helps interpret incident evidence and propose fixes.
The investigation workflow starts with an error, gathers related events, and presents a diagnosis linked to its sources. Suggested changes stay available for developer review.
Challenges we're tackling
The hardest part is distinguishing a plausible explanation from one supported by evidence. Logs can be incomplete, and events that happen close together aren't necessarily related.
We're focusing on connecting events through request and trace identifiers, making uncertainty visible, and designing regression tests that reproduce the actual failure.
What we're learning
Our central question is how to make AI-assisted debugging trustworthy. We're exploring what context a model needs, how to present evidence clearly, and how tests can help validate a proposed fix.
What's next
Our first milestone is a complete live demo: trigger a bug in a sample application, investigate it using Sentry Logs and Tracing, propose a fix, and verify the behavior with a regression test.

projects.name: Patch
projects.tagline: An embodied multimodal search rover that finds your lost stuff and checks on your home, just by asking.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Ever leave the house and wonder, "Did I leave the stove on? Did I forget to feed the cat?" or spent twenty minutes hunting for you keys?
Patch reports back with an answer, giving you peace of mind whether you're in the room next door, or across town.
Instead of controlling a robot through rigid commands, we wanted to build something that could see its surroundings, listen to what someone says, ask questions, and act on natural human intent
What it does
Patch is a small mobile robot that can see, hear, and understand what you ask, then go and act on it.
Find missing things: The rover searches the room using its camera and reports back on where it spotted the item. 
Check on your home: Ask "Is the fridge closed?" or "Did I leave the stove on?" The rover drives over, looks, and gives you a clear answer.
Talk to it naturally: Uses natural-language instructions from the user are used to interpret intent and guide the robot’s actions.
How we built it
Patch is a Raspberry Pi 5-powered rover with cameras, motor controllers, and servos, and a multimodal AI model acting as its brain.
Raspberry Pi 5:
The main computer. It streams live camera video and audio to the AI, then turns the AI's decisions into actions.
Huawei OMNI multimodal AI API:
The intelligence layer connecting what the robot sees, hears, and understands. It looks at the live camera feed and the user's speech, identifies objects and where they are in the room, and figures out what the user wants. When a request is ambiguous, it asks follow-up questions.
ESP32 motor controllers and servos:
The Pi sends movement commands to the ESP32s, which drive the wheels and servos so the rover can move, aim its camera, and get a good look at things.
Camera:
Give the rover its eyes for both searching and status checks.
The result is a real-time loop: vision → speech → language reasoning → physical action. Instead of fixed commands or pre-programmed responses, the rover reacts to what's actually happening in front of

projects.name: Hands-on learning
projects.tagline: Learn how everyday machines work through interactive 3D experiments. Change parts, test predictions, and get AI guidance grounded in what actually happens.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Reading an explanation of a machine can leave you wondering whether you really understand it. We wanted to make that understanding tangible: change something, predict what will happen, and watch the result.
Hands-On Learning explores how interactive 3D experiments and an AI tutor can help people understand everyday mechanisms.
What we're building
Our first learning experience focuses on bicycle gears.
Learners will explore a simplified 3D drive train, adjust gear combinations, and compare how those changes affect wheel rotation. Before running an experiment, they will predict the outcome. The tutor will then explain the result using their chosen configuration.
The core learning loop is: explore, predict, experiment, and explain.
## Planned implementation
We plan to use Three.js and React Three Fiber for the interactive visualization, with application code calculating the mechanical relationships.
An AI tutor will guide experiments through predefined, validated actions. Backboard is our planned integration for conversations, lesson context, and learning history.
The tutor will receive simulation results so its feedback refers to what happened in the experiment. AI output will not execute arbitrary JavaScript or generate the simulation's rules.
## Key challenges
The main challenges are keeping the mechanical behavior accurate, making the 3D controls intuitive, and connecting explanations to the learner's actions.
We are starting with one mechanism so we can focus on a complete learning experience.
## Current status
The project is in development. This initial submission describes the intended MVP; implementation details and results will be updated before final judging.
## What's next
After completing the first lesson, we hope to add reassembly challenges, fault diagnosis, and a shareable experiment notebook.

projects.name: Project Orion
projects.tagline: AI stuff
projects.body:
What it does
Tell Orion your travel preferences, then watch a little crew get to work.
What comes out is a hand-drawn travel journal with real routes, arrival times, where to eat, where to sleep, and a link for every fact. Open it, and the page lifts off into a flight over the real city in photorealistic 3D. Your guide is a small magic goose who narrates each stop and will answer if you pause and ask what's below you.
Every trip is saved to your journal shelf, so you can unfold that memory whenever you like.
How we built it
The world:
Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles for the city, Google Routes for real distances and transit, Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap for facts, food, and places to stay.
The crew:
OpenAI models scout, critique, narrate, and pick camera angles. 
The voice:
ElevenLabs gives the goose its voice, for the whole tour and for live answers when you ask a question.
The memory:
MongoDB Atlas keeps every trip, its routes, and its narration audio, so a plan made today opens again next week, on the web or in the headset.
The eyes:
Sentry traces every planning stage, AI call, and route lookup end to end, with token usage and timing per agent. It's how we tracked down a tile-server rate limit and a voice that kept changing mid-tour.
The app:
React, TypeScript, Three.js, and Motion on the web; Unity, Cesium, and OpenXR for the headset.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We built something you can actually drive. You set the destination, watch the crew argue it into shape, and then fly the result — it's a plan, a live experience, and a memory all at once.
Also: try it on a Meta Quest!

projects.name: Console
projects.tagline: Your phone becomes the right controller for whatever you’re doing on your Mac.
projects.body:
Inspiration & What it does
We do many different things on a computer, but most of them still rely on the same keyboard and mouse. Presenting, editing video, controlling music, playing games, or working in 3D all benefit from very different types of controls.
Console
turns your phone into a custom controller for whatever you’re doing on your computer. You describe what you need, and it generates a control layout on your phone using buttons, touch, gestures, motion, tilt, and other inputs.
That means your phone can become a presentation remote, a steering wheel, a media controller, a 3D navigation tool, or something completely custom depending on the task.
The idea is simple: instead of adapting yourself to the interface, the interface adapts to what you need.
How we built it
We built a Mac app and an iPhone app that speak the same controller format.
On the Mac, you open a menu-bar overlay while you’re in another app. You describe the controller you want; we capture that app’s window and use AI to propose a layout from a built-in set of controls — buttons, D-pad, stick, tilt, drag pad — wired to keyboard and mouse actions. You can tweak the layout and mappings, then pair an iPhone with a QR code over the local network.
The phone draws whatever controller you designed and sends your touches, gestures, and motion back to the Mac. AI only helps design the controller; once you’re using it, every input goes straight to the target app.

projects.tagline: Git for agent skills, safe undo, inspect, conflict resolution and installation of skills.
projects.body:
UI with lists of skill files
Conflict View
CLI Support
AI agents are increasingly powered by reusable skills, but installing a skill can silently introduce conflicting instructions or change desired behavior. Skim is a Git-native skill manager that makes those changes reviewable and reversible.
Skim imports skills pinned to exact Git commits, detects overlapping scopes, uses AI to identify semantic conflicts and lets users choose how to resolve them before anything is installed. 
I learned about designing AI workflows: structural validation happens before model calls, AI output is normalized and verified against real source files. The hardest parts were keeping previews and installs atomic, ensuring AI citations are trustworthy and learn to package the application along with its dashboard as an installable CLI and implementing a conflict-safe Undo feature.

projects.name: Carat
projects.tagline: A browser assistant that predicts your next action with one keypress.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to make typing on the web faster and more effortless. Carat predicts the next action a user is likely to take and lets them accept it with one keypress.
What it does
Carat predicts what you'll type next, using the context of the page and your recent activity to offer short, relevant completions. Pressing one key accepts the suggestion, so you can move faster without interrupting your flow.
How we built it
We built Carat as a browser-based autocomplete assistant that uses page context and recent activity to generate concise, context-aware suggestions. We focused on making the interaction light.
Challenges we faced
The biggest challenge was making suggestions useful without being distracting. We had to balance context, recency, and brevity while ensuring that Carat only completes what the user is likely to type next. We learned that the best suggestions are short, relevant, and easy to accept. Next, we would like to improve personalization and support more browsers.

Generating games with ai is still hard, because of A) hard distribution and B) lack of coherent style/trust.
Roblox is the easiest way to get your game in front of people, but the tools are a bit hard to iterate with for new developers:
How do you find assets which work together?

What it does
BloxMCP is a interactive tool for quickly building roblox games from scratch. You are able to walk around your game as it is being built in real time, letting you iterate faster and make a more playable experience.
How we built it
There are 3 layers to the project:
The frontend is a simple threejs simulation built to emulate what players would see in roblox. The idea is to immerse the builder so they can play test while building the game in real time.

The backend runs the agentic workflows, while also acting as a git forge to keep the plugin and frontend synced up (they both pull from it to update their state every so often).
When a client makes a request, it is routed through Jev to either be handled by an agent or instantly done by Jev itself. For example, building terrain is something jev can do in 0.5 seconds, but tastefully placing objects is not.

projects.name: aim
projects.tagline: Focused attention maxxing with agents
projects.body:
Do you doomscroll while your agent codes because starting anything else feels risky?
The moment you focus on something productive, your agent might finish—or get stuck waiting for a decision, forcing you to drop what you’re doing and switch back.
That’s the real problem with agentic coding: not the waiting, but the constant attention switching.
AIM is a human-first agent harness that coordinates your attention with your coding agent. While the agent works, AIM gives you useful content or tasks matched to the time you have. It tracks meaningful agent progress in the background and brings you back at a natural stopping point when your attention is actually needed.
Instead of babysitting your agent, you stay focused, and AIM handles the handoff.
How it works: AIM sits between you and your coding agent.
When you hand off a task, AIM starts a focused activity, such as a tutorial, lecture, practice problem, or other useful content. It breaks that content into semantic segments and estimates where attention is highest, where interruptions are costly, and where natural stopping points occur.
Meanwhile, the agent harness tracks meaningful state changes: progress, blockers, decisions, and completion. AIM buffers those updates instead of constantly pulling you back into the coding interface.
When the agent actually needs you, AIM reconciles both states and transitions you back at the best available breakpoint. If the agent can keep working independently, AIM lets you stay focused.
The result is a system that schedules human attention around agent work instead of forcing the human to babysit the agent.
